Canonical Landau-Ginzburg models for cominuscule homogeneous spaces
Peter Spacek, Charles Wang

Abstract
. We present a type-independent Landau-Ginzburg (LG) model ( X can ∨ , 𝒲 can ) (X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}) for any cominuscule homogeneous space X = G / P X=G/P . We give a fully combinatorial construction for our superpotential 𝒲 can \mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}} as a sum of n + 1 n+1 rational functions in the (generalized) Plücker coordinates on the “Langlands dual” minuscule homogeneous space 𝕏 ∨ = P ∨ \ G ∨ \mathbb{X}^{\vee}=P^{\vee}\backslash G^{\vee} . Explicitly, we define the denominators 𝒟 i ∗ \mathcal{D}_{i_{*}} of these rational functions using the combinatorics of order ideals of the corresponding minuscule poset, which can be interpreted as (generalized) Young diagrams, by a process that can be described by “moving boxes” and hence is easily implemented. To construct the corresponding numerators, we define derivations δ i 1 \delta_{i_{1}} on ℂ ⁡ [ 𝕏 ∨ ] \mathbb{C}[\mathbb{X}^{\vee}] that act by “adding an appropriate box if possible” and then we apply each δ i 1 \delta_{i_{1}} to the corresponding 𝒟 i ∗ \mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}} . By studying certain Weyl orbits in the fundamental representations of G ~ ∨ \widetilde{G}^{\vee} and exploiting the existence of a certain dense algebraic torus in 𝕏 ∨ \mathbb{X}^{\vee} , we show that the polynomials 𝒟 i ∗ \mathcal{D}_{i_{*}} coincide with the generalized minors ϕ i ∗ \phi_{{i_{*}}} appearing in the cluster structures for homogeneous spaces studied by Geiß-Leclerc-Schröer in [ GLS08 ] . We then define the mirror variety X can ∨ = 𝕏 ∨ ∖ D ac X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}=\mathbb{X}^{\vee}\setminus D_{\mathrm{ac}} to be the complement of the anticanonical divisor D ac = ∑ i ∗ { 𝒟 i ∗ = 0 } D_{\mathrm{ac}}=\sum_{{i_{*}}}\{\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}=0\} formed by the 𝒟 i ∗ \mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}} . Moreover, we show that the LG models ( X can ∨ , 𝒲 can ) (X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}) are isomorphic to the Lie-theoretic LG-models ( X Lie ∨ , 𝒲 Lie ) (X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}}) constructed by Rietsch in [ Rie08 ] and our models naturally generalize the type-dependent Plücker coordinate LG-models previously studied by various authors in [ MR20 , PR18 , PRW16 , PR13 ] .



1.
Introduction

Let
X=G/P
be a projective variety homogeneous under the action of a simple, semi-simple, complex algebraic group
G
and
P
the parabolic subgroup of
G
associated to
X
. There are various descriptions of the small quantum cohomologies of these varieties; see e.g.
[
Ful04
]
for a survey. In this article, we will describe the quantum cohomology
qH^{*}(X)
of
X
using a mirror symmetry isomorphism to the
Jacobi ring

\mathbb{C}[X^{\vee}\times(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{\rho}]/\langle\partial\mathcal{W}_{\mathbf{q}}\rangle
of a
Landau-Ginzburg (LG) model

(X^{\vee},\mathcal{W}_{\mathbf{q}})
consisting of a mirror space
X^{\vee}
and a superpotential
\mathcal{W}_{\mathbf{q}}:X^{\vee}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
depending on
\rho=\mathop{\mathrm{rk}}\nolimits(\mathrm{Pic}(X))
formal parameters
\mathbf{q}=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{\rho})
corresponding to the quantum parameters of
qH^{*}(X)
. Rietsch constructed LG models
(X_{\mathrm{Lie}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}})
for homogeneous spaces in
[
Rie08
]
by combining Peterson’s presentation
[
Pet97
]
of the quantum cohomology of homogeneous spaces with Lie-theoretic constructions, leading to the name
Lie-theoretic mirror models
.

In the case when
X
is
cominuscule
(i.e. when
P=P_{k}=P_{\{k\}}
is a maximal parabolic subgroup of
G
which stabilizes the highest weight vector in the cominuscule fundamental weight representation
V({\varpi_{k}})
; in this case we have
\rho=1
and hence
\mathbf{q}=q
a single parameter), the geometric Satake correspondence provides a one-to-one correspondence between generators of the cohomology of
X
and a natural set of projective coordinates on the space
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=P^{\vee}\backslash G^{\vee}
which we will refer to as
(generalized) Plücker coordinates
. Here
G^{\vee}
and
P^{\vee}
are the Langlands dual groups to
G
and
P
respectively, and hence we will refer to
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
as the
Langlands dual homogeneous space
. The geometric Satake correspondence is especially appealing due to the fact that when
X
is cominuscule, then the Langlands dual
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
is
minuscule
which endows the Plücker coordinates on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
with many useful combinatorial properties.

The geometric Satake correspondence motivated the construction of Landau-Ginzburg models
(X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}})
with
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}\subset\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
for many families of cominuscule spaces (e.g.
[
MR20
,
PR13
,
PR18
,
PRW16
]
). The mirror varieties
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
in these constructions all arise as the complement of a distinguished anticanonical divisor
D_{\mathrm{ac}}
inside
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
, and the mirror models have correspondingly been referred to as
canonical
Landau-Ginzburg models. In each case, these models have been shown to be isomorphic to Rietsch’s Lie-theoretic models
(X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}})
. Although these constructions of LG models for so many cominuscule spaces suggests the possibility of a uniform construction, the methods and objects in each case heavily relied on type-specific representation-theoretic methods. Our main result in this paper is the type-independent construction of LG models for these cominuscule cases which are isomorphic to Rietsch’s Lie-theoretic models.

In the works
[
SW23
,
SW24
]
, we have been working towards generalizing the previous approaches with the goal of obtaining a uniform, type-independent construction which applies equally well to any cominuscule homogeneous space. The main difficulty lies in identifying suitable candidates for the mirror space
X_{\mathrm{can}}
and the superpotential
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
. The starting point for our construction comes from certain
generalized minors
(up to sign)
\phi_{{i_{*}}}:G^{\vee}\to\mathbb{C}
for
{i_{*}}\in[n]
which can be defined in terms of the projection formulas

\phi_{{i_{*}}}(g)=(-1)^{h}\Delta_{w_{0}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}(g^{-1})=(-1)^{h}\Bigl\langle g^{-1}\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+},v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{-}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}\quad\text{for}\quad{i_{*}}\in[n],

along with
\phi_{0}(g)=\Delta_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}},{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}(g^{-1})
.
These generalized minors will be introduced in further detail in Section
2.2.3
. Our first step will be to identify regular functions, which we denote by
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
, corresponding to the
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
on the minuscule Langlands dual space
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
. For this, we consider
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
in its natural minimal embedding
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}\bigl(V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})^{*}\bigr)
, which is often called the
(generalized) Plücker embedding
of
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
; see equation (
2.5
) and the discussion leading up to it. The resulting projective coordinates on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
are referred to as
(generalized) Plücker coordinates
and in order to construct the
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
, we begin by computing in Section
3
the restriction of each
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
to an algebraic torus
U^{\circ}_{-}\subset G^{\vee}
, which is defined in equation (
2.8
). These computations use order ideals of the minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}
associated to
X
as introduced in Section
2.3
; they can be depicted as (skew) Young diagrams with each box labeled by a simple reflection, see Table
2.18
for examples of such diagrams. Because
\phi_{0},\phi_{k}
are defined using the representation dual to the one used to define Plücker coordinates, we directly compute

\phi_{k}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=a_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}\quad\text{and}\quad\phi_{0}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=p_{\varnothing}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=1.

We determine the restrictions of the remaining
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
for
{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}
to
U^{\circ}_{-}

\phi_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=\prod_{j=1}^{{c_{*}}}a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{j}}}

in Theorem
3.10
, where
{c_{*}}
is the coefficient of the simple root
\alpha_{{i_{*}}}
in the highest root
\alpha_{0}
for
G
and
a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{j}}}
is a monomial in the toric coordinates of
U^{\circ}_{-}
corresponding to a certain order ideal
\mathsf{w}_{i_{j}}
of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
allowing an easy combinatorial description, namely
\mathsf{w}_{i_{j}}
the maximal Young subdiagram obtained from
\mathsf{w}_{i_{j-1}}
by adding boxes with label unequal to
s_{i_{j}}
and where
\mathsf{w}_{i_{0}}=\varnothing
. (See also Corollary
3.9
.) Here, the sequence of indices
(i_{j})
is given in equation (
3.8
) and starts with
i_{1}=\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})
and
i_{2}=\sigma_{i_{1}}(k)
where
\sigma_{i}:[n]\setminus\{i\}\to[n]\setminus\{i\}
denotes the (possibly trivial) Dynkin involution of the Dynkin diagram of
G^{\vee}
after removing node
i
.)

The reason for working with these restrictions is that order ideals of the minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}
also give a combinatorial description of the restrictions of Plücker coordinates to
U^{\circ}_{-}
(considering the coordinates as
\widetilde{P}^{\vee}
-invariant functions on
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
). In Section
4
, we use the structure of order ideals to analyze the cancellation of toric terms in Plücker monomials and describe this cancellation in terms of moving boxes between Young diagrams corresponding to different Plücker coordinates. To organize these cancellations, we construct a poset
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
whose elements are all
{c_{*}}
-tuples of order ideals of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
corresponding to Plücker monomials of degree
{c_{*}}
and whose cover relations correspond to moving a single box between Young diagrams. We will construct
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
using the initial element
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\dots,\mathsf{w}_{i_{{c_{*}}}})
consisting of the order ideals
\mathsf{w}_{i_{j}}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
mentioned above and generating the remaining elements by moving boxes in all possible ways from
\mathsf{w}_{i_{l}}
to
\mathsf{w}_{i_{m}}
for
l<m
. Letting
L_{d}\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
denote the tuples
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{w}_{{c_{*}}})
obtained using
d
such moves starting from
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\dots,\mathsf{w}_{i_{{c_{*}}}})
, we establish in Theorem
4.24
that
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
is equal on the torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
to

\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}=\sum_{d\geq 0}(-1)^{d}\sum_{(\mathsf{w}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{w}_{{c_{*}}})\in L_{d}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}}\dots p_{\mathsf{w}_{{c_{*}}}},

(1.1)

and we obtain the full equality of this expression on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
via Remark
6.6
. It will follow that for all but four cases, i.e. when
{c_{*}}\leq 2
,
\mathsf{P}_{i_{*}}
either consists of a single element or else can be identified with the Bruhat order on weight spaces in a minuscule representation; see Remark
4.7
.

Using the
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
, we define our mirror space
X_{\mathrm{can}}
. For convenience, we set
\mathcal{D}_{0}=p_{\varnothing}
and
\mathcal{D}_{k}=p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}
. Then letting
D_{{i_{*}}}=\{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}=0\}
for each
0\leq{i_{*}}\leq n
, we set
X_{\mathrm{can}}
to be the complement of the divisor
D_{\mathrm{ac}}=\sum_{{i_{*}}=0}^{n}D_{{i_{*}}}
formed by the union of the
D_{{i_{*}}}
inside of
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}

X_{\mathrm{can}}=\mathbb{X}^{\vee}\setminus D_{\mathrm{ac}}.

As noted below in Remark
1.3
, it will follow from Theorem
4.24
that
D_{\mathrm{ac}}
anticanonical.

We will construct our superpotential as a sum of
n+1
rational functions in the Plücker coordinates of
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
. The denominators of these rational functions will be given by the
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
for
0\leq{i_{*}}\leq n
. In order to determine the corresponding numerators, we define for each
j\in[n]
the derivation
\delta_{j}:\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{X}^{\vee}]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{X}^{\vee}]
which acts on Plücker coordinates labeled by Young diagrams as

\delta_{j}(p_{\mathsf{w}})=\begin{cases}p_{\mathsf{w}^{+j}},&\text{$\mathsf{w}^{+j}$ is a valid Young diagram for $\mathbb{X}^{\vee}$,}\\
0,&\textrm{otherwise,}\end{cases}

(1.2)

where
\mathsf{w}^{+j}
is the result of adding a box labeled
s_{j}
to the Young diagram
\mathsf{w}
if the result is a valid Young diagram. (Recall from above that Young diagrams for
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
are naturally equipped with a labeling by simple reflections in the Weyl group of
G^{\vee}
.) We extend
\delta_{j}
to polynomials in the Plücker coordinates as a derivation via the product rule.

For each
{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}
, the numerator of the term of our superpotential with the denominator
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
will be given by
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})
, where we recall that
i_{1}=\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})
. For the term of our superpotential with denominator
\mathcal{D}_{0}=p_{\varnothing}
, the corresponding numerator will be given by
\delta_{k}(\mathcal{D}_{0})=p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}
. In Section
6.1
, we address the numerator of the “quantum” term of our superpotential which has denominator
\mathcal{D}_{k}
. Our results in Section
4
show that
\mathcal{D}_{k}
is equal to the Plücker coordinate
p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}
and we show in Corollary
6.3
that the corresponding numerator is the Plücker coordinate
p_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}
where
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
is order ideal isomorphic to the
complement
of the largest order ideal containing
exactly
one element labeled
s_{k}
. Equivalently,
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}
is the ideal corresponding to the minimal coset representative
w^{\prime}=w^{P}(w^{\prime\prime})^{-1}\in W^{P}
, where
w^{\prime\prime}\in W^{P}
is the minimal coset representative of
w_{P}s_{k}W_{P}
. Using these descriptions with
\mathcal{D}_{i}
as in (
1.1
) above, we obtain the superpotential

\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}=\frac{p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}}{p_{\varnothing}}+q\frac{p_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}}{p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}}+\sum_{{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}}\frac{\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})}{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}}.

Before stating the full extent of our results, we will illustrate our models in three well-known examples: quadrics, Lagrangian and orthogonal Grassmannians. First, we consider the Lagrangian Grassmannian
X=\mathrm{LG}(4,8)=\mathrm{Sp}_{8}/P_{4}=C_{4}^{\mathrm{sc}}/P_{4}
, describing Lagrangian subspaces in the standard eight-dimensional, complex symplectic vector space
\mathbb{C}^{8}
. The Langlands dual homogeneous space is
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=\mathrm{OG}(4,9)=P^{\vee}_{4}\backslash\mathrm{PSO}_{9}=P^{\vee}_{4}\backslash B_{4}^{\mathrm{ad}}

\mathsf{w}^{P}

This determines the mirror variety as
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}=\mathbb{X}^{\vee}\setminus D_{\mathrm{ac}}
for
D_{\mathrm{ac}}=\sum_{{i_{*}}=0}^{4}D_{i_{*}}
the anticanonical divisor defined by
D_{i_{*}}=\{\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}=0\}
. We now act by the derivations
\delta_{i_{1}}
on each of the
\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}
with
{i_{*}}\neq 4
(where
{i_{*}}=4
is the quantum term), which in terms of order ideals adds a box with index
i_{1}
if allowed by
\mathsf{w}^{P}
and maps the Plücker coordinate to
0
otherwise; in conclusion, we find:

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}

\displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{4}(\mathcal{D}_{0})}{\mathcal{D}_{0}}+\frac{\delta_{3}(\mathcal{D}_{1})}{\mathcal{D}_{1}}+\frac{\delta_{2}(\mathcal{D}_{2})}{\mathcal{D}_{2}}+\frac{\delta_{1}(\mathcal{D}_{3})}{\mathcal{D}_{3}}+q\frac{p_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}}{p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}}

We will describe the model for the eight-dimensional quadric
X=Q_{8}=\mathrm{Spin}_{10}/P_{1}=D_{4}^{\mathrm{sc}}/P_{1}
more succinctly. We have
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=Q_{8}=P^{\vee}_{1}\backslash\mathrm{PSO}_{10}=P^{\vee}_{1}\backslash D_{4}^{\mathrm{ad}}
with
{c_{*}}=1
for
{i_{*}}\in\{1,3,4\}
and
{c_{*}}=2
for
{i_{*}}=2
, giving us

\mathsf{w}^{P}=\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\tiny\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$1$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$2$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$3$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\moveright 6.7pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$4$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$2$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$1$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt},\quad\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}=\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\tiny\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$1$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$2$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$3$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\moveright 6.7pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$4$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$2$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathsf{w}^{\prime}=\raisebox{3.5pt}{\tiny\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt\hbox to6.4pt{\hfil$1$\hfil}\vrule height=5.12001pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.27997pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}.

obtained from moving boxes from
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})

height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}}

We note that although our expressions for
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
seem to distinguish the quantum and
\mathcal{D}_{0}
terms, it is possible to give a much more uniform expression for our
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
using a derivation defined via the quantum product instead. Unfortunately, the expressions obtained using the quantum derivation have many extraneous cancellations which make
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
much more difficult to compute compared to our current presentation. For more details on the quantum derivation, see Remark
1.4
. Furthermore, our current expression makes clear which term of
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
corresponds to which component of the divisor
D_{\mathrm{ac}}
, which will be useful for our comparisons with Rietsch’s Lie-theoretic LG models and also was a useful feature in the computations of Rietsch and Williams in
[
RW19
]
. For more details on this connection, see Remark
1.2
.

With our candidate LG-models in hand, we are now ready to state our main theorem.

Theorem 1.1
.

Let
X=G/P_{k}
be a cominuscule homogeneous space for
G
a simply-connected linear algebraic group of rank
n
, and let
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash G^{\vee}
be the associated “Langlands dual” homogeneous space, with the set of projective coordinates
\{p_{\mathsf{w}}~|~\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}\}
known as
(generalized) Plücker coordinates
obtained from the natural embedding
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}\bigl(V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})^{*}\bigr)
with
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
order ideals of the corresponding minuscule poset. Then:

(i)

The
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
, for
{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}
, are equal on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
to the
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
as given by equation (
1.1
) as well as
\phi_{0}=\mathcal{D}_{0}=p_{\varnothing}
and
\phi_{k}=\mathcal{D}_{k}=p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}
on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
and these polynomials form the set of frozen variables for the cluster structure on
\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{X}^{\vee}]
studied in
[
GLS11
]

(ii)

The divisor
D_{\mathrm{ac}}=\sum_{{i_{*}}=0}^{n}D_{{i_{*}}}
is anti-canonical, where
D_{{i_{*}}}=\{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}=0\}
.

(iii)

For
{i_{*}}\neq 0,k
, the derivations
\delta_{j}
defined combinatorially by (
1.2
) yield homogeneous polynomials
\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})
in Plücker coordinates, where
\sigma_{k}
is the Dynkin involution of the Dynkin diagram with the vertex
k
removed, and the rational functions

\mathcal{W}_{0}=\frac{\delta_{k}(\mathcal{D}_{0})}{\mathcal{D}_{0}}=\frac{p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}}{p_{\varnothing}}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}=\frac{\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})}{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}}\quad\text{for}\quad{i_{*}}\neq 0,k,

satisfy the following equations on the dense algebraic torus
P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash U^{\circ}_{-}\subset\mathbb{X}^{\vee}

\mathcal{W}_{0}=\sum_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}:~\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=k}a_{\mathsf{b}}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}=\sum_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}:~\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}a_{\mathsf{b}}\quad\text{for}\quad{i_{*}}\neq k,

where
a_{\mathsf{b}}
denote the toric coordinates
\{a_{\mathsf{b}}~|~\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}\}
of
P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash U^{\circ}_{-}
.

(iv)

For
{i_{*}}=k
, we find that
\phi_{k}=\mathcal{D}_{k}=p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}
on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
, and define the rational function which we refer to as the
quantum term
by

\mathcal{W}_{k}=q\frac{p_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}}{p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}}\quad\text{for a formal parameter $q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}$,}

where
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}
is the order ideal corresponding to
w^{\prime}=w^{P}(w^{\prime\prime})^{-1}\in W^{P}
defined by the minimal coset representatives
w^{P}
and
w^{\prime\prime}
of the cosets
w_{0}W_{P}
and
w_{P}s_{k}W_{P}
, with
w_{0}\in W
and
w_{P}\in W_{P}=\langle s_{i}~|~i\neq k\rangle
the respective longest Weyl group elements. Moreover,
\mathcal{W}_{k}
satisfies on the torus
P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash U^{\circ}_{-}
the equation

\mathcal{W}_{k}=q\frac{\sum_{\iota:\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}a_{\iota(\mathsf{w}^{\prime})}}{a_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}},

where
a_{\mathsf{S}}=\prod_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{S}}a_{\mathsf{b}}
for a subset
\mathsf{S}\subset\mathsf{w}^{P}
and the sum is over labeled order embeddings of the poset
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}
into the minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}
.

(v)

The pair
(X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}})
consisting of the mirror variety and superpotential

X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}=\mathbb{X}^{\vee}\setminus D_{\mathrm{ac}}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}=\sum_{{i_{*}}=0}^{n}\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}

forms an LG-model for
X
, which we refer to as the
canonical mirror model
. That is, we have the isomorphism

qH^{*}(X)_{(q)}\cong\mathbb{C}[X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}_{q}]/\langle\partial\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}\rangle.

Furthermore, the canonical mirror model
(X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}})
is isomorphic to the Lie-theoretic mirror model
(X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}})
defined in
[
Rie08
]
; moreover, on the torus
P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash U^{\circ}_{-}
the LG-model restricts to a Laurent polynomial model isomorphic to the one defined in
[
Spa21
]
.

In order to show that our canonical LG model agrees with Rietsch’s Lie-theoretic LG model, we need to establish an isomorphism between
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
and
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}
as well as an equality of the superpotentials
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
and
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}}
after pulling back along the isomorphism. Building off of our previous results in
[
SW23
]
, we establish that
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\cong X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
in Theorem
6.5
by observing that both spaces are affine varieties and then comparing coordinate rings.

To compare the superpotentials, we consider the restrictions of both superpotentials to the torus
P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash U^{\circ}_{-}
. Although many of our previous results have been established on the torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
, the proof of Theorem
6.5
implies (see Remark
6.6
) that the quotient map
\pi:G^{\vee}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
restricts to an isomorphism
U^{\circ}_{-}\cong P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash U^{\circ}_{-}
so that restrictions to
U^{\circ}_{-}
can be considered interchangeably with restrictions to
P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash U^{\circ}_{-}
. Thus, the first four parts of Theorem
1.1
follow immediately from our previous results.

The final computation we need for this comparison is the restrictions of the numerators
\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})
to the torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
. For these computations, we construct in Section
5
the poset
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
by translating the derivation
\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}
to elements of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
and then using an analogous approach as in Section
4
to study the action of
\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}
on
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
. We show in Theorem
5.16
that the restriction to
U^{\circ}_{-}
of
\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})
is given by

\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}\cdot\left(\textstyle\sum_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}:~\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}\displaystyle a_{\mathsf{b}}\right),

where the sum is over certain toric coordinates corresponding to the simple reflection
s_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}
. Thus, we obtain on the torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
the expression

\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}=\frac{\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})}{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}}=\sum_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}:~\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}a_{\mathsf{b}}

for each term of our superpotential except the quantum term, which we handle separately in Section
6.1
. Using this computation, we prove the final fifth part of our main Theorem
1.1
that for any value of the formal quantum parameter
q
our canonical superpotential agrees with Rietsch’s Lie-theoretic superpotential on the dense torus
P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash U^{\circ}_{-}
and hence on the entire space
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
. From this, we conclude that our canonical mirror models are isomorphic to Rietsch’s Lie-theoretic models. Before concluding the introduction, we describe a few features of our LG models as well as interesting connections with other works.

Remark 1.2
.

The
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
form the set of frozen variables for the cluster structure on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
as given in
[
GLS08
]
for simply-laced types and extended by
[
Dem11
]
to the general case. Note that we have introduced an extra sign and permuted the indices of
\phi_{i}
by
\sigma_{0}
compared with these references to simplify notation arising from switching from “upper” to “lower” unipotent cells. In particular, our superpotentials
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
are regular functions on the open cluster variety
X_{\mathrm{can}}
.

Thus, it would be feasible to use our LG models to attempt a type-independent generalization of the results of Rietsch and Williams relating Newton-Okounkov bodies for Grassmannians to so-called superpotential polytopes for Grassmannians in
[
RW19
]
. Importantly, both the Newton-Okounkov bodies as well as the superpotential polytopes they study depend on the choice of a divisor supposed on
D_{\mathrm{ac}}
and for the superpotential polytope in particular it was important in their computations to understand the correspondence between terms of the superpotential and components of
D_{\mathrm{ac}}
.

Remark 1.3
.

For each
{i_{*}}\in[n]
, each
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
is a homogeneous polynomial of degree
{c_{*}}=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},\alpha_{0}\rangle\!\rangle
in the Plücker coordinates and for
{i_{*}}=0
,
\mathcal{D}_{0}
is a homogeneous polynomial of degree
1
in the Plücker coordinates. Recall that
D_{{i_{*}}}=\{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}=0\}
, so as a result, the degree of the divisor

D_{\mathrm{ac}}=\sum_{{i_{*}}=0}^{n}D_{{i_{*}}}

is equal to

\sum_{0\leq{i_{*}}\leq n}\deg(\phi_{{i_{*}}})=1+\sum_{{i_{*}}\in[n]}{c_{*}}=1+\sum_{{i_{*}}\in[n]}\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},\alpha_{0}\rangle.

In order to compute the final sum on the right hand side, we list below the highest roots corresponding to each
G
with at least one cominuscule fundamental weight as well the value of the sum.

\begin{array}[]{c|c|c}G&\alpha_{0}&1+\sum_{{i_{*}}\in[n]}\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},\alpha_{0}\rangle\\
\hline\cr A_{n-1}&\alpha_{1}+\dots+\alpha_{n-1}&n\\
B_{n}&\alpha_{1}+2\alpha_{2}+\dots+2\alpha_{n}&2n\\
C_{n}&2\alpha_{1}+\dots+2\alpha_{n-1}+\alpha_{n}&2n\\
D_{n}&\alpha_{1}+2\alpha_{2}+\dots+2\alpha_{n-2}+\alpha_{n-1}+\alpha_{n}&2n-2\\
E_{6}&\alpha_{1}+2\alpha_{2}+2\alpha_{3}+3\alpha_{4}+2\alpha_{5}+\alpha_{6}&12\\
E_{7}&2\alpha_{1}+2\alpha_{2}+3\alpha_{3}+4\alpha_{4}+3\alpha_{5}+2\alpha_{6}+\alpha_{7}&18\end{array}

We now compare the quantities computed above with the indices of the Langlands dual minuscule spaces that arise in our constructions.

\begin{array}[]{c|c|c|c|c|c}G&P&X=G/P&\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=P^{\vee}\backslash G^{\vee}&\mathrm{index}(\mathbb{X}^{\vee})&1+\sum_{{i_{*}}\in[n]}\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},\alpha_{0}\rangle\\
\hline\cr A_{n-1}&\textrm{any }P_{k}&\mathrm{Gr}(k,n)&\mathrm{Gr}(n-k,n)&n&n\\
B_{n}&P_{1}&Q_{2n-1}&\mathbb{P}^{2n-1}&2n&2n\\
C_{n}&P_{n}&\mathrm{LG}(n,2n)&\mathrm{OG}(n,2n+1)&2n&2n\\
D_{n}&P_{1}&Q_{2n-2}&Q_{2n-2}&2n-2&2n-2\\
D_{n}&P_{n-1},P_{n}&\mathrm{OG}(n,2n)&\mathrm{OG}(n,2n)&2n-2&2n-2\\
E_{6}&P_{1},P_{6}&\mathbb{O}\mathbb{P}^{2}&\mathbb{O}\mathbb{P}^{2}&12&12\\
E_{7}&P_{7}&E^{\mathrm{sc}}_{7}/P_{7}&E^{\mathrm{sc}}_{7}/P_{7}&18&18\end{array}

Thus, in every case we obtain the equality

1+\textstyle\sum_{{i_{*}}\in[n]}\displaystyle\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},\alpha_{0}\rangle=\mathrm{index}(\mathbb{X}^{\vee})

showing that the divisor
D_{\mathrm{ac}}
is an anticanonical divisor in
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
. As a result,
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
is the complement of an anticanonical divisor in
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
and for this reason, these Plücker coordinate Landau-Ginzburg models have often been referred to as canonical Landau-Ginzburg models.

Remark 1.4
.

Since
X
is cominuscule, the geometric Satake correspondence gives a vector space isomorphism between the cohomology ring
H^{*}(X)
and the fundamental coweight representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{k}})
that we will use to define a uniform “quantum” derivation
\Delta
. The geometric Satake correspondence identifies the Plücker coordinate
p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}
with the Schubert class
\sigma_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}\in qH^{*}(X)
of a hyperplane. Now, for an arbitrary Plücker coordinate
p
, we denote the corresponding Schubert class by
\sigma\in qH^{*}(X)
and consider the quantum product
\sigma_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}*_{q}\sigma
which can be expressed as a linear combination of Schubert classes. By geometric Satake, we interpret this result as a linear combination of Plücker coordinates and define
\Delta(p)
to be equal to this linear combination. In other words, we use geometric Satake to pull the quantum product back to the coordinate ring of
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
; hence, we will simply write
\Delta(p)=p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}*_{q}p
for this map. We extend
\Delta
to polynomials in Plücker coordinates as a derivation.

In terms of Young diagrams, ignoring any quantum contributions, we can realize
\Delta
as the “full” derivation adding any possible box, whereas
\delta_{j}
acts as a “restricted” derivation only adding boxes with label
s_{j}
. Hence, at
q=0
, we can in fact obtain
\Delta
by the equality
\Delta=\sum_{j}\delta_{j}
. For arbitrary
q
, our quantum term
q\frac{p_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}}{p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}}
and Corollary
6.3
suggest the following generalization of the rim-hook rule for Grassmannians studied by
[
FW04
]
. The role of the rim-hook diagram in arbitrary cominuscule type is played by the (generalized) Young diagram
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
corresponding to the minimal coset representative
w_{P}s_{k}W_{P}
, which can equivalently be obtained as the unique subdiagram of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
containing
exactly
one element labeled
s_{k}
, see Example
2.18
for a table of these generalized rim-hooks.

Conjecture 1.5
.

For any cominuscule homogeneous space and (generalized) Young diagram
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
with corresponding Schubert class
\sigma_{\mathsf{w}}
, the quantum product of
\sigma_{\mathsf{w}}
with the hyperplane class
\sigma_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}
is given by

\sigma_{\mathsf{w}}*_{q}\sigma_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}=q\sigma_{\mathsf{w}^{-}}+\sum_{\mathsf{w}^{+}}\sigma_{\mathsf{w}^{+}},

where
\sigma_{\mathsf{w}^{-}}
denotes the the Schubert class of the complement of
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}
in
\mathsf{w}
if
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}\subset\mathsf{w}
and
0
otherwise and the sum is over all possible ways
\mathsf{w}^{+}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
to add a single box to
\mathsf{w}
.

It is possible to replace the derivations
\delta_{j}
in our construction of
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
with the uniform “quantum” derivation
\Delta
and to extend the derivation to the quantum term as well. Letting
\mathcal{D}=\prod_{{i_{*}}=0}^{n}\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
, we obtain the expression

\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}=\sum_{{i_{*}}=0}^{n}\frac{\Delta(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})}{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}}=\frac{\Delta(\mathcal{D})}{\mathcal{D}}.

We note in particular that with this interpretation, the superpotential terms corresponding to
\mathcal{D}_{0}
and
\mathcal{D}_{k}
are no longer distinguished from the others by having different formulas. Since Remark
1.3
above shows that the anticanonical divisor
D_{\mathrm{ac}}
is defined exactly by the vanishing of the regular function
\mathcal{D}
, we may thus interpret the superpotential
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
in some sense as a “logarithmic derivative of an anticanonical divisor.”

To give an example of this construction, we consider
X=\mathrm{LG}(3,6)=\mathrm{Sp}_{6}/P_{3}
the Lagrangian Grassmannian of type
C_{3}

1.1

height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}}{p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}}

which agrees exactly with our construction. While the uniform presentation of the superpotential appears much more elegant than the previous presentation, it severely complicates the expressions by introducing a large amount of extraneous cancellation as seen even in the relatively small example above. For this reason among others, we prefer in our construction to work with the derivations
\delta_{j}
which yield Plücker coordinate expressions without any cancellations, even though the two expressions turn out to be equivalent. In fact, we also have an equivalence at the level of individual terms terms via
\Delta(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})=\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})
, although this equality is false for general polynomials in the Plücker coordinates. Thus, we view the derivations
\delta_{\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})}
as parts of the full derivation
\Delta
which are optimized for simplicity of computation by eliminating extraneous cancellations.

Remark 1.6
.

Let
p_{1}\dots p_{d}
be a monomial in Plücker coordinates of degree
d
. Then for the action of the derivation
\Delta
defined above in Remark
1.4
, we obtain by commutivity and associativity of the quantum product that

\Delta(p_{1}\dots p_{d})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}p_{1}\dots p_{i-1}(p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}*_{q}p_{i})p_{i+1}\dots p_{d}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}*_{q}(p_{1}\dots p_{d})=d\,p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}*_{q}(p_{1}\dots p_{d}),

where all products are now interpreted to be the quantum product inside of
qH^{*}(X)
via the geometric Satake correspondence as in the previous Remark
1.4
.
In particular, we compute for the individual terms
\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}
of the potential
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
that

\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}=\frac{\Delta(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})}{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}}=\frac{\deg(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})~p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}*_{q}\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}}{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}}={c_{*}}\,p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}

and thus that if we interpret
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
inside of
qH^{*}(X)
, we obtain

\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}=\Bigl(1+\textstyle\sum_{{i_{*}}\in[n]}\displaystyle{c_{*}}\Bigr)p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}=\mathrm{index}(\mathbb{X}^{\vee})p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}.

With this interpretation, we may interpret
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
in some sense as an incarnation of the anticanonical class of
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
inside of
qH^{*}(X)
. We note that slightly different observations were made in previous works by Pech-Rietsch (
[
PR13
, §1]
and
[
PR18
, §9]
). Furthermore, from our perspective, the reason the expression for
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
is particularly simple in the case of Grassmannians
\mathrm{Gr}(k,n)
has to do with the fact that every fundamental weight in type
A_{n-1}
is minuscule, so that each term of the potential is simply a ratio of Plücker coordinates rather than the general situation which is instead a ratio of higher degree polynomials in Plücker coordinates.

Remark 1.7
.

We may consider
X^{\vee}=\Pi(R_{w_{P}}^{w_{0}})
as the projection of the Richardson variety
R_{w_{P}}^{w_{0}}
, which is defined to be the closure of the intersection of opposite Schubert cells
\Sigma_{w_{P}}
and
\Sigma^{w_{0}}
in the full flag manifold
B^{\vee}\backslash G^{\vee}
. For more details on projections of Richardson varieties, see
[
KLS14
]
. It is known (see
[
LT17
, Lemma 5.4]
) that the sum of the classes of those projected Richardson varieties which are hypersurfaces inside
\Pi=\Pi(R_{w_{P}}^{w_{0}})
forms an anticanonical divisor.

In our context, the hypersurface projected Richardson varieties are given by

\Pi_{0}=\Pi(R_{s_{k}w_{P}}^{w_{0}}),\Pi_{1}=\Pi(R_{w_{P}}^{s_{1}w_{0}}),\dots,\Pi_{n}=\Pi(R_{w_{P}}^{s_{n}w_{0}}).

We consider
\Pi_{{i_{*}}}
for
{i_{*}}\in[n]
as associated to the correspondingly labeled node of the Dynkin diagram of
G^{\vee}
. We do not, however, associate such an interpretation to
\Pi_{0}
. Although we will not use this, we believe that each hypersurface
\Pi_{{i_{*}}}
for
{i_{*}}\in[n]
is defined by
\{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}=0\}
while
\Pi_{0}
is defined by
\{p_{\varnothing}=0\}
.

We conclude with a brief outline of this article. We start by fixing notation and conventions as well as recalling relevant Lie-theoretic and order-theoretic background in Section
2
. We then prove several key components of our main theorem in Sections
3
,
4
, and
5
before assembling all the pieces into our main result in Section
6
. In Appendix
A
we apply our construction to four exceptional cases directly and in Appendix
B
we show how to recover LG models previously constructed with type-dependent methods using our type-independent construction.

2.
Preliminaries

In this section we start by summarizing all conventions and previous results that we will need for our work. We begin with some Lie-theoretic conventions in Section
2.1
followed by the results we will be building on in Section
2.2
, including the Lie-theoretic and Laurent polynomial LG-models of
[
Rie08
]
and
[
Spa21
]
respectively. Afterwards, we will introduce minuscule posets, their order ideals, and how their combinatorics can be used in our context in Section
2.3
.

2.1.
Conventions and notation

In this section we fix our notations and conventions and recall some facts from Lie theory. Unless otherwise stated, we will always use the notation and conventions fixed below. We write
[N]=\{1,2,\ldots,N\}
for any
N\in\mathbb{N}
.

Let
G
be a simple and simply-connected complex algebraic group of rank
n
and fix a maximal torus
T
and Borel subgroup
B_{+}\supset T
. We can write
B_{+}=TU_{+}
for a unipotent subgroup
U_{+}
, and we write
U_{-}
for the opposite unipotent subgroup (i.e. such that
B_{-}=TU_{-}
satisfies
B_{+}\cap B_{-}=T
). Recall that the parabolic subgroups of
G
containing
B_{+}
correspond one-to-one to subsets
I\subset[n]
, and that the Levi subgroup of the parabolic subgroup
P_{I}
is semisimple of Dynkin type given by
removing
the vertices in
I
from the Dynkin diagram of
G
. In particular, the Weyl group
W_{I}
of (the Levi subgroup of)
P_{I}
is realized as the subgroup of the Weyl group
W
of
G
generated by all simple reflections
not
in
I
; we write
w_{0,I}\in W_{I}
and similarly
w_{0}\in W
for the respective longest elements. Now, we note that these longest elements define (possibly trivial) Dynkin diagram involutions
\sigma_{I}
by
w_{0,I}\cdot{\varpi_{i}}=-{\varpi_{{\sigma_{I}}(i)}}
where
{\varpi_{i}}
is the fundamental weight of the Levi subgroup of
P_{I}
and
i\in[n]\setminus I
; we extend
\sigma_{I}
to
[n]
by
\sigma_{I}(i)=i
for
i\in I
, and write
\sigma_{0}=\sigma_{\varnothing}
.

The pair
(G,T)
defines the
Langlands dual pair

(G^{\vee},T^{\vee})
that has character and cocharacter lattices interchanged. The parabolic subgroups of
G^{\vee}
form exactly the Langlands dual pairs to
(P_{I},T)
, so we denote these simply by
P^{\vee}_{I}
. This holds in particular for
B_{+}=P_{[n]}
the Langlands dual of which we denote
B^{\vee}_{+}
; together with
T^{\vee}
this defines the opposite Borel subgroup
B^{\vee}_{-}
and the unipotent subgroups
U^{\vee}_{+}
and
U^{\vee}_{-}
. Writing
\Phi
resp.
\Phi^{\vee}
for the roots resp. coroots of
G
with respect to
T
, we note that they form the
coroots
resp.
roots
of
G^{\vee}
with respect to
T^{\vee}
. Similarly, for
\Delta=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\}\subset\Phi
the base of simple roots for
G
fixed by
B_{+}
, the simple coroots
\Delta\!^{\vee}=\{\alpha^{\vee}_{1},\ldots,\alpha^{\vee}_{n}\}\subset\Phi^{\vee}
form a base of simple roots for
G^{\vee}
; analogously fundamental weights
{\varpi_{i}}
and coweights
{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}
for
G
are fundamental coweights and weights for
G^{\vee}
. It is in particular clear from this that the Weyl groups of
G
and
G^{\vee}
are identical, so we simply write
W
for both. Finally, we remark that assuming
G
is simply-connected implies that
G^{\vee}
is
adjoint
.

We will also need to refer to the Lie algebras of the algebraic groups introduced above: we will write
\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}
,
\mathfrak{p}^{\vee}_{I}
,
\mathfrak{b}^{\vee}_{+}
,
\mathfrak{u}^{\vee}_{+}
, and
\mathfrak{t}^{\vee}
for the Lie algebras of
G^{\vee}
,
P^{\vee}_{I}
,
B^{\vee}_{+}
,
U^{\vee}_{+}
and
T^{\vee}
, respectively. The simple Lie algebra
\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}
has a root space decomposition (or Cartan decomposition) of the form
\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}=\mathfrak{t}^{\vee}\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha^{\vee}\in\Phi^{\vee}}\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}_{\alpha}
, and we choose a set of Chevalley generators
(e^{\vee}_{i},h^{\vee}_{i},f^{\vee}_{i})_{i\in[n]}
for
\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}
satisfying the Serre relations, where
e^{\vee}_{i}\in\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}_{\alpha^{\vee}_{i}}
,
f^{\vee}_{i}\in\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}_{-\alpha^{\vee}_{i}}
and
h^{\vee}_{i}=[e^{\vee}_{i},f^{\vee}_{i}]\in\mathfrak{t}^{\vee}
. Note that
\mathfrak{b}^{\vee}_{+}
is generated by
\{e^{\vee}_{i},h^{\vee}_{i}~|~i\in[n]\}
and that
\mathfrak{p}^{\vee}_{I}
is generated by
\{e^{\vee}_{i},h^{\vee}_{i},f^{\vee}_{j}~|~i,j\in[n],j\notin I\}
. The Chevalley generators define one-parameter subgroups

x^{\vee}_{i}(a)=\exp(a\,e^{\vee}_{i})\in U^{\vee}_{+}\quad\text{and}\quad y^{\vee}_{i}(a)=\exp(af^{\vee}_{i})\in U^{\vee}_{-}\quad\text{for}\quad a\in\mathbb{C}.

These subgroups in turn define representatives of
W
in
G^{\vee}
by assigning to a simple reflection
s_{i}\in W
the elements

\dot{s}_{i}=x^{\vee}_{i}(+1)\,y^{\vee}_{i}(-1)\,x^{\vee}_{i}(+1)\quad\text{and}\quad\bar{s}_{i}=x^{\vee}_{i}(-1)\,y^{\vee}_{i}(+1)\,x^{\vee}_{i}(-1),

and extending this to
\dot{w},\bar{w}\in G^{\vee}
for a general word
w\in W
by a choice of reduced expression for
w
. Note that the maps
W\to G^{\vee}
given by
w\mapsto\dot{w}
and
w\mapsto\bar{w}
are
not
homomorphisms:
s_{i}^{2}=e\in W
but
\dot{s}_{i}^{2}\in T^{\vee}
is nontrivial.

Since
G^{\vee}
is adjoint, not all fundamental representations of
\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}
give rise to representations of
G^{\vee}
; hence, we will have to consider the
universal cover

\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
of
G^{\vee}
. (Note that for simply-laced Lie types,
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}\cong G
.) We will analogously write
\widetilde{P}^{\vee}_{I}
etc. for the corresponding universal covers. Since
\widetilde{U}^{\vee}_{+}\cong U^{\vee}_{+}
and
\widetilde{U}^{\vee}_{-}\cong U^{\vee}_{-}
, we will identify
U^{\vee}_{+}
and
U^{\vee}_{-}
with the universal covers in
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
; this yields preferred lifts of the elements
\dot{s}_{i}
and
\bar{s}_{i}
to
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
as the products of the uniquely lifted one-parameter subgroups.

To finish up, we will need a small observation regarding the representatives
\dot{s}_{i}
and
\bar{s}_{i}
in
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
of the simple reflection
s_{i}\in W
: if
\mu^{\vee}
is some weight of
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
mapped to
\mu^{\vee}-d\alpha^{\vee}_{i}
by
s_{i}
with
d\in\mathbb{Z}
, then for any
extremal
vector
v_{\mu^{\vee}}
of weight
\mu^{\vee}
in an irreducible representation the actions of these representatives are related by

\dot{s}_{i}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}}=(-1)^{d}\bar{s}_{i}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{d}d!(f^{\vee}_{i})^{d}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}},&\text{if~}d\geq 0;\\
d!(e^{\vee}_{i})^{d}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}},&\text{if~}d\leq 0;\\
\end{cases}

(2.1)

see e.g.
[
GLS11
, Section 7.1]
. By extension (i.e. taking a reduced expression and repeated application), we find for a general element
w\in W
and extremal weight vector
v_{\mu^{\vee}}
that

\dot{w}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}}=(-1)^{h}\bar{w}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}}\quad\text{where}\quad h=0pt\bigl(w\cdot\mu^{\vee}-\mu^{\vee}\bigr)\in\mathbb{Z}.

(2.2)

2.2.
Related Landau-Ginzburg models and results

We now summarize the Lie-theoretic construction of LG-models in
[
Rie08
]
that applies to general homogeneous spaces. Afterwards, we specialize to cominuscule homogeneous spaces
X=G/P_{k}
and introduce Plücker coordinates on their minuscule Langlands dual homogeneous spaces
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash G^{\vee}
in Section
2.2.2
, followed by a summary of the presentation of the coordinate ring of the related unipotent cell as given in
[
GLS11
]
in Section
2.2.3
. Finally, we present the Laurent polynomial model of
[
Spa21
]
in Section
2.2.4
.

2.2.1.
Lie-theoretic Landau-Ginzburg model

We will now introduce the Lie-theoretic models defined in
[
Rie08
]
, using the presentation as given in
[
PR13
]
. Fix an
arbirtrary
(i.e. not necessarily cominuscule) homogeneous space
X=G/P
, and denote by
W_{P}=W_{I}\subset W
the parabolic Weyl subgroup corresponding to
P=P_{I}
. Consider the subvariety

\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}=B^{\vee}_{-}\bar{w}_{0}^{-1}\cap U^{\vee}_{+}T^{P}\bar{w}_{P}U^{\vee}_{-}~~\subset~~G^{\vee},

sometimes called the
geometric crystal associated to
(G^{\vee},P^{\vee})
cf.
[
LT17
]
, where we denoted
T^{P}=(T^{\vee})^{W_{P}}\subset T^{\vee}
for the locus of
T^{\vee}
invariant under the action of
W_{P}
by conjugation, and
w_{0}\in W
and
w_{P}\in W_{P}
for the respective longest elements.

Remark 2.1
.

We followed our convention in
[
SW23
]
by multiplying
\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}
as defined in
[
Rie08
]
on the right by
\bar{w}_{0}^{-1}
.

Note that
\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}
can be considered as those elements
z\in B^{\vee}_{-}\bar{w}_{0}^{-1}
that can be decomposed as
z=u_{+}t\bar{w}_{P}u_{-}
for
u_{+}\in U^{\vee}_{+}
,
t\in T^{P}
and
u_{-}\in U^{\vee}_{-}
. Furthermore, the
u_{-}
can be restricted to lie in a specific unipotent cell as follows. Let

U_{-}^{P}=U^{\vee}_{-}\cap B^{\vee}_{+}(\dot{w}^{P})^{-1}B^{\vee}_{+}~~\subset~~U^{\vee}_{-}

(2.3)

where
w^{P}\in W^{P}
is the minimal coset representative of
w_{0}W_{P}
, i.e. the Weyl group element satisfying
w_{0}=w^{P}w_{P}
with
\ell(w_{0})=\ell(w^{P})+\ell(w_{P})
.

Lemma 2.2

(
[
PR18
]
, Section 4)
.

Every
z\in\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}
is
uniquely
decomposed as
z=u_{+}t\bar{w}_{P}u_{-}
with
u_{+}\in U^{\vee}_{+}
,
t\in T^{P}
and
u_{-}\in U_{-}^{P}
. More precisely, given
(u_{-},t)\in U_{-}^{P}\times T^{P}
, there exists a
unique

u_{+}\in U^{\vee}_{+}
such that
u_{+}t\bar{w}_{P}u_{-}\in\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}
, and the map
U_{-}^{P}\times T^{P}\to\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}
sending
(u_{-},t)\mapsto u_{+}t\bar{w}_{P}u_{-}
is an isomorphism.

Remark 2.3
.

Although proven in a specific case in
[
PR18
]
, the methods carry over to the general case so the proof will be omitted here.

The
superpotential

\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}}:\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}\to\mathbb{C}
is now defined as

\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}}(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(e^{\vee}_{i})^{*}(u_{+}^{-1})+(f^{\vee}_{i})^{*}(u_{-}),\quad\text{where}\quad z=u_{+}t\bar{w}_{P}u_{-},

and where
(e^{\vee}_{i})^{*}
resp.
(f^{\vee}_{i})^{*}
are the unique characters mapping
x^{\vee}_{i}(a)
resp.
y^{\vee}_{i}(a)
to
a
and the other one-parameter subgroups to
0
. (Equivalently, these can be defined as follows: the Chevalley generators
\{e^{\vee}_{i}~|~i\in[n]\}
generate a basis for
\mathfrak{u}^{\vee}_{+}
, which in turns gives rise to a PBW basis for the completed universal enveloping algebra
\widehat{\mathcal{U}}^{\vee}_{+}\supset\mathfrak{u}^{\vee}_{+}
; let
(e^{\vee}_{i})^{*}
be the element dual to
e^{\vee}_{i}
in the dual basis; the maps
(e^{\vee}_{i})^{*}:U^{\vee}_{+}\to\mathbb{C}
are finally obtained using the embedding
U^{\vee}_{+}\hookrightarrow\widehat{\mathcal{U}}^{\vee}_{+}
.)

The results in
[
Rie08
]
now state that

Theorem 2.4

(
[
Rie08
]
, Theorem 4.1)
.

There exists an isomorphism

qH^{*}(X)_{\mathrm{loc}}\cong\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}]/\langle\partial\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}}\rangle,

where the left-hand side is the small quantum cohomology of
X
localized at the quantum parameters, and the right-hand side is the quotient of the coordinate ring of
\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}
by the ideal generated by the derivatives of
\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}}
along
U_{-}^{P}
.

The Lie-theoretic mirror model is now obtained using an isomorphism
\Psi:X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\times T^{P}\to\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}
where

X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}=\mathcal{R}^{\vee}_{w_{P},w_{0}}=\bigl(B^{\vee}_{+}w_{P}B^{\vee}_{-}\cap B^{\vee}_{-}w_{0}B^{\vee}_{-}\bigr)/B^{\vee}_{-}~~\subset~~G^{\vee}/B^{\vee}_{-}

is the open Richardson variety associated to
(w_{P},w_{0})
. (For a discussion of
\Psi
in the current notation, see Remark 3.1 of
[
Spa21
]
.) Writing
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}}=\Psi^{*}(\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}})
, we obtain

qH^{*}(X)_{\mathrm{loc}}\cong\mathbb{C}[X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\times T^{P}]/\langle\partial\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\rangle,

(2.4)

where
\langle\partial\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\rangle
is the ideal generated by the derivatives along
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}
. In other words,
(X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}})
forms a
Landau-Ginzburg model
for
X
.

We now specialize to the case that
X=G/P
for
P=P_{k}=P_{\{k\}}
a maximal parabolic subgroup (i.e. when
X
has Picard rank
\rho=1
). In this case,
G^{\vee}
being an adjoint linear algebraic group implies that the simple coroot
\alpha^{\vee}_{k}
gives an isomorphism
T^{P}\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{C}^{*}
. This isomorphism allows us to work more directly with a formal parameter
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
instead of invariant torus elements. This approach is indeed justified as the mirror symmetry isomorphism in (
2.4
) identifies
T^{P}
with the quantum parameter space of the quantum cohomology, and
\alpha^{\vee}_{k}
effectively splits this identification in this specialized case.

This allows us to move the focus away from
\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}
to
U_{-}^{P}
. First, Lemma
2.2
can be restated as

Corollary 2.5
.

For any fixed
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
let
t\in T^{P}
be such that
\alpha^{\vee}_{k}(t)=q
. Then, every
u_{-}\in U_{-}^{P}
allows a unique
u_{+}\in U^{\vee}_{+}
such that
u_{+}t\bar{w}_{P}u_{-}\in\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}
.

Similarly, the superpotential
\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}}
can be expressed as:

Definition 2.6
.

For any fixed
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
, let
\mathcal{W}_{U_{-}^{P}}:U_{-}^{P}\to\mathbb{C}
be the function given by

\mathcal{W}_{U_{-}^{P}}(u_{-})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(e^{\vee}_{i})^{*}(u_{+}^{-1})+(f^{\vee}_{i})^{*}(u_{-}),

where
u_{+}\in U^{\vee}_{+}
is the unique element determined by
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
and
u_{-}\in U_{-}^{P}
of Corollary
2.5
.

Note the shift from working over
\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}
to working over
U_{-}^{P}
for fixed
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
makes explicit that we do not think of
\mathcal{W}_{U_{-}^{P}}
as a morphism
U_{-}^{P}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}\to\mathbb{C}
but rather as a
\mathbb{C}^{*}
-family of morphisms
U_{-}^{P}\to\mathbb{C}
; this is in line with the fact that the Jacobi ideals
\langle\partial\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}}\rangle
and
\langle\partial\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\rangle
are only generated by derivatives along
U_{-}^{P}
and
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}
respectively.

2.2.2.
Minuscule homogeneous spaces and their Plücker coordinates

The Lie-theoretic mirror models introduced in the previous subsection hold for any projective homogeneous space. However, in the case of
cominuscule
homogeneous spaces, these models can be reformulated using natural coordinates on the mirror varieties. From now on, we will restrict to this case; that is, we assume that
X
can be written as
X=G/P
for
P=P_{k}=P_{\{k\}}
a maximal parabolic subgroup such that the fundamental weight
{\varpi_{k}}
of
G
is
cominuscule
. Recall that a fundamental weight
{\varpi_{k}}
is
cominuscule
if
\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}},\alpha\rangle\!\rangle\in\{-1,0,+1\}
for any root
\alpha\in\Phi
, where
\langle\!\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\!\rangle
denotes the dual coupling between the character and cocharacter lattices; in this case,
{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
is called a
minuscule
coweight and
X
is called a
cominuscule homogeneous space
or a
cominuscule (generalized) flag variety
. Note that cominusculity of
{\varpi_{k}}
is equivalent to
\alpha^{\vee}_{k}
having coefficient
1
in the highest coroot
\alpha^{\vee}_{0}
, i.e.
\langle\!\langle\alpha^{\vee}_{0},{\varpi_{k}}\rangle\!\rangle=1
.

Cominusculity of
{\varpi_{k}}
can also be considered as minusculity of the weight
{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
of
G^{\vee}
. Hence, the homogeneous space
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash G^{\vee}
is often called
minuscule
. However, since
G^{\vee}
is adjoint, the representation with highest weight
{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
of
\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}
does not necessarily induce a representation of
G^{\vee}
. Hence, we will often consider
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=\widetilde{P}^{\vee}_{k}\backslash\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
instead (note that
P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash G^{\vee}\cong\widetilde{P}^{\vee}_{k}\backslash\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
, allowing us to identify these descriptions of
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
). Finally, for simplicity, we often call an index (i.e. vertex of the Dynkin diagram)
i\in[n]

(co-) minuscule
if the corresponding fundamental weight is (co-) minuscule; the context will clarify whether we consider a fundamental weight of
G
or
G^{\vee}
. In Table
2.1
we have listed all minuscule and cominuscule weights, together with the associated homogeneous spaces.
