Table 2.1.
Table listing for each type of
G
the fundamental weights
{\varpi_{i}}
that are minuscule, cominuscule or both, the associated homogeneous spaces and their dimensions and indexes. The varieties appearing are:

Q_{n}
, the quadric of dimension
n
;

\mathrm{Gr}(k,n)
, the Grassmannian of
k
-dimensional subspaces in
\mathbb{C}^{n}
;

\mathrm{LG}(n,2n)
,

the Lagrangian Grassmannian of maximal isotropic subspaces with respect to the standard symplectic form;

\mathrm{OG}(n,2n)

and
\mathrm{OG}(n,2n+1)
, one of the two isomorphic connected components of the orthogonal Grassmannians of maximal isotropic subspaces with respect to the standard quadratic form;

\mathbb{OP}^{2}=E^{\mathrm{sc}}_{6}/P_{6}
, the Cayley plane;

E^{\mathrm{sc}}_{7}/P_{7}
, the Freudenthal variety.

Note that the two varieties that are only minuscule are redundant:

The type-
B_{n}
minuscule variety
\mathrm{OG}(n,2n+1)
is isomorphic to the variety
\mathrm{OG}(n+1,2n+2)
which is both minuscule and cominuscule as a type-
D_{n+1}
homogeneous space;

The type-
C_{n}
minuscule variety
\mathbb{CP}^{2n-1}
is the same as
\mathrm{Gr}(1,2n)
, which is both minuscule and cominuscule as a type-
A_{2n-1}
homogeneous space.

Adapted from
[
CMP08
]
and
[
Spa21
]
.

Minuscule homogeneous spaces allow for the definition of a natural set of projective coordinates called
(generalized) Plücker coordinates
. The fact that
{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
is minuscule implies that the fundamental representations
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{k}})
and
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})
of
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
are
minuscule
. (Note that these are dual representations; depending on the type, they can also be isomorphic.) A representation is minuscule if the Weyl group acts transitively on its weights.

We will consider the lowest weight of
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})
, namely
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
. Clearly, the stabilizer of
W
acting on
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
is
W_{P}=W_{k}
; hence, writing
W^{P}
for the set of minimal representatives of left cosets of
W_{P}
in
W
, we find that
W^{P}\cdot(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}})
forms the set of weights of the representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})
. In particular, choosing a lowest weight vector
v_{0}\in V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})
, the set of vectors
\{v_{w}=\dot{w}\cdot v_{0}~|~w\in W^{P}\}
forms a weight basis for the representation. The actions of
\dot{w}
and
\bar{w}
for
w\in W
on this weight basis can be described explicitly; see e.g.
[
Gre08
, Section 3]
or
[
Gec17
, Section 3]
, or for the summarized results phrased in the current notation see
[
Spa21
, Section 4]
. We will in particular need the following result:

Lemma 2.7

(
[
Spa21
]
, Corollary 4.3 and Lemma 4.4(ii) and (iii))
.

Let
v^{+}\in V({\varpi^{\vee}_{k^{\prime}}})
be the highest vector in a minuscule representation of a linear algebraic group
H
, and let
W^{\prime}\subset W
be the set of minimal coset representatives of the Weyl subgroup
W_{k^{\prime}}=\langle s_{i}~|~i\neq k^{\prime}\rangle\subset W
, then:

(i)

If the minimal coset representative
w\in W^{\prime}
has reduced expression
w=s_{j_{1}}\cdots s_{j_{\ell(w)}}
, then its representatives act on the highest weight vector by
\bar{w}\cdot v^{+}=f^{\vee}_{j_{1}}\cdots f^{\vee}_{j_{\ell(s)}}\cdot v^{+}
and
\dot{w}\cdot v^{+}=(-1)^{\ell(w)}f^{\vee}_{j_{1}}\cdots f^{\vee}_{j_{\ell(w)}}\cdot v^{+}
.

(ii)

Conversely, if
f^{\vee}_{j_{1}}\cdots f^{\vee}_{j_{\ell}}\cdot v^{+}
is nonzero of weight
\mu^{\vee}
, then
s_{j_{1}}\cdots s_{j_{\ell}}\in W^{\prime}
is a reduced expression for the (unique) element mapping the highest weight
{\varpi^{\vee}_{k^{\prime}}}
to
\mu^{\vee}
.

We now take the basis
\{v_{w}^{*}~|~w\in W^{P}\}
for
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})^{*}
dual to the weight basis just constructed; this forms a weight basis as well with
v_{0}^{*}
of highest weight
{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
under
right
-action of
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
. In particular,
\widetilde{P}^{\vee}_{k}
stabilizes the line
\mathbb{C}v_{0}^{*}
, yielding an embedding

\mathbb{X}^{\vee}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}\bigl(V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})^{*}\bigr):\quad P^{\vee}_{k}g\mapsto\mathbb{C}v_{0}^{*}\cdot P^{\vee}_{k}g,

(2.5)

where we used that
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=\widetilde{P}^{\vee}_{k}\backslash\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
; this embedding is called the
(generalized) Plücker embedding
.

Definition 2.8
.

The projective coordinates
(p_{w}~|~w\in W^{P})
on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
defined by

p_{w}(g)=v_{0}^{*}(g\cdot v_{w})\quad\text{for}\quad g\in\widetilde{G}^{\vee}

are called
(generalized) Plücker coordinates
. We will refer to the maps
p_{w}:\widetilde{G}^{\vee}\to\mathbb{C}
as Plücker coordinates as well. We will frequently suppress the arguments of these coordinates if it is clear on which domain we consider them.

2.2.3.
The coordinate ring of
U_{-}^{P}
for cominuscule
G/P

The isomorphism
\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}\cong U_{-}^{P}\times T^{P}
discussed in Lemma
2.2
will turn up again to relate the Lie-theoretic mirror model to our type-independent canonical mirror models. In particular, it will allow us to use a description of the coordinate ring of
U_{-}^{P}
. In
[
GLS11
]
, the coordinate rings of unipotent cells are described as being a polynomial ring generated by a “dual PBW basis” localized at certain
generalized minors
in the sense of
[
FZ99
]
. However,
[
GLS11
]
works with “upper” unipotent groups, i.e. those that have Lie algebras contained in the positive root spaces, whereas
U_{-}^{P}
is “lower” unipotent; we will use the transposition anti-isomorphism to translate between the two conventions. Recall from (
2.3
) that
U_{-}^{P}=U^{\vee}_{-}\cap B^{\vee}_{+}(\dot{w}^{P})^{-1}B^{\vee}_{+}
, which is mapped under the transposition map to
U_{+}^{P}=U^{\vee}_{+}\cap B^{\vee}_{-}\dot{w}^{P}B^{\vee}_{-}
(recall that
\dot{w}^{T}=\dot{w}^{-1}
). Proposition 8.5 of
[
GLS11
]
now applies to
U_{+}^{P}
directly.

Instead of presenting the construction of the dual PBW basis for
U_{+}^{P}
, we will use the type-independent characterization in terms of Plücker coordinates given in Proposition 3.8 of
[
SW23
]
: Consider the set
\Pi^{\vee}_{w^{P}}\subset\Pi^{\vee}
of positive roots mapped to negative roots by
w^{P}
(equivalently, this is the set of positive roots with coefficient
1
in front of
\alpha^{\vee}_{k}
in their decomposition into simple roots; see
[
SW23
, Lemma 3.5]
), then for every
\alpha^{\vee}\in\Pi^{\vee}_{w^{P}}
there exists a unique
w_{\alpha^{\vee}}\in W^{P}
such that
w_{\alpha^{\vee}}(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}+\alpha^{\vee}
; each of these minimal coset representatives
w_{\alpha^{\vee}}
determines a Plücker coordinate
p_{\alpha^{\vee}}=p_{w_{\alpha^{\vee}}}
on
U^{\vee}_{-}
, so writing
p_{\alpha^{\vee}}^{T}:u_{+}\mapsto p_{\alpha^{\vee}}(u_{+}^{T})
, we obtain a set of “transposed” Plücker coordinates
\{p_{\alpha^{\vee}}^{T}~|~\alpha^{\vee}\in\Pi^{\vee}_{w^{P}}\}
on
U_{+}^{P}
; by Proposition 8.5 of
[
GLS11
]
and Proposition 3.8 of
[
SW23
]
, this set forms a generating set for the coordinate ring of
U_{+}^{P}
.

In contrast to the dual PBW basis, the generalized minors appearing in the coordinate ring of
U_{+}^{P}
can be stated concisely as:

\Delta_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},(w^{P})^{-1}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})}(u_{+})=\Bigl\langle u_{+}(\dot{w}^{P})^{-1}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+},~v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}\quad\text{for}\quad i\in[n],

where
v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+}
is a choice of highest weight vector in the fundamental representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})
, and
\langle v,v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+}\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}
denotes the coefficient in front of
v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+}
in the decomposition of
v
with respect to a weight basis of the representation. (Note that this is independent of the choice of basis.)

Now, to translate these results to
U_{-}^{P}
, we pull these functions back along the transposition anti-isomorphism, yielding the generating set of Plücker coordinates
\{p_{\alpha^{\vee}}~|~\alpha^{\vee}\in\Pi^{\vee}_{w^{P}}\}
and the transposed generalized minors
u_{-}\mapsto\Delta_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},(w^{P})^{-1}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})}(u_{-}^{T})
for
i\in[n]
. We will translate each of these generalized minors calculated in
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})
into one calculated in
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}})
to remove the transpose maps.

For this, we first note that that evaluating an element
f\in V^{*}
in some dual representation at an element
g\cdot v\in V
is the same as evaluating the element
g^{T}\cdot f\in V^{*}
at
v\in V
. Subsequently, we observe that the dual representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})^{*}
is a
right
-representation, which is mapped under the inversion anti-isomorphism to the
left
-representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}})
. Note, however, that projection to the highest weight vector
v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+}
is a
lowest
weight element of the dual representation (of weight
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}
). In conclusion, we obtain the relations:

\Bigl\langle g\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+},~v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}=\Bigl\langle v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+},~g^{T}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}=\Bigl\langle g^{-T}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}^{-},~v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}^{-}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}

(2.6)

Applying this to the generalized minor in question (and recalling that
\dot{w}^{T}=\dot{w}^{-1}
for any Weyl group element
w\in W
), we find:

\Delta_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},(w^{P})^{-1}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})}(u_{-}^{T})=\Bigl\langle u_{-}^{T}(\dot{w}^{P})^{-1}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+},~v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}^{+}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}}=\Bigl\langle u_{-}^{-1}(\dot{w}^{P})^{-1}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}^{-},~v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}^{-}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}.

Next, we note that
(\dot{w}^{P})^{-1}=\bar{w}
for
w=(w^{P})^{-1}
, and hence by (
2.2
) we find that
(\dot{w}^{P})^{-1}
acts as
(-1)^{h}\dot{w}=(-1)^{h}(\bar{w}^{P})^{-1}
on the lowest weight vector (of weight
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}
), where

h=0pt\bigl(-(w^{P})^{-1}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}\bigr).

(2.7)

Combining this with the fact that
\bar{w}_{0}=\bar{w}^{P}\bar{w}_{P}
maps the highest weight vector to the lowest weight vector, we find that

\displaystyle\Delta_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},(w^{P})^{-1}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})}(u_{-}^{T})

\displaystyle=(-1)^{h}\Bigl\langle u_{-}^{-1}(\bar{w}^{P})^{-1}\bar{w}^{P}\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}^{-},~\bar{w}_{0}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}^{+}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}

\displaystyle=(-1)^{h}\Bigl\langle u_{-}^{-1}\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}^{-},~\bar{w}_{0}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}^{+}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(i)}}}.

We recognize the right-hand side as the desired generalized minor to conclude

\Delta_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},(w^{P})^{-1}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})}(u_{-}^{T})=(-1)^{h}\Delta_{w_{0}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}},w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}}(u_{-}^{-1})\quad\text{for}\quad j=\sigma_{0}(i),

and where
h
is given in (
2.7
). As
\cdot^{-1}:U^{\vee}_{-}\to U^{\vee}_{-}
is an anti-automorphism, the generalized minor is now truly taken on lower unipotent elements; however, in general
\cdot^{-1}
does
not
map
U_{-}^{P}
to itself (this only holds if
(w^{P})^{-1}=w^{P}
, i.e. when the Dynkin involution
\sigma_{0}
is trivial).

In conclusion, we obtain

Proposition 2.9

(
[
GLS11
]
, Prop. 8.5 &
[
SW23
]
, Lem. 3.5)
.

The coordinate ring of
U_{-}^{P}
is given by

\mathbb{C}[U_{-}^{P}]=\mathbb{C}\bigl[p_{\alpha^{\vee}}~\big|~\alpha^{\vee}\in\Pi^{\vee}_{w^{P}}\bigr]\bigl[\phi_{j}^{-1}~\big|~j\in[n]\bigr]

where we recall that
p_{\alpha^{\vee}}=p_{w_{\alpha^{\vee}}}
for
w_{\alpha^{\vee}}\in W^{P}
the unique element sending
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
to
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}+\alpha^{\vee}
, with
\Pi^{\vee}_{w^{P}}
the set positive roots with coefficient
+1
in front of
\alpha^{\vee}_{k}
when written as a linear combination of simple roots, and where

\phi_{j}(u_{-})=(-1)^{h}\Delta_{w_{0}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}},w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}}(u_{-}^{-1})=(-1)^{h}\Bigl\langle u_{-}^{-1}\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}}^{+},~v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}}^{-}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}}

is a generalized minor as defined in
[
FZ99
]
.

We have kept the coefficient
(-1)^{h}
in
\phi_{j}
to cancel out the additional minus signs arising from the inversion
u_{-}^{-1}
. This will be discussed further in Remarks
2.22
and
3.11
, but is immaterial for the presentation of the coordinate ring. One of the intermediate results in our construction of type-independent LG-models is the derivation of Plücker coordinate expressions for these generalized minors.

2.2.4.
Laurent polynomial expressions

We will show that the type-independent canonical mirror models are Landau-Ginzburg models by showing that they are isomorphic to these Lie-theoretic mirror models, taking advantage of the fact that the latter have type-independent descriptions when restricted to an open, dense algebraic torus defined as

\mathcal{Z}^{\circ}_{P}=B^{\vee}_{-}\bar{w}_{0}^{-1}\cap U^{\vee}_{+}T^{P}\bar{w}_{P}U^{\circ}_{-}~~\subset~~\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P},

where
U^{\circ}_{-}\subset U_{-}^{P}
(cf.
[
PR18
]
, Section 5.2, or
[
Spa21
]
, Lemma 5.2) is the algebraic torus of elements
u_{-}\in U_{-}^{P}
that allow a decomposition in the form

u_{-}=y^{\vee}_{r_{1}}(a_{1})\cdots y^{\vee}_{r_{\ell}}(a_{\ell})\quad\text{with}\quad a_{i}\in\mathbb{C}^{*}

(2.8)

and with the indices
(r_{j})_{j\in[\ell]}
forming a reduced expression
s_{r_{\ell}}\cdots s_{r_{1}}=w^{P}
. (Note that the sequence is reversed in the two expressions. Moreover, we have reversed the labeling of the reduced expression for
w^{P}
compared with
[
Spa21
]
and
[
SW23
]
.) The torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
does
not
depend on which reduced expression of
w^{P}
the sequence
(r_{j})
generates: due to the full commutativity of
w^{P}
by
[
Ste96
]
, it suffices to consider two reduced expressions differing by the reversal of a pair of simple reflections, but it is easy to see (cf.
[
Rie08
]
, proof of Prop. 7.2) that
y^{\vee}_{i}(a)y^{\vee}_{j}(a^{\prime})=y^{\vee}_{j}(a^{\prime})y^{\vee}_{i}(a)
if
s_{i}s_{j}=s_{j}s_{i}
. Hence, we will temporarily consider some
fixed
reduced expression
w^{P}=s_{r_{\ell}}\cdots s_{r_{1}}
to avoid confusion, even though the choice is immaterial. However, in Section
2.3
, we will introduce a more convenient and combinatorial notation for these toric coordinates
\{a_{i}\}_{i\in{\ell}}
, which allows us to refer to specific coordinates without the need of a fixed reduced expression for
w^{P}
.

In addition to the minimal coset representative
w^{P}\in W^{P}
of
w_{0}W_{P}
for
w_{0}\in W
the longest element, we will also need the minimal coset representative
w^{\prime\prime}\in W^{P}
of
w_{P}s_{k}W_{P}
for
w_{P}\in W_{P}
the longest element. Together, these two elements define
w^{\prime}=w^{P}(w^{\prime\prime})^{-1}\in W
of length
{\ell^{\prime}}
; denote by
\mathcal{I}=\{(i_{j})_{j\in[{\ell^{\prime}}]}~|~s_{r_{i_{{\ell^{\prime}}}}}\cdots s_{r_{i_{1}}}=w^{\prime}\}
the set of subexpressions for
w^{\prime}
inside the
fixed
reduced expression for
w^{P}
. (Note that we do
not
fix a reduced expression for
w^{\prime}
.) Then we have the following result:

Theorem 2.10

(
[
Spa21
]
, Thm 5.7)
.

For cominuscule
X=G/P_{k}
and with the notation above, the restriction
\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\circ}_{P}}
of
\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}}
to
\mathcal{Z}^{\circ}_{P}
is given in terms of toric coordinates as

\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\circ}_{P}}(z)=\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{i\in[\ell]}\displaystyle a_{i}\Bigr)+q\frac{\sum_{(i_{j})\in\mathcal{I}}\prod_{j\in[{\ell^{\prime}}]}a_{i_{j}}}{\prod_{i\in[\ell]}a_{i}},\quad\text{where}\quad z=u_{+}t\bar{w}_{P}u_{-}

with
u_{-}=y^{\vee}_{r_{1}}(a_{1})\cdots y^{\vee}_{r_{\ell}}(a_{\ell})\in U^{\circ}_{-}
and
q=\alpha^{\vee}_{k}(t)\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
.

Remark 2.11
.

Although not necessary for this theorem, we prove in Lemma
6.1
that
w^{\prime}=w^{P}(w^{\prime\prime})^{-1}\in W
is a minimal coset representative; see Section 9 of the arXiv version of
[
Spa21
]
for expressions for
w^{\prime}
in all cases.

Analogously to Section
2.2.1
, we will simplify considerations by pulling back the superpotential to
U_{-}^{P}
, where the restriction to the torus
U^{\circ}_{-}\subset U_{-}^{P}
gives us a Laurent polynomial potential, namely:

Corollary 2.12
.

For
X=G/P_{k}
cominuscule, and any fixed
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
, the superpotential
\mathcal{W}_{U_{-}^{P}}
restricts on the dense algebraic torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
to

\mathcal{W}_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{i\in[\ell]}\displaystyle a_{i}\Bigr)+q\frac{\sum_{(i_{j})\in\mathcal{I}}\prod_{j\in[{\ell^{\prime}}]}a_{i_{j}}}{\prod_{i\in[\ell]}a_{i}},

where
u_{-}=y^{\vee}_{r_{1}}(a_{1})\cdots y^{\vee}_{r_{\ell}}(a_{\ell})\in U^{\circ}_{-}
and
\mathcal{I}
is defined above.

Just like in Section
2.2.1
, note that we do not think of
\mathcal{W}_{U^{\circ}_{-}}
as a morphism
U^{\circ}_{-}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}\to\mathbb{C}
but rather as a
\mathbb{C}^{*}
-family of morphisms
U^{\circ}_{-}\to\mathbb{C}
.

In Corollary 8.12 of
[
Spa21
]
, a combinatorial method is described to obtain the elements of
\mathcal{I}
using a specific quiver defined in
[
CMP08
]
; it turns out that these combinatorics are equivalent to the well-known combinatorics of
minuscule posets
, so we will take some time to introduce these and present the above results in this language.

2.3.
Minuscule posets and local toric expressions

As we have alluded to previously, minuscule posets will provide a very effective combinatorial tool for our models, both for describing toric expressions, as well as for formulating the Plücker coordinate superpotential. Hence, we will spend some time introducing them in this section. We start with the basic order-theoretic definitions and results in Section
2.3.1
, and then use them in Section
2.3.2
to rephrase the Laurent polynomial LG-model in terms of embeddings of order ideals in minuscule posets. Finally, we use these embeddings to describe toric expressions of Plücker coordinates and generalized minors in
2.3.3

2.3.1.
The combinatorics of minuscule posets

It might seem that fixing a specific reduced expression for the minimal coset representative
w^{P}\in W^{P}
of the longest element
w_{0}\in W
is unnatural; indeed, by
[
Ste96
]
all reduced expressions can be obtained from a given one by commuting simple reflections, and the algebraic torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
does not change under such modifications. Using the combinatorics of minuscule posets will allow us to let go of this fixed expression. Hence, we will introduce the relevant order-theoretic concepts here.

Firstly, recall that an
order ideal
(or
lower set
) is a subset
\mathsf{I}
of a poset (i.e. partially ordered set)
\mathsf{P}
such that any element
x\in\mathsf{P}
such that
x\leq y
for some
y\in\mathsf{I}
satisfies
x\in\mathsf{I}
. The order ideal generated by a subset
S\subset\mathsf{P}
is all
x\in\mathsf{P}
such that
x\leq s
for some
s\in S
. We will write this as
\mathsf{I}(S)
. The
join

x\vee y\in\mathsf{P}
of
x,y\in\mathsf{P}
(if it exists) is the least upper bound of
x
and
y
in
\mathsf{P}
; equivalently, it is the minimal element
x\vee y\in\mathsf{P}
such that the order ideal generated by it contains the union of the ideals generated by
x
and by
y
. An element of
\mathsf{P}
is called
join-irreducible
if it
cannot
be written as the join of two other elements of
\mathsf{P}
. Dually, the
meet

x\wedge y\in\mathsf{P}
of
x,y\in\mathsf{P}
(if it exists) is the greatest lower bound of
x
and
y
in
\mathsf{P}
; equivalently, it is the largest element such that the ideal generated by it is contained in the intersection of the ideals generated by
x
and by
y
. If every pair of elements of a (finite) poset
\mathsf{P}
has both a meet and join, then
\mathsf{P}
is called a
lattice
. Moreover, if in a lattice the meet and join
distribute
over each other (i.e.
x\wedge(y\vee z)=(x\wedge y)\vee(x\wedge z)
), then
\mathsf{P}
is called a
distributive lattice
.

Distributive lattices appear naturally in the context of minuscule representations: Equipping the weights of a minuscule representation with the partial order given by
\mu^{\vee}_{1}>\mu^{\vee}_{2}
if and only if
\mu^{\vee}_{1}-\mu^{\vee}_{2}
is a positive linear combination of simple roots, we have the following result:

Theorem 2.13

(
[
Pro84
]
, Proposition 3 and Theorem 4)
.

The poset of weights of the minuscule representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})
is isomorphic to the set
W^{P}
with the (left) Bruhat order under the bijection
w\mapsto w(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}})
. Moreover, this poset forms a finite distributive lattice.

Recall that the (left) Bruhat order on
W^{P}
(or on
W
) is the transitive closure of the covering relation
w\gtrdot w^{\prime}
if
w=s_{i}w^{\prime}
with
\ell(w)=\ell(w^{\prime})+1
. Because of the previous result, we will also refer to the order on the weights of the minuscule representation as the Bruhat order. The structure of finite distributive lattices is in turn determined by their join-irreducible elements:

Theorem 2.14

(
[
Bir37
]
, Section 9)
.

Let
\mathsf{L}
be a finite distributive lattice and
\mathsf{P}
the induced subposet of join-irreducible elements, then
\mathsf{L}
is isomorphic to the poset of order ideals of
\mathsf{P}
ordered by inclusion.

It is easy to see when a weight for a finite-dimensional representation is join-irreducible: when there is exactly one simple reflection lowering the weight. Hence, each element of the poset of join-irreducible weights (i.e. each box of the skew Young diagram) corresponds to a simple reflection—the one that lowers that weight. Because of this, we will label the boxes of the minuscule poset by the simple reflection
s_{i}
lowering that join-irreducible weight; we write
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b})=s_{i}
if the box
\mathsf{b}
has label
s_{i}
. Note that with this labeling, the minuscule poset in fact coincides with the
heap
associated to
w^{P}\in W^{P}
as defined in
[
Ste96
]
, and hence every order ideal coincides with the heap of the corresponding minimal coset representative. As both combinatorial objects are equivalent, we will favor order ideals of the minuscule poset over heaps of minimal coset representatives in this paper.

Sometimes we will need the index of the simple reflection labeling a given element of the minuscule poset instead of the reflection itself; in these cases we will write
\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=i
for the index corresponding to the simple reflection
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b})=s_{i}
.

The two theorems above tell us that we can describe all weights of a minuscule representation by order ideals of the poset of join-irreducible weights; such a poset is called a
minuscule poset
. Minuscule posets simplify notation greatly as they can be drawn two-dimensionally: every element covers at most two elements and is covered by at most two elements. These posets are therefore usually drawn as skew Young diagrams with the top-left box representing the minimal element and a box drawn to the right or below a given box indicating that the given box is covered by the other. (Note that there exists a unique minimal element as there exists a unique weight covering the lowest weight in a fundamental weight representation, hence in particular in a minuscule representation.)

We will write
\mathsf{w}^{P}
for the minuscule poset obtained from the fundamental representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})
of
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
, where
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=\widetilde{P}^{\vee}_{k}\backslash\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
is minuscule. (We suppress the “
∨
” since this data is ultimately fixed by
P=P_{k}\subset G
defining
X
.) We write
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
if a subposet
\mathsf{w}\subset\mathsf{w}^{P}
is an order ideal, and write
\ell(\mathsf{w})
for the number of boxes (i.e. elements) in the poset
\mathsf{w}
. We hence obtain two ways to refer to the weights of the minuscule representation: by order ideals
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
of the associated minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}
, and by minimal coset representatives
w\in W^{P}
. Note that these are compatible in the sense that adding a box labeled
s_{i}
to a given order ideal
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
corresponds to multiplying the corresponding word
w\in W^{P}
by the simple reflection
s_{i}
on the left. We see from this directly that a
linear extension
of
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
(i.e. completing the partial order to a total order) gives a
reduced expression
of
w\in W^{P}
. In particular, the number of boxes in the order ideal equals the length of the corresponding word, i.e.
\ell(\mathsf{w})=\ell(w)
.

Remark 2.15
.

In fact, the correspondence between ideals of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
and minimal coset representatives in
W^{P}
giving the same weight vector can be made direct: Given an ideal
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
, choose a linear extension of the partial order and let
w\in W^{P}
be formed by multiplying the labels
s_{i}
of the elements of
\mathsf{w}
with the greatest element on the left and decreasing to the right; which we will denote as

\Pi(\mathsf{w})=\prod_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}}\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b})\in W^{P}.

Conversely, given a minimal coset representative
w\in W^{P}
, take a reduced expression
w=s_{i_{1}}\cdots s_{i_{r}}
, and let
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
be the poset with elements labeled by
s_{i_{j}}
and with partial order the transitive closure of the covering relations
s_{i_{j}}\gtrdot s_{i_{j^{\prime}}}
if
j<j^{\prime}
,
(s_{i_{j}}s_{i_{j^{\prime}}})^{2}\neq e
and
\forall j^{\prime\prime}
with
j<j^{\prime\prime}<j^{\prime}
,
s_{i_{j^{\prime\prime}}}
is distinct from and commutes with
s_{i_{j}}
and
s_{i_{j^{\prime}}}
. (Compare the quiver defined in Definition 2.1 of
[
CMP08
]
.) Due to the full-commutativity of elements of
W^{P}
, these maps are independent of the choice of linear extension of the partial order and the reduced expression.

In particular, we defined the minimal coset representative
w^{\prime\prime}
for the coset
w_{P}s_{k}W_{P}
. The corresponding order ideal
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}
is the maximal order ideal of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
containing exactly one occurrence of
s_{k}
. We will show in Corollary
6.3
that
w^{\prime}=w^{P}(w^{\prime\prime})^{-1}
is also a minimal coset representative. Its corresponding order ideal
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}
will be isomorphic (respecting the labeling) to the complement of
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}
in
\mathsf{w}^{P}
.

Example 2.16
.

We will illustrate the correspondence between weights of the minuscule representation and order ideals of the minuscule poset by considering the example of the maximal orthogonal Grassmannian
\mathrm{OG}(5,10)=\mathrm{Spin}(10)/P_{5}=D_{5}^{\mathrm{sc}}/P_{5}
, as discussed in Section 4 of
[
SW24
]
(note the shift in
n
used there).

First, consider the weights of the representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{4}})
of the universal cover
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}=\mathrm{Spin}(10)
of
G^{\vee}=\mathrm{PSO}(10)
, which is the
spin representation
: We have drawn the Hasse diagram of the poset of weights of
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{4}})
with respect to the Bruhat order below. Here the highest weight,
{\varpi^{\vee}_{4}}
, is drawn on the left whereas the lowest weight,
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{5}}
, is drawn on the right; the Bruhat covering relations
s_{i}w(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{5}})\gtrdot w(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{5}})
are denoted by edges labeled
i
.

The weights that are join-irreducible with respect to the Bruhat order are denoted by black vertices; each of these corresponds to a box in the minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}
drawn to the right of the Hasse diagram and is labeled with the
s_{i}
that decreases the weight (we have written
i
instead of
s_{i}
in the poset). Note that the minuscule poset is drawn with the smallest element top-left. The correspondence between order ideals of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
and weights of the representation is indicated in the figure as well (note that the minimal element is drawn top-left).

Finally, we illustrate the direct correspondence between ideals and minimal coset representatives: Consider the ideal
\raisebox{0.5pt}{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}\vartriangleleft\raisebox{-2.25pt}{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}
which has partial order
\mathsf{b}_{s_{2}},\mathsf{b}_{s_{4}}>\mathsf{b}_{s_{3}}>\mathsf{b}_{s_{5}}
. (Here we write
\mathsf{b}_{s_{i}}
for a box satisfying
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b}_{s_{i}})=s_{i}
.) It has two linear extensions
\mathsf{b}_{s_{2}}>\mathsf{b}_{s_{4}}>\mathsf{b}_{s_{3}}>\mathsf{b}_{s_{5}}
and
\mathsf{b}_{s_{4}}>\mathsf{b}_{s_{2}}>\mathsf{b}_{s_{3}}>\mathsf{b}_{s_{5}}
both giving the same Weyl element
s_{2}s_{4}s_{3}s_{5}=s_{4}s_{2}s_{3}s_{5}\in W^{P}
since the simple reflections
s_{2}
and
s_{4}
commute in type
D_{5}
. Conversely, considering the element
s_{2}s_{4}s_{3}s_{5}=s_{4}s_{2}s_{3}s_{5}\in W^{P}
, we get the partial order
\mathsf{b}_{s_{2}},\mathsf{b}_{s_{4}}>\mathsf{b}_{s_{3}}>\mathsf{b}_{s_{5}}
from either reduced expression, i.e. the poset
\raisebox{0.5pt}{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}\vartriangleleft\raisebox{-2.25pt}{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}
.

\lozenge

The correspondence between elements of
W^{P}
and order ideals of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
gives us a second way of denoting the natural weight basis of
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})
:
\{v_{\mathsf{w}}~|~\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}\}
instead of
\{v_{w}~|~w\in W^{P}\}
. We will favor the notation using minimal coset representatives except in explicit examples where the order ideal notation is more convenient. As for the lowest weight vector of
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})
, we will favor the notation
v_{0}
over either
v_{\varnothing}
(where
\varnothing\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
) and
v_{e}
(where
e\in W^{P}
). This alternative notation also gives rise to a similar alternative for Plücker coordinates:

Definition 2.17

(Cf. Definition
2.8
)
.

The
Plücker coordinates

(p_{\mathsf{w}}~|~\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P})
on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
are defined by the maps

p_{\mathsf{w}}(g)=v_{0}^{*}(g\cdot v_{\mathsf{w}})\quad\text{for}\quad g\in\widetilde{G}^{\vee}

(which are also called
Plücker coordinates
by abuse of notation). Note that
p_{\mathsf{w}}=p_{w}
where
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
and
w\in W^{P}
correspond to each other under Remark
2.15
. We will frequently suppress the arguments of these coordinates if it is clear on which domain we consider them.

We will end the introduction to minuscule posets with an overview of all the possible posets:

Example 2.18
.

Comparing with Table
2.1
, we see that there are five infinite families of minuscule homogeneous spaces and two sporadic ones: one family each in types
A_{n}
(Grassmannians),
B_{n}
(maximal orthogonal Grassmannians in odd dimensions) and
C_{n}
(odd dimensional projective spaces); and two families in type
D_{n}
(even dimensional quadrics and maximal orthogonal Grassmannians in even dimensions;
k=n-1
and
k=n
give isomorphic families); as well as the minuscule varieties
E_{6}/P_{6}\cong E_{6}/P_{1}
and
E_{7}/P_{7}
. Below we have given characteristic examples of each of the corresponding minuscule posets along with the corresponding “rim-hook” order ideals
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}
corresponding to the minimal coset representative
w^{\prime\prime}
for
w_{P}s_{k}W_{P}
(red labels).

Extending these to the general case should be straightforward. Note that choosing
k=n-1
in type
D_{n}
simply switches the labels
n-1
and
n
along the main diagonal of the staircase partition, and that choosing
k=1
in type
E_{6}
yields the poset obtained by reversing the order (or diagramatically by rotating the poset
180^{\circ}
).

\lozenge

2.3.2.
Minuscule posets and the Laurent polynomial Landau-Ginzburg model

As Remark
2.15
indicated, the minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}
lets us deal with the simple reflections in the reduced expressions of
w^{P}
without fixing a specific one. In Section
2.2.4
we introduced the algebraic torus
U^{\circ}_{-}\subset U_{-}^{P}
and discussed how the toric coordinates do not depend on the fixed reduced expression of
w^{P}
, despite being associated to a specific simple reflection in one of the expressions. Combining these two observations, we can uniquely associate a toric coordinate to each box of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
; the easiest way to realize this is to (temporarily) fix a reduced expression for
w^{P}
to fix the decomposition of elements in the torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
as in equation (
2.8
) as well as a linear extension of the partial order on
\mathsf{w}^{P}
, and then associating the
i
th toric coordinate to the
i
th box of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
starting from the smallest element and going up. It should be clear from our earlier discussions that this association does not depend on the fixed reduced expression of
w^{P}
, and that the toric coordinate associated to a box labeled
s_{i}
is the argument of the one-parameter subgroup
y^{\vee}_{i}
for the
same
index
i\in[n]
, in other words we can decompose
u_{-}\in U^{\circ}_{-}
as

u_{-}=\prod_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}}y^{\vee}_{\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})}(a_{\mathsf{b}}),

(2.9)

with the factors ordered by increasing elements in
\mathsf{w}^{P}
from left to right, and where factors corresponding to incomparable elements can be ordered arbitrarily.

Associating a toric coordinate
a_{\mathsf{b}}
to each of the boxes
\mathsf{b}
of the minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}
will simplify notation greatly. First of all, given a subset
\mathsf{S}\subset\mathsf{w}^{P}
, we will write

a_{\mathsf{S}}=\textstyle\prod_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{S}}\displaystyle a_{\mathsf{b}}.

(2.10)

This will be particularly useful in combination with
embeddings
of subposets into
\mathsf{w}^{P}
; here, an embedding is a
label-preserving
, order-preserving morphism from one poset into another. In other words, an embedding
\iota:\mathsf{w}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}
maps every box
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}
with a given label to a box
\iota(\mathsf{b})\in\mathsf{w}^{P}
with
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b})=\mathrm{label}(\iota(\mathsf{b}))
such that
\iota(\mathsf{b})<\iota(\mathsf{b}^{\prime})
whenever
\mathsf{b}<\mathsf{b}^{\prime}
. Now, if
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
corresponds to some minimal coset representative
w\in W^{P}
, then an embedding
\iota:\mathsf{w}\to\mathsf{w}^{P}
corresponds to a realization of
w
as a subword of
w^{P}
for any fixed reduced expression of
w^{P}
, i.e. a subset of simple reflections in the expression for
w^{P}
forming a reduced expression for
w
. Hence, we find the following reformulation of the toric expression of
\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}}
restricted to
\mathcal{Z}^{\circ}_{P}
:

Theorem 2.19

(
[
Spa21
]
, Thm 5.7; pulled back to
U^{\circ}_{-}
and rephrased using minuscule posets)
.

For cominuscule
X=G/P_{k}
, the restriction
\mathcal{W}_{U^{\circ}_{-}}
of
\mathcal{W}_{U_{-}^{P}}
to
U^{\circ}_{-}
is given in terms of toric coordinates for any fixed
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
as

\mathcal{W}_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}}\displaystyle a_{\mathsf{b}}\Bigr)+q\frac{\sum_{\iota:\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}a_{\iota(\mathsf{w}^{\prime})}}{a_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}},

with
u_{-}\in U^{\circ}_{-}
decomposed as in (
2.9
). In this equation,
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
(cf. Remark
2.11
and Corollary
6.3
) is the order ideal corresponding to
w^{\prime}=w^{P}(w^{\prime\prime})^{-1}
for
w^{\prime\prime}\in W^{P}
the minimal coset representative of
w_{P}s_{k}W_{P}
, and the sum is over all embeddings
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}
.

The first sum over all toric coordinates can be split into
n
parts corresponding to the labels of the boxes the coordinates are associated to, as follows:

\mathcal{W}_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=\textstyle\sum_{i\in[n]}\displaystyle\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}:\,\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=i}\displaystyle a_{\mathsf{b}}\Bigr)+q\frac{\sum_{\iota:\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}a_{\iota(\mathsf{w}^{\prime})}}{a_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}}.

(2.11)

Looking at the proof of
[
Spa21
, Theorem 5.7]
in detail, we notice that each of the terms in (
2.11
) corresponds to one of the terms in the Lie-theoretic mirror model as follows (as phrased in Definition
2.6
):

\begin{split}(f^{\vee}_{i})^{*}(u_{-})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}&=\textstyle\sum_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}:~\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=i}\displaystyle a_{\mathsf{b}}\quad\text{for}\quad i\in[n],\\
(e^{\vee}_{k})^{*}(u_{+})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}&=q\frac{\sum_{\iota:\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}a_{\iota(\mathsf{w}^{\prime})}}{a_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}},\\
(e^{\vee}_{i})^{*}(u_{+})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}&=0\quad\text{for}\quad i\neq k,\end{split}

(2.12)

for any fixed
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
and with
u_{+}\in U^{\vee}_{+}
fixed by
u_{-}\in U_{-}^{P}
and
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
as in Corollary
2.5
.

2.3.3.
Local toric expressions for Plücker coordinates and generalized minors

We will show that the type-independent canonical mirror models are isomorphic to the Lie-theoretic ones by showing that the superpotentials
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
restrict to the same toric expression as in (
2.11
) on the torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
. For this, we need convenient descriptions of the Plücker coordinates and generalized minors on this torus as well. These will be provided by Algorithms 3.11 and 3.12 of
[
SW23
]
, which we briefly summarize and rephrase using order ideals of minuscule posets below. For the full details, see the corresponding statements in
[
SW23
]
.

We start with Algorithm 3.12 of
[
SW23
]
, as it is the simplest case, giving a procedure to obtain the toric expressions of
p_{w}(u_{-})
for
u_{-}=y^{\vee}_{r_{1}}(a_{1})\cdots y^{\vee}_{r_{\ell}}(a_{\ell})\in U^{\circ}_{-}
. It can be summarized as finding all subwords of the fixed reduced expression for
w^{P}=s_{r_{\ell}}\cdots s_{r_{1}}
forming reduced expressions for
w\in W^{P}
(not necessarily the same expression), and taking the corresponding toric coordinates. With the current notation in terms of ideals of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
and with (
2.10
) in mind, the result of the procedure can be given in closed form as

p_{\mathsf{w}}(u_{-})=\textstyle\sum_{\iota:\mathsf{w}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}\displaystyle a_{\iota(\mathsf{w})}\quad\text{for}\quad u_{-}=y^{\vee}_{r_{1}}(a_{1})\cdots y^{\vee}_{r_{\ell}}(a_{\ell})\in U^{\circ}_{-}.

(2.13)

Note that
p_{\mathsf{w}}
is a homogeneous polynomial of degree
\ell(\mathsf{w})
, i.e. the number of boxes in the ideal
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
. The reason for this simplification is that in a minuscule fundamental representation, all powers larger than
2
of Chevalley generators act trivially so in particular all nontrivial actions of Chevalley generators are equivalent to actions of simple reflections.

On the other hand, in non-minuscule fundamental representations, powers up to
4
of the Chevalley generators may act nontrivially, and consequently the actions of Chevalley generators are no longer necessarily equivalent to the actions of simple reflections. Furthermore, since
w^{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}\neq-{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}({i_{*}})}}
for
{i_{*}}\neq k
, it may occur that nontrivial generalized minors have trivial restrictions to
U^{\circ}_{-}
. Due to these difficulties, Algorithm 3.11 of
[
SW23
]
must be slightly more complicated than Algorithm 3.12. However, since we consider restrictions to
u_{-}\in U^{\circ}_{-}
, we can still use minuscule posets after enhancing them with positive integer weights. Enhancing order ideals with weights is straightforward:

Definition 2.20
.

A
weighted subset

(\mathsf{S},\mathrm{wt})\subset\mathsf{w}^{P}
is a subset
\mathsf{S}\subset\mathsf{w}^{P}
together with a map
\mathrm{wt}:\mathsf{S}\to\mathbb{N}
which we call its
weight
.

It is somewhat more complicated to generalize embeddings of order ideals in the minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}
to “weighted embeddings”; the rough idea is to replace each element
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}
with
\mathrm{wt}(\mathsf{b})
incomparable elements which behave exactly the same with respect to the ordering as
\mathsf{b}
:

Definition 2.21
.

Given a weighted order ideal
(\mathsf{w},\mathrm{wt})
, define the poset
\mathrm{wt}\cdot\mathsf{w}
by taking
\mathrm{wt}(\mathsf{b})
copies
\mathsf{b}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{b}_{\mathrm{wt}(\mathsf{b})}
of every element
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}
with order relations
\mathsf{b}_{i}<\mathsf{b}_{j}^{\prime}
when
\mathsf{b}<\mathsf{b}^{\prime}
. (In particular, all copies
\mathsf{b}_{i}
are incomparable.) A
weighted embedding

\iota:(\mathsf{w},\mathrm{wt})\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}
is a labeled, order morphism
\iota:\mathrm{wt}\cdot\mathsf{w}\to\mathsf{w}^{P}
. The image is a subset
\iota(\mathsf{w})\subset\mathsf{w}^{P}
which we give the weight
\mathrm{wt}(\mathsf{b})=|\iota^{-1}(\mathsf{b})|
for every
\mathsf{b}\in\iota(\mathsf{w})
.

For a generalized minor
\Delta_{w_{1}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},w_{2}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}(u_{-})
with
u_{-}\in U^{\circ}_{-}
, Algorithm 3.11 can be summarized as taking the toric polynomial corresponding to all
weighted
subwords
(\underline{s},\mathrm{wt})
, i.e. non-reduced subwords
\underline{s}=(s_{r_{j_{1}}},\ldots,s_{r_{j_{m}}})
of the fixed reduced expression for
w^{P}
with a positive integer
c_{j_{i}}=\mathrm{wt}(s_{r_{j_{i}}})
, such that
(f^{\vee}_{r_{j_{1}}})^{c_{j_{1}}}\cdots(f^{\vee}_{r_{j_{m}}})^{c_{j_{m}}}\bar{w}_{2}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}=\bar{w}_{1}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}
. For our generalized minors
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
in particular, since
w^{P}(w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}})=w_{0}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}
, we are guaranteed to have nontrivial restrictions to
U^{\circ}_{-}
, and we are able to use weighted order ideals and embeddings to express these restrictions. It is clear how to associate a weighted subset
(\mathsf{S},\mathrm{wt})\subset\mathsf{w}^{P}
to a given weighted subword of
w^{P}
: let
\mathsf{S}
be the set of elements that correspond to simple reflections with non-zero weights, and let
\mathrm{wt}:\mathsf{S}\to\mathbb{N}
be the corresponding weight.

The result of Algorithm 3.11 can be given in closed form for the generalized minors
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
with
{i_{*}}\in[n]
as:

\phi_{{i_{*}}}(u_{-})=\sum_{(\mathsf{w},\mathrm{wt})}\left(\sum_{\iota:(\mathsf{w},\mathrm{wt})\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}a_{\iota(\mathsf{w})}^{\mathrm{wt}}\right),

where we generalized (
2.10
) to weighted subsets
(\mathsf{S},\mathrm{wt})\subset\mathsf{w}^{P}
as

a_{\mathsf{S}}^{\mathrm{wt}}=\prod_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{S}}a_{\mathsf{b}}^{\mathrm{wt}(\mathsf{b})}

(2.14)

and where the first sum over
(\mathsf{w},\mathrm{wt})
is over all weighted order ideals
(\mathsf{w},\mathrm{wt})
corresponding to weighted subwords
(w,\mathrm{wt})
of
w^{P}
satisfying the condition

(f^{\vee}_{r_{j_{1}}})^{c_{j_{1}}}\cdots(f^{\vee}_{r_{j_{m}}})^{c_{j_{m}}}\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}=v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{-}.

Finding such weighted order ideal is the most complicated part of the algorithm, and in Section
3
we will determine the
unique
weighted order ideal satisfying this condition for each
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
type-independently.

Remark 2.22
.

In the above discussion we ignored the sign from the definition of
\phi_{{i_{*}}}(u_{-})
for
u_{-}\in U^{\circ}_{-}
as
(-1)^{h}\Delta_{w_{0}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}(u_{-}^{-1})
since taking the inverse of
u_{-}
introduces minus signs to each of the arguments of the one-parameter subgroups
y^{\vee}_{i}
: in fact, the sign
(-1)^{h}
will exactly cancel out the minus sign arising from this inversion. In Section
3
, we will show this explicitly; see Remark
3.11
.

Finally, since we have rephrased all other results in terms of (weighted) order ideals of the minuscule poset, we will rephrase Proposition
2.9
using these order ideals as well. For this, we only need the observation that a minimal coset representative
w\in W^{P}
sends
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
to
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}+\alpha^{\vee}
for
\alpha^{\vee}\in\Pi^{\vee}_{w^{P}}
if and only if the simple reflection
s_{k}
appears
exactly once
in its reduced expression, so that the corresponding order ideal
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
will have
exactly one
box with label
s_{k}
. The largest such minimal coset representative is
w^{\prime\prime}\in W^{P}
the representative of
w_{P}s_{k}W_{P}
and every other such representative is a subword of
w^{\prime\prime}
. In other words, all order ideals corresponding to such subwords are order ideals of
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}
, and we conclude that:

Proposition 2.23

(
[
GLS11
]
, Prop. 8.5 &
[
SW23
]
, Lem. 3.5)
.

The coordinate ring of the affine variety
U_{-}^{P}
is given by

\mathbb{C}[U_{-}^{P}]=\mathbb{C}\bigl[p_{\mathsf{w}}~\big|~\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}\bigr]\bigl[\phi_{j}^{-1}~\big|~j\in[n]\bigr]

where we recall that
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
corresponds to the minimal coset representative
w^{\prime\prime}\in W^{P}
of
w_{P}s_{k}W_{P}
and therefore is the maximal order ideal containing
exactly
one box labeled
s_{k}
, and where

\phi_{j}(u_{-})=(-1)^{h}\Delta_{w_{0}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}},w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}}(u_{-}^{-1})=(-1)^{h}\Bigl\langle u_{-}^{-1}\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}}^{+},~v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}}^{-}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}}

is a generalized minor as defined in
[
FZ99
]
.

3.
Calculating toric expressions for the generalized minors

Recall from Section
2.2.3
that

\phi_{{i_{*}}}(u_{-})=(-1)^{h}\Delta_{w_{0}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}),w_{P}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}})}(u_{-}^{-1})=(-1)^{h}\Bigl\langle u_{-}^{-1}\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+},v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{-}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}.

Let us first consider the case
{i_{*}}=k
, so that
\bar{w}_{P}
acts trivially on the highest weight vector while
\bar{w}^{P}
maps the highest to the lowest weight vector, so that we find using (
2.6
) that

(-1)^{h}\phi_{k}(u_{-})=\Bigl\langle u_{-}^{-1}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}^{+},v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}^{-}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}=\Bigl\langle(\bar{w}^{P})^{T}u_{-}^{-1}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}^{+},v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}^{+}\Bigr\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}=\bigl\langle(\bar{w}^{P})^{T}u_{-}^{T}\cdot v_{0},v_{0}\bigr\rangle,

with the last minor taken in the Plücker representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(k)}})
. Now, using the dual action, we find that

(-1)^{h}\phi_{k}(u_{-})=\bigl\langle v_{0},u_{-}\bar{w}^{P}\cdot v_{0}\bigr\rangle=(-1)^{\ell}\bigl\langle v_{0},u_{-}\cdot v_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}\bigr\rangle=(-1)^{\ell}\bigl\langle u_{-}\cdot v_{\mathsf{w}^{P}},v_{0}\bigr\rangle=(-1)^{\ell}p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}(u_{-}),

where we used (
2.2
) in the second equation. However, since the Plücker representation is minuscule, we know that the height
h
as defined in (
2.7
) equals
\ell=\ell(w^{P})
since every simple reflection of
w^{P}\in W^{P}
acts as subtraction of a single simple root (cf. Lemma
2.7
), so we conclude that

\phi_{k}(u_{-})=p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}(u_{-})

(3.1)

on all of
U_{-}^{P}
. Next, in the case
{i_{*}}=0
, we have

\phi_{0}(u_{-})=\Delta_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}},{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}(u_{-}^{-1})=\langle\!\langle u_{-}^{-1}v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}^{+},v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}^{+}\rangle\!\rangle_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}=1,

where the final equality follows by noting that
u_{-}^{-1}=y^{\vee}_{r_{\ell}}(-a_{\ell})\cdots y^{\vee}_{r_{1}}(-a_{1})
acts on
v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}}^{+}
by strictly lowering the weight (with a nontrivial polynomial in
a_{i}
as coefficient) or leaving it unchanged (with coefficient
1
). Since
p_{\varnothing}(u_{-})=v_{0}^{*}(u_{-}v_{0})=1
holds similarly (recall that
v_{\varnothing}=v_{0}
), we obtain the equality

\phi_{0}(u_{-})=p_{\varnothing}(u_{-})

(3.2)

on all of
U_{-}^{P}
.

For the remainder of this section, we fix
{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}
and let
u_{-}\in U^{\circ}_{-}
. Our goal is to express
\phi_{{i_{*}}}(u_{-})
as a polynomial in the toric coordinates of
U^{\circ}_{-}
as defined in equation (
2.8
). To find these expressions, we will need to consider the various fundamental representations of
\widetilde{G}^{\vee}
. However, we will manage to avoid most of the type-dependent representation theory by focusing on the actions of the Weyl groups on the weight spaces.

Considering
U^{\circ}_{-}\subset U^{\vee}_{-}
inside the completed universal enveloping algebra
\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{-}
of
U^{\vee}_{-}
and thus the series expansions

y^{\vee}_{r_{j}}(a_{j})=\exp(af^{\vee}_{r_{j}})=1+a_{j}f^{\vee}_{r_{j}}+a_{j}^{2}f^{\vee}_{r_{j}}+\dots

for each factor
y^{\vee}_{r_{j}}(a_{j})
of
u_{-}
, we will need to find the coefficients in
u_{-}^{-1}
of all terms
f^{\vee}_{i_{1}}\cdots f^{\vee}_{i_{j}}
that map
\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}
to
\bar{w}_{0}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}
. In other words, we can compute the
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
combinatorially using strictly decreasing paths in the Hasse diagram of weights of the representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}})
with the Bruhat order. Fortunately, we have the following result:

Proposition 3.1

(Corollary of
[
FZ99
, Thm 1.10]
)
.

The restrictions
\phi_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}
of the generalized minors
\phi_{i}(u_{-})=(-1)^{h}\Delta_{w_{P}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}),w_{0}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}})}(u_{-}^{-1})
to
U^{\circ}_{-}
are monomials in the toric coordinates.

In particular, exactly one term in the expansion of
u_{-}^{-1}
will contribute a nonzero term to the toric expression of
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
, as we now explain. By definition, if
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i}\rangle\!\rangle=c
with
\mu^{\vee}
extremal, then we have that
y^{\vee}_{i}(a)
acts on a weight vector
v_{\mu^{\vee}}
of weight
\mu^{\vee}
as

\displaystyle y^{\vee}_{i}(a)\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}}

\displaystyle=v_{\mu^{\vee}}+af^{\vee}_{i}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}}+\ldots+\tfrac{1}{(c-1)!}a^{c-1}(f^{\vee}_{i})^{c-1}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}}+\tfrac{1}{c!}a^{c}(f^{\vee}_{i})^{c}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}}

\displaystyle=v_{\mu^{\vee}}+af^{\vee}_{i}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}}+\ldots+\tfrac{1}{(c-1)!}a^{c-1}(f^{\vee}_{i})^{c-1}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}}+a^{c}\,\bar{s}_{i}\cdot v_{\mu^{\vee}},

(3.3)

cf. equation (
2.1
). Applying this to
u_{-}^{-1}=y^{\vee}_{r_{\ell}}(-a_{\ell})\cdots y^{\vee}_{r_{1}}(-a_{1})
acting on the extremal weight vector
\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}
and noting that
w^{P}=s_{r_{\ell}}\cdots s_{r_{1}}
, we expand the action as

u_{-}^{-1}(\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+})=\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}+\ldots+(\text{constant})\,\bar{w}^{P}\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+},

(3.4)

for some constant depending on the toric coordinates. On the other hand, since
w_{0}=w^{P}w_{P}
, we know that
\bar{w}^{P}
sends
\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}
to

\bar{w}^{P}\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}=\bar{w}_{0}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}=v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{-},

the lowest weight vector. Thus, Proposition
3.1
tells us that only the final term of (
3.4
) can contribute to the torus expansion of
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
. In particular, we only need to determine the constant in front of it, but by equation (
3.3
) applied to
u_{-}^{-1}=y^{\vee}_{r_{\ell}}(-a_{\ell})\cdots y^{\vee}_{r_{1}}(-a_{1})
, this constant and hence
\phi_{i}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=(-1)^{h}\Delta_{w_{P}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}),w_{0}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}})}(u_{-}^{-1})
must be given by

\phi_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=(-1)^{h}\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}(-a_{j})^{\langle\!\langle s_{r_{j}}\cdots s_{r_{1}}w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},\alpha_{r_{j}}\rangle\!\rangle},

where we fixed a reduced expression
w^{P}=s_{r_{\ell}}\dots s_{r_{1}}
to label the toric coordinates.

Note however that the exponents of the toric coordinates above should not depend on this reduced expression but only on the position of their associated element in the minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}
. To find such a simplification, we recall that two commuting simple reflections
s_{i}
and
s_{j}
have corresponding Cartan integer
\langle\!\langle\alpha^{\vee}_{j},\alpha_{i}\rangle\!\rangle=0
so in particular

\langle\!\langle s_{i}s_{j}\cdot\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle s_{i}\cdot\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i}\rangle\!\rangle-\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{j}\rangle\!\rangle\langle\!\langle\alpha^{\vee}_{j},\alpha_{i}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle s_{i}\cdot\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i}\rangle\!\rangle.

Applying this repeatedly to the product
s_{r_{j}}\cdots s_{r_{1}}
, we see that only those simple reflections (from the right to the left) that do not commute with their preceding simple reflections (i.e. those to the left) will influence the result of the coefficient
\langle\!\langle s_{r_{j}}\cdots s_{r_{1}}w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},\alpha_{r_{j}}\rangle\!\rangle
. However, these simple reflections are exactly the ones corresponding to the elements of the order ideal
\mathsf{I}(\mathsf{b})\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
with
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}
corresponding to
s_{r_{j}}
. (In particular,
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b}_{r_{j}})=s_{r_{j}}
and
\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=r_{j}
.)

Now, recalling from Remark
2.15
that
\Pi(\mathsf{w})=\prod_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}}\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b})\in W^{P}
as the increasing (from right to left) ordered product of the labels (i.e. simple reflections) of elements in the order ideal
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
equals the minimal coset representative corresponding to the ideal, the above discussion allows us to simplify the coefficient

\langle\!\langle s_{r_{j}}\cdots s_{r_{1}}w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},\alpha_{r_{j}}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle\Pi(\mathsf{I}(\mathsf{b}))\,w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},\alpha_{\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})}\rangle\!\rangle,

removing the need to take a reduced expression for
w^{P}
or a total order on
\mathsf{w}^{P}
. As a result, we can simplify the exponents of the toric coordinates and label the toric coordinates according to elements of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
in the expression for
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
as

\phi_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=(-1)^{h}\prod_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}}(-a_{\mathsf{b}})^{\langle\!\langle\Pi(\mathsf{I}(\mathsf{b}))\,w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},\alpha_{\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})}\rangle\!\rangle}.

Now, we observe that this expression is written as the product of toric coordinates taken to a certain power, which we recall was how we defined the toric monomial associated to a
weighted
order ideal in (
2.14
). So, we can summarize this expression even further by setting

\mathrm{wt}:\begin{array}[]{c}\mathsf{w}^{P}\longrightarrow\{0\}\cup\mathbb{N}\\
\mathsf{b}\mapsto\langle\!\langle\Pi(\mathsf{I}(\mathsf{b}))\,w_{P}\cdot{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},\alpha_{\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})}\rangle\!\rangle\end{array}

and considering the weighted subset of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
given by the subset
\mathrm{wt}^{-1}(\mathbb{N})\subset\mathsf{w}^{P}
with weight function
\mathrm{wt}
, yielding:

\phi_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}(u_{-})=(-1)^{h}(-a)_{\mathrm{wt}^{-1}(\mathbb{N})}^{\mathrm{wt}},

(3.5)

using the notation defined in (
2.14
), applied to the toric coordinates
(-a_{\mathsf{b}}~|~\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P})
.

Hence, the calculation of the restriction of
\phi_{i}
to
U^{\circ}_{-}
reduces to determining the extremal path in the fundamental representation
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}})
taken by
\bar{w}^{P}
from the extremal weight vector
\bar{w}_{P}\cdot v_{{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}}^{+}
to the lowest weight vector, and determining how many times each simple reflection
\bar{s}_{r_{i}}
in
\bar{w}^{P}
acts as
f^{\vee}_{r_{i}}
. In order to do this, we will first study the actions of the Weyl group elements
w_{0,j}
, which were defined in Section
2.1
. Recall that for
j\in[n]
,
w_{0,j}
is the longest element of the parabolic Weyl subgroup
W_{j}=\langle s_{i}~|~i\neq j\rangle\subset W
and
\sigma_{j}:[n]\setminus\{j\}\to[n]\setminus\{j\}
is the corresponding (possibly trivial) Dynkin subdiagram involution defined by
w_{0,j}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{j}(i)}}
and extended by
\sigma_{j}(j)=j
to the full Dynkin diagram of
W
. Note that for
k\in[n]
such that
P=P_{k}
, we have
W_{k}=W_{P}
,
w_{0,k}=w_{P}
and
\sigma_{k}=\sigma_{P}
. We begin with a lemma regarding the action of these elements on the fundamental co-weights.

Lemma 3.2
.

Let
i\neq j\in[n]
. Then there is some positive constant
c
such that

w_{0,j}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{j}(i)}}+c{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}.

Proof.

Consider the subgroup
G^{\vee}_{j}\subset G^{\vee}
corresponding to the Dynkin diagram of
G^{\vee}
with the
j
th vertex removed. (More precisely, let
G^{\vee}_{j}\subset P^{\vee}_{j}
be the Levi subgroup of the parabolic subgroup corresponding to the
j
th vertex.) Write
{\pi^{\vee}_{i}}
for the fundamental weights of
G^{\vee}_{j}
considered as a group in its own right, then the inclusion
G^{\vee}_{j}\subset G^{\vee}
gives a natural projection
{\pi_{j}}
of weight lattices satisfying
{\pi_{j}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})={\pi^{\vee}_{i}}
and
{\pi_{j}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{j}})=0
. As
w_{0,j}\in W_{j}
is the longest element, it maps
{\pi^{\vee}_{i}}
to
-{\pi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{j}(i)}}
; pulling this back along
{\pi_{j}}
, we find that
w_{0,j}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{j}(i)}}+c{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}
for some
c
.

The coefficient of
{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}
is only affected by the actions of
s_{j}
or
s_{m}
which does not commute with
s_{j}
. Furthermore, the action of
s_{j}
decreases the coefficient of
{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}
while the action of
s_{m}
not commuting with
s_{j}
increases the coefficient of
{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}
. Since
w_{0,j}
doesn’t allow the action of
s_{j}
, then
c\geq 0
. If
c=0
, then
w_{0,j}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})
is the lowest weight of
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})
, meaning that
w_{0,j}W_{i}=w^{i}W_{i}
, where
w^{i}=w_{0}W_{i}
is the minimal coset representative of
w_{0}
in
W_{i}
. In particular, this implies that
w^{i}
has no occurrence of
s_{j}
, meaning that
s_{j}
acts trivially on
V({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})
. However, this would imply that the lie subalgebra of
\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}
generated by
f^{\vee}_{i},e^{\vee}_{i}
lies in the kernel of the lie algebra morphism
\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}\rightarrow\mathrm{End}(V({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}))
, contradicting the fact that
\mathfrak{g}^{\vee}
is a simple lie algebra.
∎

The constant
c
of Lemma
3.2
is particularly easy to find when either
i
or
j
corresponds to a minuscule weight of
G^{\vee}
.

Lemma 3.3
.

For
k^{\prime}
minuscule and
i\in[n]\setminus\{k^{\prime}\}
, we have:

\displaystyle w_{0,i}({\varpi^{\vee}_{k^{\prime}}})

\displaystyle=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{i}(k^{\prime})}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},

(3.6)

\displaystyle w_{0,k^{\prime}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}})

\displaystyle=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{k^{\prime}}(i)}}+c_{i}{\varpi^{\vee}_{k^{\prime}}},\quad\text{where}\quad c_{i}=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},\alpha_{0}\rangle\!\rangle.

(3.7)

Note that
c_{i}
is also the coefficient of the simple root
\alpha_{i}
in the highest root
\alpha_{0}
.

Proof.

Both equations are relatively easy consequences of Lemma
3.2
together with the observation that

\langle\!\langle-{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}+c{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},\alpha_{i}\rangle\!\rangle=c

for any
i\neq j
and the fact that
\sigma_{i}(j)\neq i
. Equation (
3.6
) follows from the well-known fact that in a minuscule fundamental weight representation all weights have
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i}\rangle\!\rangle\in\{-1,0,+1\}
. For equation (
3.7
), the observation above becomes:

c=\langle\!\langle-{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{k^{\prime}}(i)}}+c{\varpi^{\vee}_{k^{\prime}}},\alpha_{k^{\prime}}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle w_{0,k^{\prime}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i}}),\alpha_{k^{\prime}}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i}},w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\alpha_{k^{\prime}})\rangle\!\rangle.

(Recall that
w_{0,k^{\prime}}^{T}=w_{0,k^{\prime}}^{-1}=w_{0,k^{\prime}}
since it is the longest element of
W_{k^{\prime}}
.) Hence, the claim reduces to showing that
w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\alpha_{k^{\prime}})=\alpha_{0}
for
k^{\prime}
minuscule.

For this, we note that
k^{\prime}
minuscule means that the set
\Pi
of positive roots can be split into two disjoint parts: the set
\Pi_{k^{\prime}}=\{\sum_{i=0}^{n}d_{i}\alpha_{i}\in\Pi^{\vee}~|~d_{k^{\prime}}=0\}
and the set
\Pi^{k^{\prime}}=\{\sum_{i=0}^{n}d_{i}\alpha_{i}\in\Pi~|~d_{i}=1\}
. Note that these sets are equivalently characterized by
w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\Pi_{k^{\prime}})=-\Pi_{k^{\prime}}
and
w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\Pi^{k^{\prime}})=\Pi^{k^{\prime}}
. In particular,
w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\alpha_{k^{\prime}})\in\Pi^{k^{\prime}}
.

Now, suppose that
w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\alpha_{k^{\prime}})\neq\alpha_{0}
, then there must be a
j\neq k^{\prime}
such that
\alpha=w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\alpha_{k^{\prime}})+\alpha_{j}
is a root. Clearly,
\alpha\in\Pi^{k^{\prime}}
and hence
w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\alpha)
as well. On the other hand,
\alpha_{j}\in\Pi_{k^{\prime}}
, so that
w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\alpha_{j})=-\beta\in-\Pi_{k^{\prime}}
is a negative root with coefficient
0
in front of
\alpha_{k^{\prime}}
. Hence, we find that
\Pi\ni w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\alpha)=w_{0,k^{\prime}}\bigl(w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\alpha_{k^{\prime}})+\alpha_{j})=\alpha_{k^{\prime}}-\beta
, but this is a linear combination of simple roots with
both
positive and negative coefficients, which is impossible for a root. Hence,
w_{0,k^{\prime}}(\alpha_{k^{\prime}})=\alpha_{0}
.
∎

The following indices will be of particular interest for the calculation of
\phi_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}
:

i_{-1}={i_{*}},\quad i_{0}=k\quad\text{and}\quad i_{j}=\sigma_{i_{j-1}}(i_{j-2})\quad\text{for}\quad j\in\{1,\ldots,{c_{*}}+2\},

(3.8)

where
{c_{*}}=c_{i_{*}}=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},\alpha_{0}\rangle\!\rangle
denotes the coefficient of
\alpha_{i_{*}}
in
\alpha_{0}
.

Remark 3.4
.

Since we are assuming the existence of a minuscule coweight
{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
,
{c_{*}}
is at most
4
: namely
\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{4}},\alpha_{0}\rangle\!\rangle=4
for
G^{\vee}
of type
E_{7}
. For the classical Lie groups,
{c_{*}}
is at most
2
.

The Weyl group elements
w_{0,i_{j}}
satisfy the following relations:

Lemma 3.5
.

With the conventions above, the elements
w_{0,i_{j}}
satisfy the following relations:

\displaystyle w_{0,i_{0}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{-1}}})

\displaystyle=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{1}}}+{c_{*}}{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{0}}},\quad\text{where}\quad{c_{*}}=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}},\alpha_{0}\rangle\!\rangle

(3.9)

\displaystyle w_{0,i_{1}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{0}}})

\displaystyle=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{2}}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{1}}},

(3.10)

\displaystyle w_{0,i_{j}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{j-1}}})

\displaystyle=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{j+1}}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{j}}},\quad\text{for}\quad j\in\{2,\ldots,{c_{*}}\}

(3.11)

\displaystyle w_{0,i_{{c_{*}}+1}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{{c_{*}}}}})

\displaystyle=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{c_{i}+2}}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{{c_{*}}+1}}}.

(3.12)

Proof.

Since
i_{0}=k
is minuscule, equation (
3.9
) is simply a restatement of equation (
3.7
), while (
3.10
) is a restatement of (
3.6
).

The remaining equations will be checked by type. For the reader’s convenience we recall the highest roots for the types allowing a minuscule fundamental weight:

\begin{array}[]{r|l}A_{n}&\alpha_{0}=\alpha_{1}+\ldots+\alpha_{n}\\
B_{n}&\alpha_{0}=\alpha_{1}+2\alpha_{2}+\ldots+2\alpha_{n}\\
C_{n}&\alpha_{0}=2\alpha_{1}+\ldots+2\alpha_{n-1}+\alpha_{n}\\
D_{n}&\alpha_{0}=\alpha_{1}+2\alpha_{2}+\ldots+2\alpha_{n-2}+\alpha_{n-1}+\alpha_{n}\\
E_{6}&\alpha_{0}=\alpha_{1}+2\alpha_{2}+2\alpha_{3}+3\alpha_{4}+2\alpha_{5}+\alpha_{6}\\
E_{7}&\alpha_{0}=2\alpha_{1}+2\alpha_{2}+3\alpha_{3}+4\alpha_{4}+3\alpha_{5}+2\alpha_{6}+\alpha_{7}\end{array}

In type
A_{n}
,
{c_{*}}=1
for all
{i_{*}}
, so every fundamental weight is minuscule. Hence, (
3.11
) is vacuous, and (
3.12
) follows from either of the equations of Lemma
3.3
.

In type
B_{n}
, only
{\varpi^{\vee}_{n}}
is minuscule, whereas
{c_{*}}=2
for every
{i_{*}}\neq n
. Hence, taking any
{i_{*}}\neq n
, we find that the sequence starting on
i_{-1}={i_{*}}
and
i_{0}=n
proceeds as:

i_{1}=\sigma_{n}({i_{*}})=n-{i_{*}},\quad i_{2}=\sigma_{n-{i_{*}}}(n)=n,\quad i_{3}=\sigma_{n}(n-{i_{*}})={i_{*}},\quad\text{and}\quad i_{4}=\sigma_{{i_{*}}}(n)=n.

Thus, we need to show that
w_{0,n}({\varpi^{\vee}_{n-{i_{*}}}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{n}}
and
w_{0,{i_{*}}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{n}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{n}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}
, but these follow from Lemma
3.3
since
n
is minuscule.

In type
C_{n}
,
{\varpi^{\vee}_{1}}
is minuscule, while
{c_{*}}=2
for all
i\neq 1
. Thus, let
{i_{*}}\neq 1
, then the sequence
i_{-1}={i_{*}}
,
i_{0}=1
proceeds as

i_{1}=\sigma_{1}({i_{*}})={i_{*}},\quad i_{2}=\sigma_{{i_{*}}}(1)={i_{*}}-1,\quad i_{3}=\sigma_{{i_{*}}-1}({i_{*}})={i_{*}},\quad\text{and}\quad i_{4}=\sigma_{{i_{*}}}({i_{*}}-1)=1.

Hence, we need to show that
w_{0,{i_{*}}-1}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}-1}}
and
w_{0,{i_{*}}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}-1}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{1}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}
. Now,
w_{0,{i_{*}}-1}\in W_{{i_{*}}-1}
is the longest element, and
W_{{i_{*}}-1}
is of type
A_{{i_{*}}-2}\times C_{n-{i_{*}}+1}
, so that
w_{0,{i_{*}}-1}
can be written as the product of the the longest words of these two subgroups. The longest word of the
A_{{i_{*}}-2}
-subgroup clearly acts trivially on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}
(since any
s_{i}
in this subgroup has
i<{i_{*}}
so
s_{i}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}})={\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}
) and we find
w_{0,{i_{*}}-1}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}})=s_{i_{*}}s_{{i_{*}}+1}\cdots s_{n}\cdots s_{{i_{*}}+1}s_{i_{*}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}})
which equals
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}-1}}
. To show that
w_{0,{i_{*}}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}-1}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{1}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}
, we note that
W_{{i_{*}}}
is of type
A_{{i_{*}}-1}\times C_{n-{i_{*}}}
, with the
C_{n-{i_{*}}}
-subgroup acting trivially on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}-1}}
, hence
w_{0,{i_{*}}}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}-1}})=s_{1}(s_{2}s_{1})\cdots(s_{{i_{*}}-1}\cdots s_{1})({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}-1}})=s_{1}\cdots s_{{i_{*}}-1}({\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}-1}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{1}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{{i_{*}}}}
.

In type
D_{n}
,
{\varpi^{\vee}_{1}}
,
{\varpi^{\vee}_{n-1}}
and
{\varpi^{\vee}_{n}}
are minuscule, while
{c_{*}}=2
for
{i_{*}}\neq\{1,n-1,n\}
. Hence, we will need to consider three cases depending on
k\in\{1,n-1,n\}
. First, we consider
k=1
. Let
{i_{*}}\notin\{1,n-1,n\}
, then the sequence
i_{-1}={i_{*}}
,
i_{0}=1
proceeds as

i_{1}=\sigma_{1}({i_{*}})={i_{*}},\quad i_{2}=\sigma_{{i_{*}}}(1)={i_{*}}-1,\quad i_{3}=\sigma_{{i_{*}}-1}({i_{*}})={i_{*}},\quad\text{and}\quad i_{4}=\sigma_{{i_{*}}}({i_{*}}-1)=1.

For these, one of the two subsequent indices is always minuscule, so the statements follow from Lemma
3.3
. Now, let
{i_{*}}\in\{n-1,n\}
, then the sequence
i_{-1}={i_{*}}
,
i_{0}=1
continues as
i_{1}\in\{n-1,n\}
(for
n-1
even,
i_{1}={i_{*}}
; for
n-1
odd,
i_{1}
is the other element of
\{n-1,n\}
) and
i_{2}=1
. Equation (
3.11
) is vacuous and (
3.12
) follows from Lemma
3.3
since all indices are minuscule.

Secondly, we should consider
k=n-1
, but this case is the same as
k=n
with all occurrences of
n-1
and
n
interchanged, so we will disregard it here.

Finally, we have the case
k=n
. Let
{i_{*}}\notin\{1,n-1,n\}
, then the sequence
i_{-1}={i_{*}}
,
i_{0}=n
proceeds as
i_{1}=\sigma_{n}({i_{*}})=n-{i_{*}}
,
i_{2}=\sigma_{n-{i_{*}}}(n)\in\{n-1,n\}
(depending on
n-{i_{*}}
odd or even, analogously to above),
i_{3}=\sigma_{i_{2}}(n-{i_{*}})={i_{*}}
and
i_{4}=\sigma_{{i_{*}}}(i_{2})=n
. Again, every second index is minuscule, so the equations follow from Lemma
3.7
. Now, let
{i_{*}}=1
, then
i_{-1}=1
,
i_{0}=n
give
i_{1}=\sigma_{n}(1)=n-1
,
i_{2}=\sigma_{n-1}(n)=1
,
i_{3}=\sigma_{1}(n-1)\in\{n-1,n\}
(depending on
n-1
even or odd); all indices are minuscule, so the equations follow from Lemma
3.3
(equation (
3.11
) being vacuous). Lastly, let
{i_{*}}=n-1
, then
i_{-1}=n-1
and
i_{0}=n
give
i_{1}=\sigma_{n}(n-1)=1
,
i_{2}=\sigma_{1}(n)\in\{n-1,n\}
(depending on
n-1
odd or even) and
i_{3}=\sigma_{i_{2}}(1)\in\{n-1,n\}
(depending on
n-1
even or odd). This case also has all indices minuscule, so the equations follow from Lemma
3.3
. This completes all the cases for type
D_{n}
.

Types
E_{6}
and
E_{7}
can be considered more concretely. In type
E_{6}
, both
1
and
6
are minuscule, but we can disregard
1
due to the isomorphism
E_{6}/P_{1}\cong E_{6}/P_{6}
. Thus, for
k=6
, then we have following sequences:

\begin{array}[]{c|c||c|c|c|c|c|c|c}{i_{*}}&{c_{*}}&\hskip-3.01385pti_{-1}&i_{0}&i_{1}&i_{2}&i_{3}&i_{4}&i_{5}\\
\hline\cr&&&&&&&\\
\hline\cr 1&1&1&6&1&6&1&&\\
\hline\cr 2&2&2&6&5&6&2&1&\\
3&2&3&6&3&2&5&1&\\
5&2&5&6&2&1&3&1&\\
\hline\cr 4&3&4&6&4&5&3&4&1\\
\end{array}

(3.13)

For
{i_{*}}=1
, all indices in the sequence are minuscule, while for
{i_{*}}=2
and
{i_{*}}=5
every second index is minuscule, so the statement follows from Lemma
3.3
in these cases. For
{i_{*}}=3
, we need to show that
w_{0,2}({\varpi^{\vee}_{3}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{5}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{2}}
and
w_{0,5}({\varpi^{\vee}_{2}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{1}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{5}}
. We note that
W_{2}
is of type
A_{5}
, and hence
w_{0,2}
acts on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{3}}
as
(s_{5}s_{4}s_{3}s_{1})(s_{6}s_{5}s_{4}s_{3})
; on the other hand
W_{5}
is of type
A_{4}\times A_{1}
, so
w_{0,5}
acts on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{2}}
as
s_{1}s_{3}s_{4}s_{2}
; in both cases it is easy to verify that the resulting weights are the ones listed above. For
{i_{*}}=4
, we need to show
w_{0,5}({\varpi^{\vee}_{4}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{3}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{5}}
,
w_{0,3}({\varpi^{\vee}_{5}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{4}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{3}}
and finally
w_{0,4}({\varpi^{\vee}_{3}})=-{\varpi^{\vee}_{1}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{4}}
. We have
W_{5}
of type
A_{4}\times A_{1}
, so
w_{0,5}({\varpi^{\vee}_{4}})=(s_{3}s_{4}s_{2})(s_{1}s_{3}s_{4})({\varpi^{\vee}_{4}})
;
W_{3}
is of type
A_{1}\times A_{4}
, so
w_{0,3}({\varpi^{\vee}_{5}})=(s_{4}s_{5}s_{6})(s_{2}s_{4}s_{5})({\varpi^{\vee}_{5}})
; and
W_{4}
is of type
A_{2}\times A_{1}\times A_{2}
, so
w_{0,4}({\varpi^{\vee}_{3}})=s_{1}s_{3}({\varpi^{\vee}_{3}})
. In all cases, the calculations are straightforward.

In type
E_{7}
only
7
is minuscule, so we set
k=7
and find the following sequences:

\begin{array}[]{c|c||c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c}{i_{*}}&{c_{*}}&\hskip-3.01385pti_{-1}&i_{0}&i_{1}&i_{2}&i_{3}&i_{4}&i_{5}&i_{6}\\
\hline\cr&&&&&&&\\
\hline\cr 1&2&1&7&6&7&1&7&&\\
2&2&2&7&2&1&2&7&&\\
6&2&6&7&1&7&6&7&&\\
\hline\cr 3&3&3&7&5&6&2&3&7&\\
5&3&5&7&3&2&6&5&7&\\
\hline\cr 4&4&4&7&4&5&3&5&4&7\end{array}

(3.14)

The sequences for
{i_{*}}=1
and
{i_{*}}=6
are covered by Lemma
3.3
. For the others, we note that the Weyl subgroups are of the following types:

\begin{array}[]{c|c|c|c|c|c|c}W_{1}&W_{2}&W_{3}&W_{4}&W_{5}&W_{6}&W_{7}\\
\hline\cr D_{6}&A_{6}&A_{1}\times A_{5}&A_{2}\times A_{1}\times A_{3}&A_{4}\times A_{2}&D_{5}\times A_{1}&E_{6}\end{array}

Hence, for
{i_{*}}=2
, we have that
w_{0,1}
acts on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{2}}
as
s_{2}(s_{7}s_{6}s_{5}s_{4})s_{3}(s_{6}s_{5}s_{4})s_{2}(s_{5}s_{4})s_{3}(s_{4})s_{2}
, yielding

on

w_{0,6}

, yielding

(s_{3}s_{4}s_{5}s_{6}s_{7})(s_{1}s_{3}s_{4}s_{5}s_{6})
, yielding
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{3}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{2}}
; finally,
w_{0,3}
acts on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{2}}
as
s_{7}s_{6}s_{5}s_{4}s_{2}
, yielding
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{7}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{3}}
. For
{i_{*}}=5
, we find that
w_{0,2}
acts on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{3}}
as
(s_{6}s_{5}s_{4}s_{3}s_{1})(s_{7}s_{6}s_{5}s_{4}s_{3})
, yielding
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{6}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{2}}

w_{0,6}
acts on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{2}}
as
s_{5}(s_{1}s_{3}s_{4})s_{2}(s_{3}s_{4})s_{5}(s_{4})s_{2}
, yielding
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{5}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{6}}
; finally,
w_{0,5}
acts on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{6}}
as
s_{7}s_{6}
, yielding
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{7}}+{\varpi^{\vee}_{6}}
. For the last sequence, starting with
{i_{*}}=4
, we find that
w_{0,5}
acts on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{4}}
as
(s_{3}s_{4}s_{2})(s_{1}s_{3}s_{4})
, yielding
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{3}}+2{\varpi^{\vee}_{5}}
;
w_{0,3}

{\varpi^{\vee}_{5}}

(s_{5}s_{6}s_{7})(s_{4}s_{5}s_{6})(s_{2}s_{4}s_{5})
, yielding

acts on

, yielding

; finally,
w_{0,4}
acts on
{\varpi^{\vee}_{5}}
