\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathsf{C}\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}}(-1)^{d_{\mathsf{C}}}\sum_{j=0}^{|S_{\mathsf{C}}|}(-1)^{j}\binom{|S_{\mathsf{C}}|}{j}\sum_{(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\in T_{\mathsf{C}}^{S_{\mathsf{C}}}}a_{\tau_{1}}a_{\tau_{2}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathsf{C}\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}}(-1)^{d_{\mathsf{C}}}\sum_{(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\in T_{\mathsf{C}}^{S_{\mathsf{C}}}}a_{\tau_{1}}a_{\tau_{2}}\sum_{j=0}^{|S_{\mathsf{C}}|}(-1)^{j}\binom{|S_{\mathsf{C}}|}{j}.

The alternating sum of coefficients is equal to

\sum_{j=0}^{S_{\mathsf{C}}}(-1)^{j}\binom{|S_{\mathsf{C}}|}{j}=(1+(-1))^{|S_{\mathsf{C}}|}=\begin{cases}0&|S_{\mathsf{C}}|>0\\
1&|S_{\mathsf{C}}|=0\end{cases}.

Thus, the only contributions to the overall sum come from
0
-cubes with
S_{\mathsf{C}}=\varnothing
. By Lemmas
4.15
and
4.16
, the only nonempty
0
-cube is
\mathsf{C}_{0}=\{(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})\}
with
T^{\varnothing,\varnothing}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}=\{(\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}},\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}})\}
, so the right-hand side above reduces to

\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}=\phi_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}},

as claimed.
∎

5.
Using derivations to obtain toric expressions for the numerators

In this section, we will define for each
{i_{*}}\in[n]
a derivation
\delta_{i_{1}}
on the coordinate ring
\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{X}^{\vee}]
, where we recall from Section
3
that
i_{1}=\sigma_{k}({i_{*}})
for
{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}
and
i_{1}=\sigma_{k}(k)=k
for
{i_{*}}=k
. As we have mentioned in Section
1
, this derivation will play a central role in defining the canonical potentials, and hence we will need to investigate its action specifically on monomials appearing in
\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}
. To simplify this investigation, we will translate the derivation
\delta_{i_{1}}
on
\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{X}^{\vee}]
into a map on
\mathsf{P}_{i_{*}}
and investigate the induced poset structure of its image. More precisely, our aim will be showing that the torus expansion of
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}})
restricted to
U^{\circ}_{-}
is closely related to that of
\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}
. For each
{i_{*}}\in[n]
, we define the derivation
\delta_{i_{1}}:\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{X}^{\vee}]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{X}^{\vee}]
as follows. First, for a Plücker coordinate
p_{\mathsf{w}}\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{X}^{\vee}]
labeled by
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
, the derivation
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts either by adding the minimal element
\mathsf{b}
of
\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
if
\mathsf{w}\sqcup\mathsf{b}
is a valid order ideal or trivially otherwise

\delta_{i_{1}}(p_{\mathsf{w}})=\begin{cases}p_{\mathsf{w}\sqcup\{\mathsf{b}\}},&\text{if $\mathsf{w}\sqcup\{\mathsf{b}\}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}$,}\\
0,&\textrm{otherwise.}\end{cases}

We extend
\delta_{i_{1}}
to polynomials in the Plücker coordinates as a derivation. With this definition, it is immediately clear that:

Corollary 5.1
.

\delta_{k}(\mathcal{D}_{0})=\delta_{k}(p_{\varnothing})=p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}
.

For the remainder of this section, we will work with
{i_{*}}\neq 0,k
and study the action of
\delta_{i_{1}}
on
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
. Recall from (
4.2
) that we defined
\mu^{\vee}_{i}
to be the weight
\Pi(\mathsf{w}_{i})(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}})
corresponding to the order ideal
\mathsf{w}_{i}
. First, we will make the following easy observation regarding the action of
\delta_{i_{1}}
:

Lemma 5.2
.

Let
p_{\mathsf{w}}\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{X}^{\vee}]
be a Plücker coordinate on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
, then
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on
p_{\mathsf{w}}
if and only if
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=-1
.

Proof.

Since our Plücker coordinates come from a minuscule representation, we must have
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle\in\{-1,0,+1\}
and in particular we have
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=-1
if and only if
s_{i_{1}}
acts by adding
\alpha^{\vee}_{i_{1}}
to
\mu^{\vee}
, which in turn is equivalent to
\ell(s_{i_{1}}\Pi(\mathsf{w}))=\ell(\Pi(\mathsf{w}))+1
, where
\Pi(\mathsf{w})\in W^{P}
corresponds to
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
as in Remark
2.15
. This last statement is equivalent to the existence of a
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
such that
\mathsf{w}\sqcup\mathsf{b}
is a valid order ideal.
∎

Thus, we will frequently be interested in the coefficient
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle
when investigating the action of
\delta_{i_{1}}
on the polynomial
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
. This action is straightforward when
{c_{*}}=1
:

Lemma 5.3
.

If
{c_{*}}=1
and
{i_{*}}\neq k
, then the restriction to
U^{\circ}_{-}
of
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})
is given by

\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\left(\textstyle\sum_{\mathsf{b}:\,\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=i_{1}}\displaystyle a_{\mathsf{b}}\right)a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}},

where the sum is over all elements
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
.

Proof.

Since
{c_{*}}=1
, by Corollary
4.2
, we have
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}=p_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}
, where we recall from Proposition
3.7
that
p_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}
corresponds to the weight
{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{2}}}-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{1}}}
. Thus, by Lemma
5.2
, there is
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
such that
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})=\delta_{i_{1}}(p_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}})=p_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\sqcup\mathsf{b}}
. Since
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}
has no element with label
s_{i_{1}}
,
\mathsf{b}
must be the minimal element of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
.

Furthermore, any embedding
\tau:\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\sqcup\mathsf{b}\rightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}
must restrict to the identity on
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\sqcup\mathsf{b}
by Lemma
4.1
, while
\tau(\mathsf{b})
may be any element of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
since
\mathsf{b}
is the minimal such element of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
. Thus in the case
{c_{*}}=1
, we immediately obtain the restriction

\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\sum_{\tau:\,\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\sqcup\mathsf{b}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}a_{\tau}=\sum_{\tau:\,\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\sqcup\mathsf{b}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}a_{\tau(\mathsf{b})}a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}=\left(\sum_{\mathsf{b}}a_{\mathsf{b}}\right)a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}

where the final sum is over all
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
.
∎

Studying the action of
\delta_{i_{1}}
on the polynomial
\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}
for
{c_{*}}>1
will be more complicated, but the first monomial can be considered directly. Recall that
p_{i_{j}}
refers to the Plücker coordinate
p_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{j}}}
.

Lemma 5.4
.

For any
{i_{*}}\in[n]
, the action of
\delta_{i_{1}}
on
p_{i_{j}}
is nontrivial if and only if
j=1
. In particular,

\delta_{i_{1}}(p_{i_{1}}\dots p_{i_{c_{*}}})=p_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\sqcup\mathsf{b}}p_{i_{2}}\dots p_{i_{{c_{*}}}},

where
\mathsf{b}
is the minimal element of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
.

Proof.

By Proposition
3.7
, we have that
p_{i_{j}}
corresponds to the weight
{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{j+1}}}-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{j}}}
. Since these are weights in a minuscule representation, then by definition of the derivation action, we have that
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on
p_{i_{j}}
if and only if
i_{j}=i_{1}
, in which case there is
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
such that
\mathsf{w}_{i_{w}}\sqcup\mathsf{b}
is an order ideal. Furthermore,
\mathsf{b}
is the minimal element of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
since
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}
has no element with label
s_{i_{1}}
. By the proof of Lemma
3.5
, we have that
i_{1}\neq i_{2},\dots,i_{{c_{*}}}
, so the derivation action acts nontrivially only on
p_{i_{1}}
by Lemma
5.2
.
∎

Although our construction applies to the general case, it is again more straightforward to apply our construction directly to the four exceptional cases with
{c_{*}}>2
. Hence, as in the previous section, we will restrict ourselves to the case
{c_{*}}=2
from now on and defer four exceptional cases to Appendix
A
.

With this restriction, we will now establish the more general statement that
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on at most one Plücker coordinate of each monomial
p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}}
corresponding to an element
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
.

Lemma 5.5
.

For any
{i_{*}}\in[n]
and any
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
, the derivation
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on at most one factor of the quadratic monomial
p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}}
.

Proof.

Because the Plücker coordinates
p_{\mathsf{w}}
that we consider come from a minuscule representation, the corresponding weights
\mu^{\vee}
satisfy that
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{m}\rangle\!\rangle\in\{-1,0,+1\}
for any
m
. By Lemma
5.2
,
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts on
p_{\mathsf{w}}
nontrivially if and only if
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=-1
so it suffices to show that at most one of the Plücker coordinates
p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}},p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}}
satisfies this property for any
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
.

By Lemma
5.4
, we have

\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee}_{i_{1}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{2}}}-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{1}}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=-1\quad\text{and}\quad\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee}_{i_{2}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{3}}}-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{2}}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle\in\{0,+1\}.

Therefore, we have
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee}_{i_{1}}+\mu^{\vee}_{i_{2}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{3}}}-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{1}}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle\in\{-1,0\}
when
i_{1}\neq i_{3}
respectively
i_{1}=i_{3}
. Now by Lemma
4.10
, letting
\mu^{\vee}_{i}
denote the weight corresponding to
\mathsf{w}_{i}
, we have

\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee}_{1}+\mu^{\vee}_{2},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{3}}}-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{1}}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle\in\{-1,0\}.

Since this is a sum of the two integers
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee}_{1},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee}_{2},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle\in\{-1,0,1\}
, we cannot have that both of these integers are equal to
-1
, so by Lemma
5.2
,
\delta_{i_{1}}
can act nontrivially on at most one of the Plücker coordinates
p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}},p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}}
for any
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
.
∎

In this proof we used arguments about the coefficient
\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle
where
\mu^{\vee}=\Pi(\mathsf{w})\cdot(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}})
. These coefficients will be a useful tool for our upcoming arguments as well, and for notational convenience we will sometimes use the tuple
(c_{\mathsf{w}_{1}},c_{\mathsf{w}_{2}})
to refer to these coefficients; i.e.

c_{\mathsf{w}_{1}}=\langle\!\langle\Pi(\mathsf{w}_{1})\cdot(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}),\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle\quad\text{and}\quad c_{\mathsf{w}_{2}}=\langle\!\langle\Pi(\mathsf{w}_{2})\cdot(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}),\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle.

(5.1)

Using Lemma
5.5
, we will now translate the action of
\delta_{i_{1}}
to elements
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
.

Definition 5.6
.

The map
\delta_{i_{1}}:\mathsf{P}_{i_{*}}\to(W^{P})^{2}\cup\{0\}
is given by

\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})=\begin{cases}(\mathsf{w}_{1}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})&\text{if $\delta_{i_{1}}(p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}})=p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{1}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}}$,}\\
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{2})&\text{if $\delta_{i_{1}}(p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}})=p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{2}}$,}\\
0&\text{else,}\end{cases}

where
\mathsf{b}_{1}
and
\mathsf{b}_{2}
are elements of
\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{1}
and
\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{2}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
such that
\mathsf{w}_{1}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{1}
and
\mathsf{w}_{2}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{2}
are order ideals respectively. When
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\neq 0
, we will often refer to its image as
(\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+},\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+})=\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\neq 0
.

In the remainder of this section, we will mainly be interested in the image of this map
\delta_{i_{1}}
.

Definition 5.7
.

Let
\mathsf{P}_{i_{*}}^{+}
denote the poset obtained from
\mathsf{P}_{i_{*}}
by applying
\delta_{i_{1}}
as follows: The elements of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
will be the set
\{\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})~|~\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\neq 0\}
and the partial order
>_{+}
will be the one inherited from
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
:

\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})>_{+}\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})>(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4}).

We also identify
\delta_{i_{1}}
with the (partial) function
\delta_{i_{1}}:\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}\dashrightarrow\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
obtained by ignoring those elements of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
on which
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts trivially.

Lemma
5.5
says that for any pair
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{i_{*}}
,
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on at most one element of the pair
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})
. As a result, the poset
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
may contain strictly fewer elements than
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
and this case will require special care. We first identify exactly when this case will occur.

Lemma 5.8
.

The order ideal
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}
contains exactly one element whose label
s_{j}
does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
.

Proof.

Recall that
\Pi(\mathsf{w}_{i_{j}})=w_{i_{j}}
. We will prove this statement by computing the coefficient
\langle\!\langle w_{i_{1}}(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}),\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle
in two ways, where we recall that
w_{i_{1}}
has no occurrence of the simple reflection
s_{i_{1}}
. First, Lemmas
5.4
and
5.2
immediately imply that
\langle\!\langle w_{i_{1}}(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}),\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=-1
.

Second, we consider the action of
w_{i_{1}}
on
-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}
. Since
w_{i_{1}}
is a minimal coset representative, any simple reflection
s_{m_{j}}
in any reduced expression for
w_{i_{1}}
acts by adding
\alpha^{\vee}_{m_{j}}
, and we find

\langle\!\langle w_{i_{1}}(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}),\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{k}}+\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{\ell(w_{i_{1}})}\displaystyle\alpha^{\vee}_{m_{j}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell(w_{i_{1}})}\langle\!\langle\alpha^{\vee}_{m_{j}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle.

Equating these results yields

-1=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell(w_{i_{1}})}\langle\!\langle\alpha^{\vee}_{m_{j}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle.

Since
w_{i_{1}}
has no occurrences of
s_{i_{1}}
, then the right hand side above is a sum of nonpositive integers. Thus, there must be exactly one
j
such that
\langle\!\langle\alpha^{\vee}_{m_{j}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=-1
. The lemma follows immediately since each simple reflection in
w_{i_{1}}
corresponds to a unique element of
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}
.
∎

We can now describe when
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts trivially on
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
.

Lemma 5.9
.

For
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
,
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts trivially on
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
if and only if
i_{1}=i_{3}
and there is a sequence of moves from the top element
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
to
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})

\mathsf{b}_{1}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}},~\mathsf{b}_{2}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\setminus\mathsf{b}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{1}^{\prime}},~\ldots,~\mathsf{b}_{d}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\setminus\{\mathsf{b}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{b}_{d-1}\},\mathsf{w}_{2}\sqcup\{\mathsf{b}_{1}^{\prime},\dots,\mathsf{b}_{d-1}^{\prime}\}}

such that
\mathsf{w}_{1}=\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\setminus\{\mathsf{b}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{b}_{d}\}
and
\mathsf{w}_{2}=\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}\sqcup\{\mathsf{b}_{1}^{\prime},\dots,\mathsf{b}_{d}^{\prime}\}
, and the label of one of the
\mathsf{b}_{j}
does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
.

Proof.

Suppose first that
\delta_{i_{1}}(p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}})=0
. Then by Lemma
5.2
, it must be the case that the coefficients
(c_{\mathsf{w}_{1}},c_{\mathsf{w}_{2}})
as defined in equation (
5.1
) are
0
or
+1
. On the other hand, by Lemma
5.4
the coefficients

c_{i_{1}}=\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee}_{i_{1}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{2}}}-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{1}}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle\quad\text{and}\quad c_{i_{2}}=\langle\!\langle\mu^{\vee}_{i_{2}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{3}}}-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{2}}},\alpha_{i_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle

satisfy
(c_{i_{1}},c_{i_{2}})\in\{(-1,0),~(-1,+1)\}
. Thus, since the coefficients
(c_{\mathsf{w}_{1}},c_{\mathsf{w}_{2}})
differ from
(c_{i_{1}},c_{i_{2}})
, any sequence of moves
\mathsf{b}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{b}_{d}
between
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
and
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})
must contain one move
\mathsf{b}_{j}
whose label affects these coefficients.

By Lemma
4.9
,
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b}_{j})
can only affect the values of these coefficients if
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b}_{j})=s_{i_{1}}
or if
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b}_{j})
does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
. Since
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}
contains no element with label
s_{i_{1}}
, we conclude that
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b}_{j})
does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
. Furthermore, since
c_{i_{2}}-1\in\{0,+1\}
, we must have had
c_{i_{2}}=+1
. Since the weight corresponding to
p_{i_{2}}
is
{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{3}}}-{\varpi^{\vee}_{i_{2}}}
by Proposition
3.7
, the equality
c_{i_{2}}=+1
can only occur if if
i_{3}=i_{1}
.

Conversely, suppose that
i_{1}=i_{3}
and that there is a sequence of moves
\mathsf{b}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{b}_{d}
as in the statement such that one of the
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b}_{j})
does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
. Since
i_{1}=i_{3}
, we have
(c_{i_{1}},c_{i_{2}})=(-1,1)
. Then Lemma
4.9
implies that
(c_{\mathsf{w}_{1}},c_{\mathsf{w}_{2}})=(0,0)
, so by Lemma
5.2
, the derivation acts trivially on the Plücker monomial
p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}}
.
∎

The following corollary is an immediate consequence of Lemma
5.9
.

Corollary 5.10
.

As posets,
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}\cong\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
if and only if
i_{1}\neq i_{3}
. If
i_{1}=i_{3}
, then
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
is isomorphic to the connected (by cover relations) component of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
that contains the top element
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
after deleting all cover relations corresponding to moves
\mathsf{b}
whose labels do not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
.

As we did in the previous section, we now partition the toric terms for any
(\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+},\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
. While we could define these partitions from scratch, it will turn out to be much more convenient to define them in terms of our existing sets
T^{A_{1},A_{2}}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
as follows. For each pair of embeddings
(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})
of
(\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+},\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+})
,
\tau_{i}^{+}:\mathsf{w}_{i}^{+}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}
, we obtain a pair of embeddings
(\tau_{1}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{1}},\tau_{2}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{2}})
of
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})
by restriction.

Definition 5.11
.

For each
(\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+},\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+})=\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
,
A_{1}\subset A_{\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{1}}
, and
A_{2}\subset A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
, we define the set

T^{A_{1},A_{2},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}=\Bigl\{(\tau_{1}^{+}:\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P},\tau_{2}^{+}:\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P})~\Big|~(\tau_{1}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{1}},\tau_{2}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{2}})\in T^{A_{1},A_{2}}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}\Bigr\}.

Since the restrictions are well-defined for every pair of embeddings
(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})
, these sets partition the toric terms of
p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}}
and we will use them to organize the cancellation of terms in
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}
. We will be able to use the same strategy as we used in Section
4
, but we first need a few preparatory lemmas. The first statement we will need for the cancellation is an immediate corollary of the analogous statements in Section
4
.

Corollary 5.12
.

Let
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
such that
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\neq 0
. Then the sets
T^{\varnothing,\varnothing,+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
are empty unless
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})=(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
is the top element of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
, in which case we have

T^{\varnothing,\varnothing,+}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}=\bigl\{(\tau_{1}^{+},\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}})~\big|~\tau_{1}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}\bigr\}.

Moreover, for every
\mathsf{b}_{i_{1}}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}
with
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b}_{i_{1}})=s_{i_{1}}
there exists a (necessarily unique) embedding
\tau_{1}^{+}
with
(\tau_{1}^{+},\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}})\in T^{\varnothing,\varnothing,+}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}
such that
\tau_{1}^{+}(\mathsf{b})=\mathsf{b}_{i_{1}}
, where
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}
is such that
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\sqcup\{\mathsf{b}\}
.

Proof.

The first part of the statement follows immediately from Lemmas
4.15
and
4.16
, because only the toric set
T^{\varnothing,\varnothing}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}
is nonempty among all the toric sets
T^{\varnothing,\varnothing}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
.

For the second part, Lemma
5.4
gives
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}^{+},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}^{+})=\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})=(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\sqcup\mathsf{b},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
, where
\mathsf{b}
is the minimal element of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
. Now let
(\tau_{i_{1}}^{+},\tau_{i_{2}}^{+})\in T^{\varnothing,\varnothing,+}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}
, so that by Lemma
4.15
we have
\tau_{i_{1}}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}
and
\tau_{i_{2}}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}
since
(\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}},\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}})
is the only element in
T_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}^{\varnothing,\varnothing}
. Since
\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}
, we thus also have
\tau_{i_{2}}^{+}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}
.

Finally, note that for
every

\mathsf{b}_{*}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
the assignment
\mathsf{b}\mapsto\mathsf{b}_{*}
defines a valid embedding of
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}^{+}
since
\tau_{i_{1}}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}
places no restrictions on the image of
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}^{+}
under
\tau_{i_{1}}^{+}
.
∎

Cubes are defined the same way for
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
as they were for
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
. However, it will be more convenient for us to study cubes in
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
by considering cubes
\mathsf{C}\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
and applying
\delta_{i_{1}}
to
\mathsf{C}
. Because
\delta_{i_{1}}
may act trivially on some elements of
\mathsf{C}
, we first verify that the image
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{C})
is a cube in
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
.

Lemma 5.13
.

For any
m
-cube
\mathsf{C}\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
with set
S_{\mathsf{C}}
of labels, the non-zero image
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{C})\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
of
\mathsf{C}
under
\delta_{i_{1}}
is one of the following:

(1)

an
m
-cube if
i_{1}\neq i_{3}
or if
i_{1}=i_{3}
and every minimal length sequence
\mathsf{b}_{1},\mathsf{b}_{2},\dots
of moves between
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
and the bottom element of
\mathsf{C}
consists of moves whose labels commute with
s_{i_{1}}
,

(2)

an
(m-1)
-cube if
i_{1}=i_{3}
and
S_{\mathsf{C}}
contains an label not commuting with
s_{i_{1}}
,

(3)

or empty if
i_{1}=i_{3}
and there is a minimal length sequence
\mathsf{b}_{1},\mathsf{b}_{2},\dots
of moves between
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
and the top element of
\mathsf{C}
which contains a move whose label does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
.

Proof.

We consider first the cases that
i_{1}\neq i_{3}
or the cases that
i_{1}=i_{3}
but every minimal length sequence

\mathsf{b}_{1}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}},~\mathsf{b}_{2}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\setminus\mathsf{b}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{1}^{\prime}},~\ldots

between
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
and the bottom element of
\mathsf{C}
consists only of moves
\mathsf{b}_{j}
whose labels commute with
s_{i_{1}}
. In these cases, Lemma
5.9
implies that
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on each element of
\mathsf{C}
, and thus
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{C})
is an
m
-cube in
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
since every cover relation between elements of
\mathsf{C}
is also a cover relation between the corresponding elements of
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{C})
by definition of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
.

We now consider the case where
i_{1}=i_{3}
and there is a minimal length sequence

\mathsf{b}_{1}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}},~\mathsf{b}_{2}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\setminus\mathsf{b}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{1}^{\prime}},~\ldots

between
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
and the bottom element of
\mathsf{C}
such that the label of some
\mathsf{b}_{j}
,
s_{m_{j}}=\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b}_{j})
does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
. Letting
S_{\mathsf{C}}
denote the set of labels of the cube
\mathsf{C}
, we consider the cases that
s_{m_{j}}\in S_{\mathsf{C}}
or
s_{m_{j}}\notin S_{\mathsf{C}}
. If
s_{m_{j}}\notin S_{\mathsf{C}}
, then by Lemma
2.7
there must be a sequence of moves between
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
and the top element of
\mathsf{C}
containing
\mathsf{b}_{j}
, which by Lemma
5.9
implies that
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts trivially on every element of
\mathsf{C}
and hence that
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{C})=\varnothing
.

Finally suppose
s_{m_{j}}\in S_{\mathsf{C}}
. Since
\mathsf{C}
is an
m
-cube, we may identify it with the set of subsets of
S_{\mathsf{C}}
ordered by inclusion by Corollary
4.20
. Explicitly, we identify an element
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{C}
with the labels
\mathrm{label}(A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}})\cap S_{\mathsf{C}}
corresponding to cover relations
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\gtrdot(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})
in the partial ordering on
\mathsf{C}
. Then by Lemmas
5.8
and
5.9
, we have that
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts trivially on
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{C}
if and only if
s_{m_{j}}\notin\mathrm{label}(A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}})
, so that

\{\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})~|~(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{C}:~\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\neq 0\}=\{\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{C}~|~\mathrm{label}(A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}})\ni s_{m_{j}}\}

can be identified with the sub-cube of
\mathsf{C}
consisting of elements
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})
with
s_{m_{j}}\in\mathrm{label}(A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}})
, which is an
(m-1)
-cube. Again,
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{C})
is a cube in
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
because every cover relation between elements of
\mathsf{C}
in which
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on both elements corresponds to a cover relation between the corresponding elements of
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{C})
by definition of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
.
∎

In fact, it is an immediate consequence of Corollary
5.10
that every cube in
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
arises in this way, since this corollary implies that the Hasse diagram of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}^{+}
is isomorphic to a connected component of the Hasse diagram of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
. With this lemma, we can use
\delta_{i_{1}}
to lift the bijections of Lemma
4.23
to the sets
T^{A_{1},A_{2},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
. Recall that as before we will write
A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}(S)
to denote the set
\{\mathsf{b}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}\mid\mathsf{b}\in S\}
of moves in
A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
with labels in
S
.

Lemma 5.14
.

Let
\mathsf{C}\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
be an
m
-cube with set of labels
S
. For any two distinct elements
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}),(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})\in\mathsf{C}
such that
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on both, consider the sets
A_{21}=A_{\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{1}}(S)
,
A_{12}=A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}(S)
,
A_{43}=A_{\mathsf{w}_{4},\mathsf{w}_{3}}(S)
, and
A_{34}=A_{\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4}}(S)
. Then there is a bijection

\kappa_{A_{21},A_{12}}^{A_{43},A_{34},+}:T^{A_{21},A_{12},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}T^{A_{43},A_{34},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4}}

such that for any
(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\in T^{A_{21},A_{12},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
, we have
(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\overset{t}{=}\kappa_{A_{21},A_{12}}^{A_{43},A_{34},+}(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})
, where
\overset{t}{=}
denotes toric equality as in Definition
4.22
.

Proof.

As in the proof of Lemma
4.23
, we may immediately reduce to the case where
(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})
can be obtained from
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})
by a single move
\mathsf{b}
with label
s_{m}=\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b})\in S
, corresponding to a cover relation of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
. Furthermore, we will similarly simplify notation by writing
T_{12}^{+}=T^{A_{21},A_{12},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
and
T_{34}^{+}=T^{A_{43},A_{34},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4}}
, while writing
\kappa_{12}^{34,+}=\kappa_{A_{21},A_{12}}^{A_{43},A_{34},+}
for the remainder of this proof.

We now consider two cases depending on whether
s_{m}
commutes with
s_{i_{1}}
. If
s_{m}
commutes with
s_{i_{1}}
, then both the construction and proof of Lemma
4.23
can be applied directly, with
(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})
in place of
(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})
, to construct
\kappa_{12}^{34,+}
and show that it satisfies the required properties.

Now suppose that
s_{m}
does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
. In this case since we are assuming that
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on both
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})
and
(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})
, then by Lemmas
5.2
,
5.8
, and
4.9
, we have that

\begin{cases}\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{1},~\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{2}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{2},~\mathsf{w}_{3}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{3}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{3}~\text{and}~\mathsf{w}_{4}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{4},&\text{if $(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\lessdot(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})$,}\\
\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{1}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{1},~\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{2},~\mathsf{w}_{3}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{3}~\text{and}~\mathsf{w}_{4}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{4}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{4},&\text{if $(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\gtrdot(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})$,}\end{cases}

where in each case,
\mathsf{b}_{i}
denotes the minimal element of
\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{i}
with label
i_{1}
.

First, consider the case
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\lessdot(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})
corresponding to the move
\mathsf{b}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4}}
with label
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b})=s_{m}
. This means that
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})=(\mathsf{w}_{3}\setminus\mathsf{b},\mathsf{w}_{4}\sqcup\mathsf{b}^{\prime})
, so that we obtain (since
\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{1}
and
\mathsf{w}_{4}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{4}
)

\mathsf{w}_{3}^{+}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}=\{\mathsf{b}_{3},\mathsf{b}\}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{4}^{+}=\{\mathsf{b}_{2},\mathsf{b}^{\prime}\}.

Then given a pair of embeddings
(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\in T_{12}^{+}
of
\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}
and
\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}
, we define

\tau_{3}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}}=\tau_{1}^{+},\quad\tau_{3}^{+}(\mathsf{b}_{3})=\tau_{2}^{+}(\mathsf{b}_{2})\quad\text{and}\quad\tau_{3}^{+}(\mathsf{b})=\tau_{2}^{+}(\mathsf{b}^{\prime}),\quad\text{while}\quad\tau_{4}^{+}=\tau_{2}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{4}^{+}},

and set
\kappa_{12}^{34,+}(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})=(\tau_{3}^{+},\tau_{4}^{+})
. The image lies in
T_{34}^{+}
, since
\tau_{3}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{3}}
and
\tau_{4}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{4}}
are clearly embeddings of
\mathsf{w}_{3}
and
\mathsf{w}_{4}
and
(\tau_{3}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{3}},\tau_{4}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{4}})\in T_{34}
by the definitions of
A_{\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{1}}
and
\textup{I}^{\mathsf{b}}_{{}_{,}\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
along with Corollary
4.20
as in the proof of Lemma
4.23
.

In the second case, we have
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\gtrdot(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})
corresponding to the move
\mathsf{b}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
with label
s_{m}
.
This means that
(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})=(\mathsf{w}_{1}\setminus\mathsf{b},\mathsf{w}_{2}\sqcup\mathsf{b})
, so that we obtain (since
\mathsf{w}_{3}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{3}
and
\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}=\mathsf{w}_{2}
)

\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{3}^{+}=\{\mathsf{b},\mathsf{b}_{1}\}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathsf{w}_{4}^{+}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}=\{\mathsf{b}_{4},\mathsf{b}^{\prime}\}.

Then given a pair of embeddings
(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\in T_{12}^{+}
of
\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}
and
\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}
, we define

\tau_{3}^{+}=\tau_{1}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{3}^{+}},\quad\text{while}\quad\tau_{4}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}}=\tau_{2}^{+},\quad\tau_{4}^{+}(\mathsf{b}_{4})=\tau_{1}^{+}(\mathsf{b}_{1})\quad\text{and}\quad\tau_{4}^{+}(\mathsf{b}^{\prime})=\tau_{1}^{+}(\mathsf{b}),

and set
\kappa_{12}^{34,+}(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})=(\tau_{3}^{+},\tau_{4}^{+})
. Again, the image clearly lies in
T_{34}^{+}
.

Showing that
\kappa_{12}^{34,+}
defines a bijection and that
\kappa_{12}^{34,+}(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\overset{t}{=}(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})
is completely analogous to the proof of Lemma
4.23
.
∎

Before we can compute the toric restrictions of the
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})
, we need one final technical detail in the situation of Lemma
5.13
where a
1
-cube in
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
becomes a
0
-cube, since as we saw before in the proof of Theorem
4.24
,
0
-cubes correspond to the toric terms which do not cancel.

Lemma 5.15
.

Let
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\gtrdot(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})\in\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
be a
1
-cube corresponding to a move
\mathsf{b}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
with label
s_{m}
which does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
and suppose that
i_{1}=i_{3}
. Then
T^{\varnothing,s_{m},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}=\varnothing
.

Proof.

Suppose
(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\in T^{\varnothing,s_{m},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
and let
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}_{1}
which moves to
\mathsf{b}^{\prime}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{2}
be as in the statement. By the proof of Lemma
5.9
, we have that
(\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+},\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+})=\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})=(\mathsf{w}_{1}\sqcup\mathsf{b}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{2})
, where
\mathsf{b}_{i_{1}}
is the minimal element of
\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{1}
with label
s_{i_{1}}
. Let
\tau_{i}=\tau_{i}^{+}|_{\mathsf{w}_{i}}
. Then by definition of
T^{\varnothing,s_{m},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
, we have
(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\in T^{\varnothing,s_{m}}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
, so that extending
\tau_{2}
by
\tau_{2}(\mathsf{b}^{\prime})=\tau_{1}(\mathsf{b})
defines a valid embedding of
\mathsf{w}_{2}\sqcup\mathsf{b}
. Since
\mathsf{w}_{2}\supset\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}
, we must have in particular that
\tau_{1}(\mathsf{b}_{1})\in\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}
.

Since
s_{m}
does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
, then
\mathsf{b}_{i_{1}}
and
\mathsf{b}
must be comparable in
\mathsf{w}^{P}
. Furthermore, since
\mathsf{b}_{i_{1}}
is maximal in
\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}
, we must have that
\tau_{1}^{+}(\mathsf{b}_{i_{1}})>\tau_{1}^{+}(\mathsf{b})=\tau_{1}(\mathsf{b})
. Combined with
\tau_{1}(\mathsf{b})\in\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}
, we thus have that
\tau_{1}^{+}(\mathsf{b}_{i_{1}})\in\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}
. However, this is a contradiction since
i_{1}=i_{3}
implies that
\mathsf{w}^{P}\setminus\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}
has no elements with label
s_{i_{1}}=s_{i_{3}}
.
∎

We now come to the main theorem in this section computing the toric expression of
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})
.

Theorem 5.16
.

For each
{i_{*}}\neq k\in[n]
, the restriction of
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})
to the torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
is given by

\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}\left(\textstyle\sum_{\mathsf{b}:\,\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})={i_{1}}}\displaystyle a_{\mathsf{b}}\right),

where the sum is over all
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}
with index
i_{1}
or equivalently
\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b})=s_{i_{1}}
.

Proof.

This proof is entirely analogous to the proof of Theorem
4.24
using the results proved so far in this section. Recall that we defined
L_{d}\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
to be the subset of elements of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
which can be obtained from the top element
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
by a minimal length sequence of
d\geq 0
moves

\mathsf{b}_{1}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}},~\ldots,~\mathsf{b}_{d}\in A_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}\setminus\{\mathsf{b}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{b}_{d-1}\},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}\sqcup\{\mathsf{b}_{1}^{\prime},\dots,\mathsf{b}_{d-1}^{\prime}\}}.

We begin by applying
\delta_{i_{1}}
to
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
:

\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})=\sum_{d\geq 0}(-1)^{d}\sum_{(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in L_{d}}\delta_{i_{1}}(p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}})=\sum_{d\geq 0}(-1)^{d}\sum_{(\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+},\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+})\in L_{d}^{+}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+}}p_{\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+}},

where we write
L_{d}^{+}=\delta_{i_{1}}(L_{d})
and used Lemma
5.5
in the last equality. Since the toric sets
T^{A_{1},A_{2},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
partition the toric terms of
p_{w_{1}^{+}}p_{w_{2}^{+}}
, we obtain the following expression for the restriction

\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\sum_{d\geq 0}(-1)^{d}\sum_{(\mathsf{w}_{1}^{+},\mathsf{w}_{2}^{+})\in L_{d}^{+}}~\sum_{A_{1},A_{2}}~\sum_{(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{1}^{+})\in T^{A_{1},A_{2},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}^{\prime}}}a_{\tau_{1}^{+}}a_{\tau_{2}^{+}},

where the third sum is over all
A_{1}\subset A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
and
A_{2}\subset A_{\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{1}}
.

For each pair
A_{1},A_{2}
, by Lemma
4.21
, there is a unique
(|A_{1}|+|A_{2}|)
-cube in
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
containing
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})
, and this cube has set of labels
\{\mathrm{label}(\mathsf{b})\mid\mathsf{b}\in A_{1}\cup A_{2}\}
. For any cube
\mathsf{C}\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
, let
d_{\mathsf{C}}
denote the minimum number of moves in
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
between the top element
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})
of
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
and the top element of
\mathsf{C}
and let
S_{\mathsf{C}}
denote the set of labels of
\mathsf{C}
. Then we may rewrite the sum above by summing over all cubes contained in
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
. Before rewriting it like this, we first note that by Lemma
5.14
, we have for all cubes
\mathsf{C}\subset\mathsf{P}_{i_{*}}
and all pairs
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}),(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})\in\mathsf{C}
such that
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on both
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})
and
(\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4})
that

\sum_{(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\in T^{A_{1},A_{2},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}}a_{\tau_{1}^{+}}a_{\tau_{2}^{+}}=\sum_{(\tau_{3}^{+},\tau_{4}^{+})\in T^{A_{3},A_{4},+}_{\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4}}}a_{\tau_{3}^{+}}a_{\tau_{4}^{+}}

where
A_{1}=A_{\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{1}}(S_{\mathsf{C}})
,
A_{2}=A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}(S_{\mathsf{C}})
,
A_{3}=A_{\mathsf{w}_{4},\mathsf{w}_{3}}(S_{\mathsf{C}})
and
A_{4}=A_{\mathsf{w}_{3},\mathsf{w}_{4}}(S_{\mathsf{C}})
. Thus, the sum of monomials corresponding to pairs of embeddings in the toric set
T^{A_{\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{1}}(S_{\mathsf{C}}),A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}(S_{\mathsf{C}}),+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
is independent of the particular element
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{C}
and instead only depends on whether
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})
or not. Thus, for each cube
\mathsf{C}
, we will simply use the notation
T_{\mathsf{C}}^{S_{\mathsf{C}},+}
to denote any one of the torically equivalent toric sets
T^{A_{\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{1}}(S_{\mathsf{C}}),A_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}(S_{\mathsf{C}}),+}_{\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2}}
where
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts on
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})
nontrivially or the empty set if
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts trivially on every
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{C}
. We may now rewrite the sum as

\displaystyle\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathsf{C}\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}}\sum_{(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{C}:\,\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\neq 0}(-1)^{d_{\mathsf{C}}+|A_{\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{1}}(S_{\mathsf{C}})|}\sum_{(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\in T^{S_{\mathsf{C}},+}_{\mathsf{C}}}a_{\tau_{1}^{+}}a_{\tau_{2}^{+}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathsf{C}\subset\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}}\sum_{(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\in T^{S_{\mathsf{C}},+}_{\mathsf{C}}}a_{\tau_{1}^{+}}a_{\tau_{2}^{+}}\sum_{(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\in\mathsf{C}:\,\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\neq 0}(-1)^{d_{\mathsf{C}}+|A_{\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{1}}(S_{\mathsf{C}})|}.

By Lemma
5.13
, the innermost sum above is the alternating sum over the levels of an
m^{\prime}=|S_{\mathsf{C}}|
-cube, an
m^{\prime}=(|S_{\mathsf{C}}|-1)
-cube, or an empty cube, which again by the binomial theorem we may evaluate as

\sum_{j=0}^{m^{\prime}}(-1)^{j}\binom{m^{\prime}}{j}=(1+(-1))^{m^{\prime}}=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if $m^{\prime}>0$,}\\
1,&\text{if $m^{\prime}=0$.}\end{cases}

The sum above is nonzero only when
m^{\prime}=0
, which can occur in two cases by Lemma
5.13
: either when
\mathsf{C}=\mathsf{C}_{0}
is a
0
-cube where
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially; or else when
\mathsf{C}=\mathsf{C}_{1}
is a
1
-cube where
\delta_{i_{1}}
acts nontrivially on the top element of
\mathsf{C}
and trivially on the bottom element of
\mathsf{C}
, that is, the case where the unique label
s_{m}
of
\mathsf{C}
does not commute with
s_{i_{1}}
. Hence, we can split the nonzero terms into two sums depending on these cases:

\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\left(\sum_{\mathsf{C}=\mathsf{C}_{0}}\sum_{(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\in T_{\mathsf{C}}^{\varnothing,+}}a_{\tau_{1}^{+}}a_{\tau_{2}^{+}}\right)+\left(\sum_{\mathsf{C}=\mathsf{C}_{1}}\sum_{(\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{2}^{+})\in T_{\mathsf{C}}^{s_{m},+}}a_{\tau_{1}^{+}}a_{\tau_{2}^{+}}\right).

However, the second sum over
\mathsf{C}=\mathsf{C}_{1}
is zero since
T_{\mathsf{C}}^{s_{m},+}=\varnothing
by Lemma
5.15
. Furthermore, by Corollary
5.12
, there is only one nonzero term in the first sum coming from
\mathsf{C}_{0}=\{(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})\}
, so we obtain

\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\sum_{(\tau_{i_{1}}^{+},\tau_{i_{2}}^{+})\in T_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}^{\varnothing,\varnothing,+}}a_{\tau_{i_{1}}^{+}}a_{\tau_{i_{2}}^{+}}=a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}}a_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}\left(\textstyle\sum_{\mathsf{b}:\,\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})={i_{1}}}\displaystyle a_{\mathsf{b}}\right)

where the rightmost sum is over
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}
with index
i_{1}
.
∎

6.
Proof of main theorem

In the previous Section
5
, we explicitly avoided
{i_{*}}=k
because the corresponding term
\mathcal{W}_{k}
behaves slightly differently than the terms
\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}
where
{i_{*}}\neq k
in our construction. Before we can present the proof of our main theorem, we handle this special term which we often call the “quantum term” directly in the first subsection.

6.1.
The quantum term

Comparing Theorem
3.10
and Theorem
5.16
with the terms of toric restriction of the Lie-theoretic superpotential as given in (
2.12
), we can see that the terms
\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}
for
{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}
of
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
deal with the terms
(f^{\vee}_{i_{1}})^{*}(u_{-})
and it is clear that
\mathcal{W}_{k}=p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=3.52pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.87997pt\hbox to4.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=3.52pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.87997pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}/p_{\varnothing}
takes care of the term
(f^{\vee}_{k})^{*}(u_{-})
. Hence, the remaining term in the Lie-theoretic superpotential is
(e^{\vee}_{k})^{*}(u_{+}^{-1})
where
k
is such that
P=P_{k}
. We will start with the toric expression for this term as stated in equation (
2.12
):

(e^{\vee}_{k})^{*}(u_{+}^{-1})=q\frac{\sum_{\iota:\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}a_{\iota(\mathsf{w}^{\prime})}}{a_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}}.

In our case, this term is the only one containing the quantum parameter, so it is often referred to as the
quantum term
. Note that this is the only term of the Lie-theoretic potential (or more precisely its restriction to
U^{\circ}_{-}
) that depends on the formal quantum paramter
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
.

Both the numerator and the denominator of the toric expression above are given by summing over the products of toric coordinates corresponding to embeddings of a poset into the minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}
: for the numerator it is the subposet
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}
, whereas for the denominator it is the order ideal
\mathsf{w}^{P}
itself. Hence, we directly see using (
2.13
) and (
3.1
) that the denominator equals
\phi_{k}=p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}
on the torus and therefore on all of
U_{-}^{P}
since
U_{-}^{P}
is irreducible and
U^{\circ}_{-}\subset U_{-}^{P}
is dense. On the other hand, for the numerator to correspond to a Plücker coordinate, the subset
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}
must be an order ideal, or equivalently
w^{\prime}
must be a minimal coset representative, a fact which we foreshadowed already in Remark
2.11
. We will establish this by showing a more general result, which does require
k
to be a minuscule vertex of
G^{\vee}
.

For
j\in[n]
, recall that we wrote
w_{0,j}\in W_{j}
for the longest elements of the parabolic Weyl subgroups. Write
W^{(j)}
for the set of minimal coset representatives of the cosets in
W/W_{j}
, with
w^{(j)}\in W^{(j)}
the representative of
w_{0}W_{j}
. Moreover, let
w_{j}^{\prime\prime}\in W^{(j)}
be the representative of
w_{0,j}s_{j}W_{j}
, and let
w_{j}^{\prime}=w^{(j)}(w_{j}^{\prime\prime})^{-1}\in W
. Then:

Lemma 6.1
.

The element
w_{j}^{\prime}=w^{(j)}(w_{j}^{\prime\prime})^{-1}\in W
lies in
W^{(j)}
.

Proof.

We begin by excluding the trivial case where
w_{j}^{\prime\prime}=w^{(j)}
, since
w_{j}^{\prime}=e\in W^{(j)}
. (This only occurs for type
A_{n}
with
j\in\{1,n\}
; cf.
[
Spa21
, Remark 7.3]
.)

Working from contradiction, assume that
w_{j}^{\prime}\notin W^{(j)}
, i.e. there exists an
i\in[n]\setminus\{j\}
such that
w_{j}^{\prime\prime\prime}=w_{j}^{\prime}s_{i}
has
\ell(w_{j}^{\prime\prime\prime})=\ell(w_{j}^{\prime})-1
. On the other hand, since
w_{0,j}\in W_{j}
is the longest element of the parabolic Weyl subgroup, we have
\ell(s_{i}w_{0,j})=\ell(w_{0,j})-1
, so that
s_{i}w_{0,j}s_{j}(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}})=w_{j}^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}})
with
\ell(w_{j}^{\prime\prime\prime\prime})\leq\ell(w_{j}^{\prime\prime})
.
However, now we find that

{\varpi^{\vee}_{\sigma_{0}(j)}}=w^{(j)}(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}})=w_{j}^{\prime}w_{j}^{\prime\prime}(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}})=w_{j}^{\prime\prime\prime}w_{j}^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}(-{\varpi^{\vee}_{j}}).

In other words,
w_{j}^{\prime\prime\prime}w_{j}^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}
and
w^{(j)}
are both coset representatives of
w_{0}W_{j}
, with lengths related by
\ell(w_{j}^{\prime\prime\prime}w_{j}^{\prime\prime\prime\prime})\leq\ell(w^{(j)})-1
, which contradicts the minimality of the coset representative
w^{(j)}
.
∎

Remark 6.2
.

The above proof generalizes straightforwardly to parabolic Weyl subgroups
W_{J}
with
J\subset[n]
having
|J|>1
.

Since
W_{P}=W_{k}
,
w^{P}=w^{(k)}
,
w_{P}=w_{0,k}
,
w^{\prime}=w_{k}^{\prime}
and
w^{\prime\prime}=w_{k}^{\prime\prime}
, we combine Lemma
6.1
with the preceding discussion to obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 6.3
.

The element
w^{\prime}=w^{P}(w^{\prime\prime})^{-1}\in W
lies in
W^{P}
and hence
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}
is an order ideal of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
. In particular, the complement of the ideal
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
defined by
w^{\prime\prime}
is isomorphic to the ideal
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
defined by
w^{\prime}
.

Since equation (
2.13
) tells us that
p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}(u_{-})=a_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}
and
p_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}(u_{-})=\sum_{\iota:\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}a_{\iota(\mathsf{w}^{\prime})}
for
u_{-}\in U^{\circ}_{-}
, we directly conclude the following:

Proposition 6.4
.

For any fixed
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
, the following equality holds on the open dense torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
and hence on
U_{-}^{P}

(e^{\vee}_{k})^{*}(u_{+}^{-1})=q\frac{p_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}(u_{-})}{p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}(u_{-})},

where
u_{+}\in U^{\vee}_{+}
is determined by
u_{-}\in U_{-}^{P}
and
q\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
as in Corollary
2.5
.

We now have descriptions for all the terms of the superpotential in Plücker coordinates, so we can put these together and prove that the Lie-theoretic and canonical mirror models are isomorphic type-independently.

6.2.
The canonical mirror variety

In order to relate our LG models to Rietsch’s LG models, we first establish that the mirror spaces
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
and
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}
are isomorphic. Our strategy will follow the outline used for the proof of
[
SW23
, Theorem 3.1]
, although we will need to make several adjustments to generalize the statement to all cominuscule types simultaneously without relying on type-specific computations.

We will construct the isomorphism via the composition

X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}=\mathcal{R}^{\vee}_{w_{P},w_{0}}\xrightarrow{\varphi}U_{-}^{P}\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=\widetilde{P}^{\vee}_{k}\backslash\widetilde{G}^{\vee}\supset X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}},

where
\pi
is the quotient map given by
u_{-}\mapsto\widetilde{P}^{\vee}_{k}u_{-}
and where
\varphi:X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\rightarrow U_{-}^{P}
is the isomorphism obtained via restricting the composition of isomorphisms
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\times T^{P}\xrightarrow{\Psi}\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}\xrightarrow{\sim}U_{-}^{P}\times T^{P}
to the first factor via
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\cong X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\times\{\mathrm{id}\}
. See
[
Spa21
, Remark 3.1]
for a discussion of the isomorphism
\Psi
with our current conventions or
[
Rie08
, Section 4]
for the original definition of
\Psi
; the isomorphism
\mathcal{Z}^{\vee}_{P}\xrightarrow{\sim}U_{-}^{P}\times T^{P}
is discussed in Lemma
2.2
.

Since
\varphi
is an isomorphism, it suffices to show that
\pi
is an isomorphism
U_{-}^{P}\to X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
to allow us to conclude
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\cong X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
. Proposition 8.5 of
[
GLS11
]
implies that
U_{-}^{P}
is affine while we know from the fact that
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}=\mathbb{X}^{\vee}\setminus D_{\mathrm{ac}}
is the complement in
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
of an anticanonical (hence ample, since
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
is Fano) divisor that
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
is also affine. Thus, it suffices to prove at the level of coordinate rings that the induced map
\pi^{*}:\mathbb{C}[X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[U_{-}^{P}]
is an isomorphism.

To see that
\pi^{*}
is injective, we observe that the dimensions of
U_{-}^{P}
and
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
are both equal to the dimension of
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
as well as the fact that
\pi
is an open map since it is the quotient by the action of
\widetilde{P}^{\vee}
. Hence,
\pi(U_{-}^{P})\cap X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
is an open, dense subset of
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
so that
\pi:U_{-}^{P}\dashrightarrow X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
is dominant and hence
\pi^{*}
is injective.

On the other hand, to see that
\pi^{*}
is surjective, we first recall Proposition
2.23
, which gives a presentation of the coordinate ring of
U_{-}^{P}
as

\mathbb{C}[U_{-}^{P}]=\mathbb{C}\bigl[p_{\mathsf{w}}~\big|~\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}\bigr]\bigl[\phi_{j}^{-1}~\big|~j\in[n]\bigr]

where we recall that
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
is the order ideal corresponding to
w^{\prime\prime}\in W^{P}
the minimal coset representative of
w_{P}s_{k}W_{P}
.

Each generator of this coordinate ring is a Plücker coordinate
p_{\mathsf{w}}
which is a priori also a well-defined function on
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
. Furthermore, we proved in Theorem
4.24
that each of the generalized minors
\phi_{j}
is equal to the polynomial in Plücker coordinates
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}
on
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
. Furthermore, the zero set
D_{j}=\{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}=0\}
is contained in
D_{\mathrm{ac}}
which was removed from
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
to obtain
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
. Thus, each
\phi_{j}
is a well-defined function on
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
which is nonzero everywhere on
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
and hence invertible. Therefore
\pi^{*}
is surjective, so we conclude that
\pi^{*}
and hence
\pi
is an isomorphism. Hence:

Theorem 6.5
.

The spaces
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}
and
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
are isomorphic via the composition

X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}\xrightarrow{\varphi}U_{-}^{P}\xrightarrow{\pi}X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}.

This isomorphism justifies many of the computations we have performed up to this point, especially the restrictions of various functions to the torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
.

Remark 6.6
.

Since the quotient map
\pi:U_{-}^{P}\rightarrow X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
is an isomorphism, the dense torus
U^{\circ}_{-}\subset U_{-}^{P}
maps to an isomorphic dense torus
P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash U^{\circ}_{-}\subset X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}
which can thus be endowed with the same toric coordinates
\{a_{\mathsf{b}}\mid\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}\}
as
U^{\circ}_{-}
. This allows for the simultaneous interpretations of the toric expressions obtained in Theorems
3.10
and
5.16
on both the tori
U^{\circ}_{-}
and
P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash U^{\circ}_{-}
.

6.3.
The canonical superpotential

We finally have all the results necessary to prove our main Theorem
1.1
.

Proof of Thm.
1.1
.

In light of Theorem
6.5
and Remark
6.6
, parts (i), (ii), (iii), and (iv) of Theorem
1.1
immediately follow from equations
3.2
,
3.1
, and Theorem
4.24
; Remark
1.3
; Theorem
5.16
; and Proposition
6.4
respectively. Furthermore, using these tools, we will now establish part (v) as well.

We verified in Theorem
6.5
that
X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}}\cong X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{Lie}}
, so it remains to check that the superpotentials
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
and
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}}
agree under this isomorphism, i.e. that for any value of the formal quantum parameter
q
, the two potentials agree. As with many computations we have performed, we will check this statement by restricting the pullbacks
\varphi^{*}(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}})
and
\pi^{*}(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}})
of both superpotentials to the torus
U^{\circ}_{-}
, and thus comparing the restriction of our potential
\pi^{*}(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}
to the restriction

\varphi^{*}(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}})|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\textstyle\sum_{i\in[n]}\displaystyle\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}:\,\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=i}\displaystyle a_{\mathsf{b}}\Bigr)+q\frac{\sum_{\iota:\mathsf{w}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{w}^{P}}a_{\iota(\mathsf{w}^{\prime})}}{a_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}}

determined in equation (
2.11
).

First, for
\mathcal{W}_{0}
we have

\delta_{k}(\mathcal{D}_{0})=\delta_{k}(p_{\varnothing})=p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathcal{W}_{0}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\frac{p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}}{p_{\varnothing}}\bigg|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\sum_{\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=k}a_{\mathsf{b}},

where the sum is over all elements
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}
with index
k
. Next, for any
{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}
, we obtain from Theorems
4.24
and
5.16
the equality

\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\frac{\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}})}{\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}}\bigg|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\sum_{\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=i_{1}}a_{\mathsf{b}},

where the sum is over all elements
\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}
with index
i_{1}
. Since we never have
i_{1}=k
for
{i_{*}}\neq k
, we thus have so far that

\mathcal{W}_{0}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}+\sum_{{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}}\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}|_{U^{\circ}_{-}}=\sum_{\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=k}a_{\mathsf{b}}+\sum_{{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}}\sum_{\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=i_{1}}a_{\mathsf{b}}=\sum_{i\in[n]}\sum_{\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=i}a_{\mathsf{b}},

where the final equality follows from the fact that
\sigma_{k}
is an involution on
[n]\setminus\{k\}
. Thus we obtain exactly the first term

\textstyle\sum_{i\in[n]}\displaystyle\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{\mathsf{b}\in\mathsf{w}^{P}:\mathrm{index}(\mathsf{b})=i}\displaystyle a_{\mathsf{b}}\Bigr)

of the Lie-theoretic potential via the terms
\mathcal{W}_{0}+\sum_{{i_{*}}\in[n]\setminus\{k\}}\mathcal{W}_{{i_{*}}}
.

The remaining quantum term is exactly equal to
\mathcal{W}_{k}
for any value of the quantum parameter
q
by Proposition
6.4
. This establishes the equality between
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{Lie}}
and
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
for any choice of the quantum parameter
q
, completing the proof of the isomorphism of Landau-Ginzburg models.
∎

\enddoc@text

Appendix A
Cubic and quartic terms

While there are infinitely many minuscule homogeneous spaces
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=P^{\vee}_{k}\backslash G^{\vee}
that have
{i_{*}}\in[n]
such that
{c_{*}}\leq 2
, only two homogeneous spaces allow
{i_{*}}
with
{c_{*}}>2
. Namely, the Cayley plane
\mathbb{OP}^{2}=P^{\vee}_{6}\backslash E_{6}^{\mathrm{ad}}
has
{c_{*}}=3
for
{i_{*}}=4
, and the Freudenthal variety
P^{\vee}_{7}\backslash E_{7}^{\mathrm{ad}}
has
{c_{*}}=3
for
{i_{*}}\in\{3,5\}
and
{c_{*}}=4
for
{i_{*}}=4
. In these four cases, Corollary
3.12
tells us that the toric expression of
\phi_{{i_{*}}}
on
U^{\circ}_{-}
is a single term contained in a cubic resp. quartic Plücker monomial. While the same techniques as used in Sections
4
and
5
apply to the cancellations of the corresponding Plücker polynomials
\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}
, the fact that the posets
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
consists of triples resp. quadruples of order ideals makes the arguments and notation quite a bit more technical. Since there are only four such cases, we will instead deal with them explicitly by giving the corresponding posets
\mathsf{P}_{i_{*}}
and Plücker polynomials
\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}
and
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}})
. We will then argue in Appendix
B
that the resulting potentials agree with the potentials in
[
SW23
]
, confirming that these are LG models isomorphic to the Lie-theoretic model of
[
Rie08
]
.

The Cayley plane

{i_{*}}=4
in type
E_{6}
with
k=6
, we find the sequence
(i_{j})=(4,5,3)
as calculated in the proof of Lemma
3.5
. Hence, we find

In fact, here we see two elements
(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{3})\in\mathsf{P}_{3}
on which the derivation
\delta_{5}
acts nontrivially on two of the order ideals instead of just one, namely the third and fourth elements from the top moving right.
This means that the derivation applied to the corresponding Plücker monomials yields two terms each; however, one pair of these terms cancels out, so we only indicated the pair which does not cancel.

Appendix B
Relation to previous type-dependent LG models

We claimed that our models naturally generalize the previous models given in
[
MR20
,
PR18
,
PRW16
,
PR13
,
SW23
,
SW24
]
and we now describe how to recover each of these type-dependent models from our formalism, using the Dynkin diagram combinatorics as calculated in the proof of Lemma
3.5
; for representative examples of the minuscule posets
\mathsf{w}^{P}
, see Example
2.18
.

Grassmannians

In
[
MR20
]
, an LG model is defined for
\mathrm{Gr}(n-k,n)=\mathrm{SL}_{n}/P_{n-k}=A_{n}^{\mathrm{sc}}/P_{n-k}
using the standard Plücker embedding of
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
into
\mathbb{P}\bigl(\bigwedge^{k}(\mathbb{C}^{n})^{*}\bigr)
with the resulting Plücker coordinates labeled by Young diagrams inside the
(n-k)\times k
-rectangle; it is straightforward to see that this labeling agrees with our labeling by order ideals after forgetting the simple reflection labels. The LG model in
[
MR20
]
is defined using the Young diagrams
\mu_{i}
and
\hat{\mu}_{i}
, defined as follows:

\mu_{i}=\begin{cases}\text{the first $i$ rows,}&\text{for $i\in\{1,\ldots,n-k\}$,}\\
\text{the first $n-i$ columns,}&\text{for $i\in\{n-k,\ldots,n\}$.}\end{cases}

(Note that
\mu_{n}=\varnothing
and that both descriptions yield the full
(n-k)\times k
-rectangle for
\mu_{n-k}
.) On the other hand,
\hat{\mu}_{i}
is the unique diagram that can be obtained by adding a box to
\mu_{i}
for
i\neq n-k
, and
\hat{\mu}_{n-k}
is the
(n-k-1)\times(k-1)
-subrectangle. With this, the superpotential is defined as

\mathcal{W}_{\text{MR}}=\sum_{i\neq n-k}\frac{p_{\hat{\mu}_{i}}}{p_{\mu_{i}}}+q\frac{p_{\hat{\mu}_{n-k}}}{p_{\mu_{n-k}}}.

In our formalism, we find that
\mathsf{w}^{P}
is the
(n-k)\times k
-rectangle with the bottom-left element labeled
s_{1}
, the top-left element labeled
s_{n-k}
and the top-right element labeled
s_{n}
(labels increasing over diagonals from left to right). In the proof of Lemma
3.5
, we see that Grassmannians always have
{c_{*}}=1
for any
{i_{*}}\in[n]
. (Note that we considered
\mathrm{Gr}(k,n)
instead of
\mathrm{Gr}(n-k,n)
.) Moreover, we have that
i_{1}=n-k-{i_{*}}
for
{i_{*}}\in\{1,\ldots,n-k-1\}
and
i_{1}=n-({i_{*}}-n+k)=2n-k-{i_{*}}
for
{i_{*}}\in\{n-k+1,\ldots,n\}
, so we find that
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}
consists of of the first
i_{1}
rows in the first case and the first
i_{1}
columns in the second case. Hence we find
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}=\mu_{i_{1}}
for all
{i_{*}}\neq n-k
(forgetting the simple reflection labeling), and therefore we conclude
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}})=\hat{\mu}_{i_{1}}
as well. For
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}
, we note that
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}
is the union of the first column and first row—being the maximal order ideal containing exactly one occurrence of an element labeled
s_{n-k}
—so its complement
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}
is the
(n-k-1)\times(k-1)
-rectangle, i.e.
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}=\hat{\mu}_{n-k}
. Together with
\mathsf{w}^{P}=\mu_{n-k}
, we conclude that the potential
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}
is identically equal to
\mathcal{W}_{\text{MR}}
.

Quadrics

In
[
PRW16
]
, LG models for odd and even quadrics are given using the (generalized) Plücker embeddings of
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
. The models for odd and even quadrics are fairly similar, but since
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}
is isomorphic to a projective plane for odd quadrics whereas for even quadrics it is isomorphic to another even quadric, the labeling of Plücker coordinates in each case is slightly different.

For the odd quadric
Q_{2m-1}=\mathrm{SO}_{2m+1}/P_{1}=B_{m}^{\mathrm{sc}}/P_{1}
, the coordinates on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=\mathbb{CP}^{2m-1}=P^{\vee}_{1}\backslash C_{m}^{\mathrm{ad}}
are labeled
p_{i}
for
i\in\{0,\ldots,2m-1\}
, and it is straightforward to see that
p_{i}
coincides with the Plücker coordinate
p_{[i]}
labeled by the order ideal
[i]
consisting of
i
elements, where the minuscule poset
\mathsf{w}^{P}=[2m-1]
is the row of
2m-1
boxes labeled
s_{1},\ldots,s_{m-1},s_{m},s_{m-1},\ldots,s_{1}
. The potential is given there as

\mathcal{W}_{\text{PRW},\text{odd}}=\frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac{p_{j+1}p_{2m-1-j}}{\mathcal{D}_{\text{PRW},j}}+q\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2m-1}},\quad\text{where}\quad\mathcal{D}_{\text{PRW},j}=\sum_{i=0}^{j}(-1)^{i}p_{j-i}p_{2m-1-j+i}.

In our formalism, we see that
{c_{*}}=2
except for the minuscule vertex
{i_{*}}=1
; hence all terms are ratios of quadratic homogeneous polynomials in the Plücker coordinate, except for the quantum term and the term
p_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}/p_{\varnothing}=p_{1}/p_{0}
. Since
\mathsf{w}^{\prime\prime}
is the maximal order ideal containing a single occurrence of the label
s_{1}
, we see that it has a single box as complement, so that the quantum terms agree as well:
qp_{\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}/p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}=qp_{1}/p_{2m-1}
.

For the remaining terms (
{i_{*}}\in\{2,\ldots,m\}
), we start by noting that
i_{1}={i_{*}}
and
i_{2}={i_{*}}-1
. Hence, we find that
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}=[{i_{*}}-1]
while
\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}=[2m-1-({i_{*}}-1)]=[2m-{i_{*}}]
. Inspecting the labels, we see that from
(\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}},\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}})=([{i_{*}}-1],[2m-{i_{*}}])
we can move a single element at a time until we reach
(\varnothing,\mathsf{w}^{P})=([0],[2m-1])
; hence, we see

\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}=\sum_{j=0}^{{i_{*}}-1}(-1)^{j}p_{[{i_{*}}-1-j]}p_{[2m-{i_{*}}+j]}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{PRW},{i_{*}}-1}.

Next, it is clear that
\delta_{i_{1}}([j])=0
for all
j\notin\{{i_{*}}-1,2m-{i_{*}}-1\}
, the only nonzero action of
\delta_{i_{1}}
on
\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}
is on the first factor of the first term, i.e.

\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}})=\delta_{i_{1}}(p_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}})p_{\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}}=p_{[{i_{*}}]}p_{[2m-{i_{*}}]},

and hence we find that
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}=\mathcal{W}_{\text{PRW},\text{odd}}
for odd quadrics.

For the even quadric
Q_{2m-2}=\mathrm{Spin}_{2m}/P_{1}=D_{m}^{\mathrm{sc}}/P_{1}
, the Plücker coordinates
(p_{0}:\ldots:p_{m-1}:p_{m-1}^{\prime}:p_{m}:\ldots:p_{2m-2})
on
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=P^{\vee}_{1}\backslash\mathrm{PSO}_{2m}=P^{\vee}_{1}\backslash D_{m}^{\mathrm{ad}}
are defined using the same method, so we only need to identify the minimal coset representatives as defined in
[
PRW16
, Section 3.1]
with the corresponding order ideals. Recalling Example
2.18
,
\mathsf{w}^{P}
consist of
2m-2
elements: it starts with a chain of
m-2
elements labeled
s_{1},\ldots,s_{m-2}
; the last element is covered by two elements labeled
s_{m-1}
and
s_{m}
respectively; both of these are covered by an element labeled
s_{m-2}
followed by a chain of
m-3
elements labeled
s_{m-3},\ldots,s_{1}
. With this in mind, define for
i\in\{0,\ldots,m-2\}
the order ideal
[i]
as the chain of the first
i
elements, define
[m-1]
to be the chain
s_{1}<\ldots<s_{m-2}<s_{m-1}
and
[m-1]^{\prime}
as the chain
s_{1}<\ldots<s_{m-2}<s_{m}
, while we define
[m]=[m-1]\cup[m-1]^{\prime}
, and finally for
i\in\{m+1,\ldots,2m-2\}
we define
[i]
to be the order ideal
s_{1}<\ldots<s_{m-2}<s_{m-1},s_{m}<s_{m-1}<\ldots<s_{2m-1-i}
consisting of
i
elements. This convention will let
p_{i}=p_{[i]}
as well as
p_{m-1}^{\prime}=p_{[m-1]^{\prime}}
.

Now, comparing the potentials, the one in
[
PRW16
]
is given as

\mathcal{W}_{\text{PRW},\text{even}}=\frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\frac{p_{m}}{p_{m-1}}+\frac{p_{m}}{p_{m-1}^{\prime}}+\sum_{j=1}^{m-3}\frac{p_{j+1}p_{2m-2-j}}{\mathcal{D}_{\text{PRW},j}}+q\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2m-2}},

where
\mathcal{D}_{\text{PRW},j}=\sum_{i=0}^{j}(-1)^{i}p_{j-i}p_{2m-2-j+i}
is the (
2m-2
)-dimensional analogue. In our formalism, we find
{c_{*}}=1
for
{i_{*}}\in\{1,m-1,m\}
and
{c_{*}}=2
otherwise. We directly see
p_{[1]}/p_{[0]}=p_{1}/p_{0}
and the quantum term is analogous to the case of the odd quadric. Recalling the proof of Lemma
3.5
, we see that
{i_{*}}\in\{m-1,m\}
gives
i_{1}\in\{m-1,m\}
(depending on
m-1
even resp. odd) so we find that
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}
is either
[m-1]
or
[m-1]^{\prime}
, both of which have
\delta_{i_{1}}([m-1])=\delta_{i_{1}}([m-1]^{\prime})=[m]
(note that
i_{1}
depends on
{i_{*}}
, so the equality contains two distinct actions of
\delta_{i_{1}}
). Hence, we conclude
\mathcal{W}_{m-1}+\mathcal{W}_{m}=p_{[m]}/p_{[m-1]}+p_{[m]}/p_{[m-1]^{\prime}}=p_{m}/p_{m-1}+p_{m}/p_{m-1}^{\prime}
.

For
{i_{*}}\notin\{1,m-1,m\}
, we find
i_{1}={i_{*}}
and
i_{2}={i_{*}}-1
, so that
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}=[{i_{*}}-1]
and
\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}=[2m-2-({i_{*}}-1)]=[2m-{i_{*}}-1]
. Concluding that
\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{PRW},{i_{*}}-1}
and
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}})=p_{[{i_{*}}]}p_{[2m-{i_{*}}-1]}
is entirely analogous to the case of the odd quadric. With this, we arrive at
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}=\mathcal{W}_{\text{PRW},\text{even}}
for even quadrics as well.

Lagrangian Grassmannians

The models presented in
[
PR13
]
for the Lagrangian Grassmannians
\mathrm{LG}(m,2m)=\mathrm{Sp}_{2m}/P_{m}=C_{m}^{\mathrm{sc}}/P_{m}
use the same embedding of
\mathbb{X}^{\vee}=P^{\vee}_{m}\backslash\mathrm{PSO}_{2m+1}=P^{\vee}_{m}\backslash B_{m}^{\mathrm{ad}}
in
\mathbb{P}\bigl(V({\varpi^{\vee}_{m}})^{*}\bigr)
as is used for the models
(X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}})
. (Note that the adjoint and simply-connected groups are reversed compared to that reference.) Hence, it suffices to identify the labelings of the corresponding Plücker coordinates and show that the superpotentials agree.

In
[
PR13
]
, the Plücker coordinates
p_{\lambda}
are labeled by strict partitions
(\lambda)=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{j})
with
1\leq\lambda_{i+1}<\lambda_{i}\leq m
; here the empty partition corresponds to the lowest weight vector and the maximal partition
(m,m-1,\ldots,1)
corresponds to the highest weight vector. On the other hand, in the order ideal formalism,
\mathsf{w}^{P}
is the “decreasing staircase” consisting of
m
columns with
m,m-1,\ldots,1
elements respectively, aligned along the bottom elements; the elements are labeled
1
to
m
along diagonals starting from the bottom-left element to the main diagonal. (Cf. Example
2.18
.) For comparison, we will denote by
[\lambda]=[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{j}]
the order ideal consisting of
j
columns with sizes
\lambda_{i}
satisfying
1\leq\lambda_{i+1}<\lambda_{i}\leq m
(ignoring empty columns). Thus we identify the Plücker coordinate
p_{(\lambda)}
of
[
PR13
]
with our Plücker coordinate
p_{[\lambda]}
. The reason for this translation between Young diagrams is because we view our order ideals as arising from the corresponding minuscule poset which we orient to place the smallest element in the upper left and the largest element in the lower right.

The potential in
[
PR13
]
is defined using a set of specific partitions (note that the notation used here slightly deviates from the source): First, they define
(\rho_{l})=(l,l-1,\ldots,1)
as the length
l
staircase partition, and take
(\rho_{l}^{+})=(l+1,l-1,l-2,\ldots,1)
to be the unique strict partition obtained from
(\rho_{l})
for
l<m
by adding a single box. Next, for
J\subset[l]
, they define
(\rho_{l})^{J}
and
(\rho_{l}^{+})^{J}
to be the partitions obtained by deleting the parts
(\rho_{l})_{j}
from
(\rho_{l})
and
(\rho_{l}^{+})_{j}
from
(\rho_{l}^{+})
for each
j\in J
. Next, they define the partition
(\mu_{l})=(m,m-1,\ldots,m+1-l)
to be the maximal partition with
l
parts, and set
(\mu_{l}^{J})=(m,m-1,\ldots,m+1-l,l+1-j_{1},\ldots,l+1-j_{i})
and
(\mu_{l}^{J})^{+}=(m,m-1,\ldots,m+1-l,l+1-j_{1}+\delta_{j_{1},1},\ldots,l+1-j_{i})
, where
J=\{j_{1}<\ldots<j_{i}\}
and
\delta_{j_{1},1}=1
for
j_{1}=1
and
0
otherwise. Whenever these constructions do
not
result in a strict partition
(\mu)
, they set
p_{(\mu)}=0
for notational ease. With this, they define

\mathcal{W}_{\text{PR}}=\frac{p_{(\rho_{0}^{+})}}{p_{(\rho_{0})}}+\sum_{l=1}^{m-1}\frac{\mathcal{D}_{\text{PR},l}^{+}}{\mathcal{D}_{\text{PR},l}}+q\frac{p_{(\rho_{m-1})}}{p_{(\rho_{m})}},\quad\text{where}\quad\mathcal{D}_{\text{PR},l}=\sum_{J\subset[l]}(-1)^{s(J)}p_{(\rho_{l})^{J}p_{(\mu_{l}^{J})}}

with
s(J)=\sum_{j\in J}j
and with
\mathcal{D}_{\text{PR},l}^{+}
obtained from
\mathcal{D}_{\text{PR},l}
by replacing
(\rho_{l})^{J}
by
(\rho_{l}^{+})^{J}
and
(\mu_{l}^{J})
by
(\mu_{l}^{J})^{+}
.

Returning to the order ideal formalism, we directly see that
(\rho_{0})=\varnothing
and
(\rho_{1})=\hskip 0.0pt{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt\hbox to2.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=1.92pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.47998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt
, so we find that the first term agrees with the potential presented here. Moreoever,
\mathsf{w}^{\prime}
is the complement of a single column, i.e. the staircase of length
m-1
, so that
qp_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}/p_{\mathsf{w}^{P}}=qp_{(\rho_{m-1})}/p_{(\rho_{m})}
for the quantum term as well.

For the remaining terms (
{i_{*}}\neq m
), we find from the proof of Lemma
3.5
that
{c_{*}}=2
, and that
i_{1}=m-{i_{*}}
and
i_{2}=m
. Hence, we find that
\mathsf{w}_{i_{1}}=[\rho_{{i_{*}}}]
(the staircase order ideal of length
{i_{*}}
) and
\mathsf{w}_{i_{2}}=[\mu_{{i_{*}}}]
(the order ideal consisting of the first
{i_{*}}
columns of
\mathsf{w}^{P}
). This immediately tells us that the initial term of
\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}
agrees with the
J=\varnothing
term of
\mathcal{D}_{\text{PR},{i_{*}}}
; for the remaining terms, we note that written as Young diagrams, the pair of partitions
\bigl((\rho_{l})^{J},(\mu_{l})^{J}\bigr)
can be thought of as
moving

s(J)
boxes in the rows indexed by
J
from
(\rho_{l})
to
(\mu_{l})
whenever such a move is valid, so it follows that the identification
(\lambda)\mapsto[\lambda]
maps the set
\{(\rho_{{i_{*}}})^{J},(\mu_{{i_{*}}}^{J})~|~J\subset[{i_{*}}]\}
to
\mathsf{P}_{{i_{*}}}
, and hence we find
\mathcal{D}_{{i_{*}}}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{PR},{i_{*}}}
for
{i_{*}}\in[m-1]
. For the numerators, we note that
(\rho_{i_{*}}^{+})
is obtained by adding a single box, and that this box in
[\rho_{i_{*}}^{+}]
has label
m-{i_{*}}=i_{1}
, so that
\delta_{i_{1}}([\rho_{i_{*}}])=[\rho_{i_{*}}^{+}]
and we conclude that the initial terms of
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}})
and
\mathcal{D}_{\text{PR},{i_{*}}}
agree; for the remaining terms, we find an analogous interpretation of moving boxes for the numerators as for the denominators, and we conclude that the potentials
\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}}=\mathcal{W}_{\text{PR}}
agree.

Orthogonal Grassmannians

The models presented in
[
SW24
]
were obtained by applying the model
(X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}})
presented here to the specific case of
\mathrm{OG}(n,2n)=\mathrm{Spin}_{2n}/P_{n}=D_{n}^{\mathrm{sc}}/P_{n}
, and hence require no further verifications.

The exceptional family

The models presented in
[
SW23
]
formed the direct inspiration for the models
(X^{\vee}_{\mathrm{can}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{can}})
presented here, so relating the two formalisms is straightforward. Firstly, comparing Definition
2.17
here with Definition 2.12 of
[
SW23
]
, we see that the latter is a special case of the former. Hence, we only need to translate the labeling used in both papers, but this is straightforward as well: given an order ideal
\mathsf{w}\vartriangleleft\mathsf{w}^{P}
, consider the corresponding minimal coset representative
\Pi(\mathsf{w})\in W^{P}
(as defined in Remark
2.15
) and follow the action of its simple reflections through the Hasse diagrams as given in equations (2.25) and (2.27) of
[
SW23
, Section 2.4]
to find the corresponding weight vector
v_{i}^{(j)}
; then
p_{\mathsf{w}}=p_{i}^{(j)}
. Establishing that the models agree thus reduces to showing that the potentials are equal.

For the Cayley plane
\mathbb{OP}^{2}=E_{6}^{\mathrm{sc}}/P_{6}
, we have written out the values of
{c_{*}}
and the sequences
(i_{j})
in equation (
3.13
) of the proof of Lemma
3.5
. Hence, we find the following order ideals
\mathsf{w}_{i_{j}}

The posets
\mathsf{P}_{i_{*}}
are now obtained by moving boxes; instead of showing the posets, we directly translate the resulting
\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}}
and
\delta_{i_{1}}(\mathcal{D}_{i_{*}})
into the
p_{i}^{(j)}
notation as used in
[
SW23
]
:

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{0}

\displaystyle=\frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}},\qquad\mathcal{W}_{1}=\frac{p_{9}^{\prime}}{p_{8}},\qquad\mathcal{W}_{6}=q\frac{p_{5}^{\prime\prime}}{p_{16}},\qquad\mathcal{W}_{2}=\frac{p_{2}p_{11}^{\prime\prime}-p_{0}p_{13}}{p_{1}p_{11}^{\prime\prime}-p_{0}p_{12}},

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{3}

\displaystyle=\frac{p_{5}^{\prime}p_{12}^{\prime}-p_{4}^{\prime\prime}p_{13}+p_{2}p_{15}}{p_{4}^{\prime}p_{12}^{\prime}-p_{3}p_{13}+p_{2}p_{14}-p_{1}p_{15}+p_{0}p_{16}},\qquad\mathcal{W}_{5}=\frac{p_{6}^{\prime\prime}p_{15}-p_{5}^{\prime}p_{16}}{p_{5}p_{15}-p_{4}p_{16}},

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{4}

\displaystyle=\frac{p_{3}(p_{8}^{\prime\prime}p_{14}-p_{7}^{\prime\prime}p_{15}+p_{6}^{\prime}p_{16})+p_{1}(-p_{10}^{\prime\prime}p_{14})+p_{0}(p_{11}^{\prime}p_{14})}{p_{2}(p_{8}^{\prime\prime}p_{14}-p_{7}^{\prime\prime}p_{15}+p_{6}^{\prime}p_{16})+p_{1}(-p_{9}^{\prime\prime}p_{14}+p_{8}^{\prime}p_{15}-p_{7}^{\prime}p_{16})+p_{0}(p_{10}^{\prime}p_{14}-p_{9}^{\prime}p_{15}+p_{8}p_{16})}.

Comparing these expressions with the potential as given in equations (3.1), (3.2) and (3.3) in
[
SW23
, Section 3.1]
, we find that the above expressions for
\mathcal{W}_{i_{*}}
already agree for
{i_{*}}\in\{0,1,2,5,6\}
. For the remaining terms, we require a number of Plücker relations as given in Remark 3.14 of
[
SW23
]
, but the simplification is straightforward.

The story for the Freudenthal variety
E_{7}^{\mathrm{sc}}/P_{7}
is analogous, but somewhat more elaborate. For the order ideals
\mathsf{w}_{i_{j}}
we find the following using equation (
3.14
) from the proof of Lemma
3.5

Hence, we obtain the following terms of the potential, written in the
p_{i}^{(j)}
notation of
[
SW23
]
:

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{1}

\displaystyle=\frac{p_{2}p_{17}-p_{0}p_{19}^{\prime}}{p_{1}p_{17}-p_{0}p_{18}},\qquad\mathcal{W}_{6}=\frac{p_{11}p_{26}-p_{10}^{\prime}p_{27}}{p_{10}p_{26}-p_{9}p_{27}},\qquad\mathcal{W}_{7}=q\frac{p_{10}}{p_{17}},

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{p_{7}^{\prime\prime}p_{21}^{\prime\prime}-p_{6}^{\prime\prime}p_{22}^{\prime\prime}+p_{5}^{\prime}p_{23}}{p_{6}^{\prime\prime}p_{21}^{\prime\prime}-p_{5}^{\prime\prime}p_{22}^{\prime\prime}+p_{4}p_{23}-p_{3}p_{24}+p_{2}p_{25}-p_{1}p_{26}+p_{0}p_{27}},

and the remaining terms can be obtained from Appendix
A
:

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{3}

\displaystyle=\textstyle\frac{p_{3}(p_{12}^{\prime\prime}p_{22}^{\prime}-p_{11}^{\prime\prime}p_{23}+p_{10}^{\prime\prime}p_{24}-p_{9}^{\prime\prime}p_{25})-p_{1}(p_{14}p_{22}^{\prime}-p_{13}^{\prime}p_{23}+p_{11}^{\prime}p_{25}-p_{10}^{\prime\prime}p_{26})+p_{0}(p_{15}^{\prime}p_{22}^{\prime}-p_{14}^{\prime\prime}p_{23}+p_{12}p_{25}-p_{10}^{\prime\prime}p_{27})}{p_{2}(p_{12}^{\prime\prime}p_{22}^{\prime}-p_{11}^{\prime\prime}p_{23}+p_{10}^{\prime\prime}p_{24}-p_{9}^{\prime\prime}p_{25})-p_{1}(p_{13}^{\prime\prime}p_{22}^{\prime}-p_{12}^{\prime}p_{23}+p_{11}^{\prime}p_{24}-p_{9}^{\prime\prime}p_{26})+p_{0}(p_{14}^{\prime}p_{22}^{\prime}-p_{13}p_{23}+p_{12}p_{24}-p_{9}^{\prime\prime}p_{27})},

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{5}

\displaystyle=\textstyle\frac{(p_{6}^{\prime}p_{15}^{\prime\prime}-p_{5}^{\prime\prime}p_{16}^{\prime\prime}+p_{3}p_{18}^{\prime}-p_{2}p_{19}^{\prime\prime})p_{25}+(-p_{6}^{\prime}p_{14}^{\prime\prime}+p_{5}^{\prime\prime}p_{15}^{\prime}-p_{3}p_{17}^{\prime}+p_{1}p_{19}^{\prime\prime})p_{26}+(p_{6}^{\prime}p_{13}^{\prime}-p_{5}^{\prime\prime}p_{14}+p_{3}p_{16}-p_{0}p_{19}^{\prime\prime})p_{27}}{(p_{5}^{\prime}p_{15}^{\prime\prime}-p_{4}p_{16}^{\prime\prime}+p_{3}p_{17}^{\prime\prime}-p_{2}p_{18}^{\prime\prime})p_{25}-(p_{5}^{\prime}p_{14}^{\prime\prime}-p_{4}p_{15}^{\prime}+p_{3}p_{16}^{\prime}-p_{1}p_{18}^{\prime\prime})p_{26}+(p_{5}^{\prime}p_{13}^{\prime}-p_{4}p_{14}+p_{3}p_{15}-p_{0}p_{18}^{\prime\prime})p_{27}}.

We suppress the translated expression for
\mathcal{W}_{4}
due to its length. Comparing these expressions with the potential as given in equation (3.4), (3.5) and (3.6) in
[
SW23
, Section 3.2]
, we see that the
\mathcal{W}_{i_{*}}
already agree for
{i_{*}}\in\{1,2,3,6,7\}
(up to adding minus signs in the numerator a denominator of
{i_{*}}=2
and reorganizing the terms for
{i_{*}}=3
). The remaining terms agree after simplifying using the Plücker relations as given in Remark 3.18 of
[
SW23
]
.
